mechanics.name: Conveyor routing
mechanics.summary: Route materials around obstacles and across junctions to keep machines supplied.
mechanics.rules: Players connect producers to consumers with directional belts. Space, crossing options and capacity constrain routes; starvation and queues expose weak links.
decisions: A short route saves space but may block expansion.
Dedicated lines are readable; mixed lines save construction but complicate control.

parameters.name: Crossing freedom
parameters.effect: More bridges or tunnels shift difficulty from avoiding obstacles to managing throughput.

parameters.name: Belt capacity
parameters.effect: Lower capacity encourages parallel routes; higher capacity supports central trunks.

cases.implementation: Two-lane belts occupy a 2D ground plane; underground belts let routes cross.
Three-dimensional belts, supports and lifts allow vertically separated logistics.

mechanics.contrast: Factorio emphasizes planar space and two lanes; Satisfactory adds height as routing space.
mechanics.combination: Design a floating-island factory where puzzles unlock transport bridges after players solve compact routing layouts.

walkthrough.setup: The mine is left of the furnace, with a busy conveyor crossing the direct route.
walkthrough.action: Route a one-way belt around the crossing and check every segment’s direction.
walkthrough.result: Ore reaches the furnace; a reversed segment causes a visible queue upstream.
walkthrough.next: Observe sustained delivery, then reserve a connection for the next machine.

prototype.firstStep: Use a small grid, one source, one sink and directional belt tiles; dots can represent items.
prototype.pitfall: Verify direction and blockage before adding layered transport or complex crossings, which complicate diagnosis.
prototype.test: Give players one reversed segment and see whether they diagnose it from the queue.

mechanics.name: Flow splitting and ratios
mechanics.summary: Divide limited input among machines without starving one branch.
mechanics.rules: Players split one input among consumers with different consumption rates. Blocked exits change actual distribution; sustained operation matters more than machine count.
decisions: Equal distribution is simple but mismatched demand can waste supply.
A manifold is compact but needs its upstream buffers to fill.

parameters.name: Demand imbalance
parameters.effect: Larger differences make equal splits insufficient and reward priorities or staged division.

parameters.name: Buffer size
parameters.effect: Larger buffers smooth interruptions but delay steady-state behavior.

cases.implementation: Splitters divide items between two outputs and support input and output priorities.
A standard splitter has three outputs; chained splitters can feed a row of machines.

mechanics.contrast: Two outputs with priority help allocate contested supply; three outputs make three-way layouts straightforward.
mechanics.combination: Build an automated kitchen that divides ingredients between a canteen and premium orders with different late penalties.

walkthrough.setup: A belt supplies six ore per round; two machines need two and four respectively.
walkthrough.action: Adjust the split toward one-to-two instead of dividing evenly.
walkthrough.result: Both machines run continuously, reducing both upstream queues and downstream starvation.
walkthrough.next: Recalculate demand and branches when adding another machine.

prototype.firstStep: Use one fixed source, two consumers with different rates and an adjustable splitter, displaying uptime.
prototype.pitfall: Do not start with dozens of recipes; two different demands can reveal whether allocation matters.
prototype.test: When one machine queues and another stalls, do players change allocation rather than simply add input?

mechanics.name: Item-filtered transport
mechanics.summary: Assign routing rules so mixed items reach the correct destinations.
mechanics.rules: Players define item rules and separate mixed input into dedicated routes. Unmatched items need an exit or can jam the line; correct sorting and overflow reveal rule quality.
decisions: Strict allowlists are predictable but need updating for new products.
A reject route costs space but prevents one stray item stopping the line.

parameters.name: Item variety
parameters.effect: More item types increase rule-management demands.

parameters.name: Misrouting consequence
parameters.effect: Automatic returns encourage experiments; irreversible contamination encourages testing first.

cases.implementation: A splitter can filter an item type toward a designated output.
Smart Splitters assign rules to individual outputs, including overflow behavior.

mechanics.contrast: Factorio separates a selected item across two outputs; Satisfactory combines multiple output rules with overflow.
mechanics.combination: Mix hazardous fragments into ore; players learn visual traits and build filters before contaminants damage product quality.

walkthrough.setup: A mixed belt carries ore and coal; the furnace fuel input accepts only coal.
walkthrough.action: Route coal to fuel, ore to a separate branch, and provide an outlet for unexpected items.
walkthrough.result: Correct items reach their inputs, while an unexpected item does not block the whole line.
walkthrough.next: Review filter coverage when a new item type enters the network.

prototype.firstStep: Use three item types, one filter and a default outlet, showing each item’s destination.
prototype.pitfall: Make rule priority and unmatched behaviour visible so players need not repeatedly rebuild to debug.
prototype.test: Introduce an unfamiliar item and see whether players route it without breaking the existing flow.

mechanics.name: Multi-stage production chains
mechanics.summary: Turn one process output into another input to manufacture complex products.
mechanics.rules: Players work backward from a target product, configure recipes and connect supply. Missing prerequisites stall downstream machines; a complete chain continuously produces the target.
decisions: Shared intermediates are reusable but create shared bottlenecks.
Expanding upstream early builds headroom at an immediate material cost.

parameters.name: Dependency depth
parameters.effect: Deeper chains increase planning and make failures harder to trace.

parameters.name: Intermediate reuse
parameters.effect: Higher reuse makes local expansion more likely to affect other products.

cases.implementation: Assemblers use chosen recipes while inserters supply ingredients and remove outputs; complex products consume intermediates.
Constructors process basic materials, while assemblers and other machines combine intermediates through direct belt ports.

mechanics.contrast: Factorio makes insertion a separate layer; Satisfactory uses machine ports and emphasizes layout.
mechanics.combination: Reveal only a final product and deadline, letting players choose between shared intermediates and a temporary dedicated chain.

walkthrough.setup: The goal is gears, which require plates made by smelting ore.
walkthrough.action: Work backward from gears to add smelting, ore input and intermediate transport.
walkthrough.result: The final machine produces steadily once all prerequisite stages keep supplying it.
walkthrough.next: Find the stage that stalls most and invest there next.

prototype.firstStep: Start with ore-to-plate-to-gear, one machine per stage, showing missing inputs and output per round.
prototype.pitfall: Recipes, logistics and machine rates compound debugging; hold two fixed while varying the third.
prototype.test: When the final machine starves, can players trace the dependency to the actual upstream shortage?

mechanics.name: Fluid routing
mechanics.summary: Use pipes, pumps and junctions to deliver fluids to machines.
mechanics.rules: Players connect fluid sources to consumers under distance, elevation or junction constraints. Starvation halts production and wrong connections can introduce unwanted fluids; flow readings guide revisions.
decisions: A shared network saves construction but spreads failures.
Extra pumps and separate branches improve control at a power and maintenance cost.

parameters.name: Elevation limit
parameters.effect: When elevation matters, factory siting becomes part of logistics.

parameters.name: Flow visibility
parameters.effect: Visible direction and bottlenecks turn guessing into diagnosis.

cases.implementation: Pipes form fluid networks, with pumps providing directional transfer and segmentation; version 2.0 differs from older pipe-by-pipe flow assumptions.
Pipeline pumps supply head lift, making elevation part of pump placement.

mechanics.contrast: Factorio emphasizes network segmentation and direction; Satisfactory makes elevation explicit.
mechanics.combination: Build irrigation for hillside greenhouses: valuable uphill crops require additional lift and backup tanks.

walkthrough.setup: The source is low, two machines are higher, and the current pipes cannot deliver enough water.
walkthrough.action: Add a pump at an appropriate point and separate the overloaded branch.
walkthrough.result: Liquid reaches the machines, and flow indicators reveal any remaining restriction.
walkthrough.next: Check spare supply capacity before connecting another consumer.

prototype.firstStep: Use a node-based network, stored volume and one explicit height restriction; no free-surface fluid simulation is needed.
prototype.pitfall: Physical accuracy, loops and mixed liquids create many more state problems; add them in stages.
prototype.test: Can players distinguish insufficient supply, limited throughput and an invalid height lift?

mechanics.name: Power supply balancing
mechanics.summary: Match generation, storage and load so expansion does not cripple the factory.
mechanics.rules: Players wire machines and generators, comparing demand with available supply. Peaks or fuel loss cause slowdowns or outages; spare capacity, storage and separate grids are alternatives.
decisions: Overbuilding power improves resilience but delays other investments.
Separate grids isolate faults but cannot freely share all spare capacity.

parameters.name: Demand variation
parameters.effect: Large swings make storage and startup order more important than average power.

parameters.name: Shortage behavior
parameters.effect: Slowdowns allow recovery time; total trips emphasize warnings and backups.

cases.implementation: Insufficient power slows most electric machinery; grid statistics show production, consumption and storage.
A grid can trip when demand exceeds available capacity, requiring supply-demand repair and a restart.

mechanics.contrast: Slowdown allows degraded operation; tripping makes power headroom a sharper constraint.
mechanics.combination: Have returning expedition teams charge at once, forcing a choice between overnight production and next-day exploration range.

walkthrough.setup: The grid supplies ten power units, existing machines use eight, and a new one needs four.
walkthrough.action: Switch off a nonessential machine while gathering materials for more generation.
walkthrough.result: Essential machines stabilise, but the disabled process stops producing.
walkthrough.next: Restore loads after expansion and reserve capacity for the next peak.

prototype.firstStep: Use total supply, three different loads and switches, clearly showing how overload affects equipment.
prototype.pitfall: Choose a clear outage rule; unexplained switching between total and random failures undermines planning.
prototype.test: During a shortage, can players choose a process to pause and explain the outputs they preserve?

mechanics.name: Sensor-driven control
mechanics.summary: Make machines start and stop in response to temperature, stock or other signals.
mechanics.rules: Players read sensor values, choose thresholds or logic, and connect signals to equipment. Machines change state when conditions match; oscillation, lag and false triggers guide tuning.
decisions: Close start and stop thresholds track the target closely, but will the machine toggle repeatedly near the boundary?
Control only by stock, or also require enough power? Is that extra condition worth the debugging work?

parameters.name: Signal delay
parameters.effect: More delay demands anticipation and safety margins.

parameters.name: Logic complexity
parameters.effect: Simple conditions aid learning; combined logic enables custom controllers.

cases.implementation: Circuit networks carry signals such as item counts and conditionally control inserters, pumps and other connectable entities.
Thermo Sensors send red or green signals around a chosen threshold to control equipment such as heaters.

mechanics.contrast: Factorio lends itself to production and inventory controls; ONI directly turns environmental conditions into control inputs.
mechanics.combination: Design a hatchery controller that balances temperature and power, then test it with species requiring different conditions.

walkthrough.setup: The warehouse only needs five to ten parts, but continuous production fills it completely.
walkthrough.action: Set production to start below five and stop at ten, then connect the control to the machine.
walkthrough.result: Stock is replenished automatically after use and production stops at the target.
walkthrough.next: Change consumption speed and check for repeated toggling or late replenishment.

prototype.firstStep: Use one inventory sensor, one switched machine and adjustable thresholds, displaying readings and switching reasons.
prototype.pitfall: Many gates and sensors make faults hard to locate; ensure a single chain can be traced first.
prototype.test: Can players remove rapid toggling by adjusting thresholds and explain each switching event?

mechanics.name: Autonomous aerial logistics
mechanics.summary: Delegate hauling to flying units, then plan around coverage, energy and throughput.
mechanics.rules: Players configure supply, demand and transport facilities so flying units move items. Coverage or routes, energy and handling capacity limit throughput; queues and shortages show where to expand.
decisions: Flight bypasses terrain, but distance and small frequent loads can reduce efficiency.
Central hubs are easy to manage; distributed nodes sit closer to consumers.

parameters.name: Payload
parameters.effect: Larger payloads favor bulk transport; small payloads amplify round-trip cost.

parameters.name: Energy constraint
parameters.effect: Sparse charging or fuel points can matter more than straight-line distance.

cases.implementation: Logistic robots move items according to chest supply and demand inside a logistics network and need charging.
Drones carry items between a home port and selected destination, turning terrain-crossing logistics into port routing.

mechanics.contrast: Factorio uses requests within network coverage; Satisfactory uses designated trips between ports.
mechanics.combination: Supply mountain research stations by choosing expensive roads or drone ports constrained by weather windows.

walkthrough.setup: Two workshops need parts; the only drone keeps making long trips while the nearby workshop runs dry.
walkthrough.action: Add a buffer stock and adjust requests so the drone delivers useful batches.
walkthrough.result: Tiny repeated trips decrease, though the added node still needs energy and upkeep.
walkthrough.next: Inspect queues and shortages before adding capacity or moving nodes.

prototype.firstStep: Use map nodes, fixed travel times and one drone with a charge state; omit free-flight pathfinding initially.
prototype.pitfall: Large autonomous fleets, collisions and dynamic routes can create performance problems; test dispatch rules first.
prototype.test: With near and far requests active, can players reduce shortages by changing buffers or routes?

mechanics.name: Reusable factory blueprints
mechanics.summary: Save a proven production module, then replicate and adapt it elsewhere.
mechanics.rules: Players build a working module, save its layout and settings, then place copies. Materials, space and external connections still matter; output verifies that interfaces are connected.
decisions: A reusable module fits more situations but may be less compact than a custom layout.
Test one copy and its connections, or place many at once? How many copies would inherit an existing fault?

parameters.name: Template size
parameters.effect: Small templates reward standardized interfaces; large ones reduce repetition.

parameters.name: Replication cost
parameters.effect: Keeping material costs makes blueprints save actions without bypassing resource management.

cases.implementation: Selected entities become blueprints; placement creates ghosts that players or construction robots complete.
Blueprint Designers save modules within a bounded volume for placement from the build menu.

mechanics.contrast: Factorio captures layouts in the world for later construction; Satisfactory uses a designated design volume.
mechanics.combination: Let players save disaster-proof modules after stress tests, then rearrange their interfaces for new terrain.

walkthrough.setup: One small plate line works reliably, and you now need three times its output.
walkthrough.action: Save the module, place two copies and connect their input and power one at a time.
walkthrough.result: Layouts need no rebuilding, but unconnected copies still cannot run.
walkthrough.next: Once the new copies work, update the blueprint rather than reproducing old faults.

prototype.firstStep: Implement selection, saving and placement on a small grid with material and occupancy checks, supporting a few building types.
prototype.pitfall: Rotation, mirroring, multiple floors and version compatibility complicate saves; make exact copying reliable first.
prototype.test: Do players inspect interfaces after copying and correct the source module when a repeated fault appears?

mechanics.name: Byproduct consumption and recirculation
mechanics.summary: Find a destination for unwanted outputs so they do not stall the main product.
mechanics.rules: A process produces several outputs, and players provide uses, storage or disposal for each. Full byproduct outputs constrain production; conversion and recirculation turn waste into another input.
decisions: Disposal is simple; reuse saves resources but couples systems.
A large temporary buffer delays imbalance without solving it.

parameters.name: Byproduct ratio
parameters.effect: A higher ratio makes waste handling central to the factory.

parameters.name: Disposal options
parameters.effect: Easy disposal lowers stall risk; mandatory reuse emphasizes closed-loop planning.

cases.implementation: Advanced oil processing produces several oil fractions; cracking converts excess fractions toward downstream demand.
Some refinery recipes produce solids and fluids; either output needs a destination for sustained operation.

mechanics.contrast: Factorio balances oil fractions through cracking; Satisfactory often requires both solid and fluid output handling.
mechanics.combination: Run a sugar mill whose residue can be sold as feed or burned for power, with changing demand rewarding flexible outlets.

walkthrough.setup: Every main product produces waste liquid, and the waste tank is almost full.
walkthrough.action: Add a disposal outlet, then route some waste into a process that can consume it.
walkthrough.result: The main line resumes, but insufficient recycling demand can create another backlog.
walkthrough.next: Compare generation and consumption rates and adjust recycling or the fallback outlet.

prototype.firstStep: Use one main output, one byproduct and finite storage, with disposal and reuse routes.
prototype.pitfall: Complex recycling can deadlock; first ensure every output has an understandable destination.
prototype.test: Pause the recycling consumer; can players diagnose the backlog and restore production without merely adding storage?

mechanics.name: Structural support and collapse
mechanics.summary: Find adequate support before building taller or extending farther.
mechanics.rules: Players place walls, beams and floors subject to support rules. Long spans or weak support can collapse; feedback guides reinforcement.
decisions: Extra pillars improve safety but occupy usable space.
Stronger materials enable larger spans at a processing cost.

parameters.name: Support reach
parameters.effect: Longer supported spans loosen engineering constraints.

parameters.name: Collapse loss
parameters.effect: Recoverable materials encourage experiments; cascading damage encourages prototypes.

cases.implementation: Pieces gain stability through connections to grounded and supporting pieces, with color feedback.
Roofs need walls or columns for support; removing supports can collapse the roof and injure characters beneath.

mechanics.contrast: Valheim propagates stability through connected pieces; RimWorld constrains large rooms through roof support from walls and columns.
mechanics.combination: Build a retreat bridge that carries the party but can lose a selected support to stop pursuers.

walkthrough.setup: You extend a walkway; its outermost floor is too far from the support column.
walkthrough.action: Add a column below before extending farther.
walkthrough.result: The stability indicator improves; removing a key support destabilises dependent pieces.
walkthrough.next: Recheck support paths before each extension or demolition.

prototype.firstStep: Start with a two-dimensional grid and support based on connection distance from foundations, without rigid-body collapse.
prototype.pitfall: Structural evaluation, failure propagation and physics debris are separate costs; first align rules with safety feedback.
prototype.test: Can players infer where to reinforce and predict what removing a support will affect?

mechanics.name: Room qualification rules
mechanics.summary: Turn enclosed space and required fixtures into a functional room.
mechanics.rules: Players enclose space, add access and furnish it. Area, enclosure and contents determine room roles or eligibility; failed requirements block intended functions.
decisions: Compact rooms are cheap but constrain expansion.
Shared spaces save area but may alter the recognized role.

parameters.name: Rule transparency
parameters.effect: Showing missing requirements reduces blind rebuilding.

parameters.name: Qualification tiers
parameters.effect: Binary eligibility is readable; quality tiers provide ongoing goals.

cases.implementation: NPC housing needs enclosure, space and furnishings; housing queries check validity.
Enclosure and contents determine room roles; stats such as space and beauty affect residents.

mechanics.contrast: Terraria emphasizes eligibility; RimWorld also considers role and quality.
mechanics.combination: Run an inn with different guest requirements, rearranging walls and furniture in a fixed building.

walkthrough.setup: Your bedroom has a bed and lamp but fails recognition because one wall cell is missing.
walkthrough.action: Inspect the unmet conditions, close the gap and keep a valid entrance.
walkthrough.result: The room changes from invalid to usable and its function becomes available.
walkthrough.next: Recheck qualification after expanding or rearranging furniture.

prototype.firstStep: Detect enclosed areas with an entrance and two required furniture items, displaying each condition separately.
prototype.pitfall: Conflicting uses, nested spaces and multiple floors add edge cases; begin on one simple floor.
prototype.test: Given a room missing one condition, can players fix it using the feedback and explain why?

mechanics.name: Terrain shaping
mechanics.summary: Reshape elevation and ground for buildings and water.
mechanics.rules: Players raise, lower or fill terrain to create space and routes. Tools and materials constrain changes to buildable land, slopes and waterways.
decisions: Following terrain saves cost; flattening simplifies layout.
Local changes can displace water problems elsewhere.

parameters.name: Reshaping cost
parameters.effect: High costs reward adaptation; low costs encourage expression.

parameters.name: Reversibility
parameters.effect: Easy restoration encourages experiments; irreversible changes demand previews.

cases.implementation: The hoe levels or raises terrain to prepare foundations and paths.
Dynamite removes terrain blocks for channels or settlement reshaping.

mechanics.contrast: Valheim emphasizes local preparation; Timberborn links block excavation to water and settlement planning.
mechanics.combination: Give a cliff village limited earthworks to divide among farmland, roads and reservoirs.

walkthrough.setup: A house cannot be placed: a slope occupies one side and a ditch cuts through the other.
walkthrough.action: Level only the required footprint, keeping a nearby channel for drainage.
walkthrough.result: The buildable area expands, spending fill material and changing the terrain.
walkthrough.next: Check that access and drainage still work before planning the next building.

prototype.firstStep: Use tile heights, cut/fill costs and building-level requirements before adding deformable terrain meshes.
prototype.pitfall: Terrain linked to water, navigation and vegetation triggers many updates; expand those links gradually.
prototype.test: Do players use limited earthworks to save materials and anticipate affected routes?

mechanics.name: Service coverage placement
mechanics.summary: Reach more demand with facilities while reducing wasted overlap.
mechanics.rules: Players place facilities and users within effective reach. Boundaries, access and capacity constrain benefits; overlays and unserved users guide new sites.
decisions: Central sites cover broadly but use valuable land.
Peripheral sites fill gaps at the cost of duplication.

parameters.name: Coverage shape
parameters.effect: A radius is readable; road-based reach rewards network planning.

parameters.name: Capacity
parameters.effect: Limited capacity can require more facilities within covered areas.

cases.implementation: Workbenches support nearby building and repair, so expansion can require more benches.
Services require planning around reach, road access and processing capacity; proximity alone is insufficient.

mechanics.contrast: Workbenches provide local construction support; city services add access and capacity limits.
mechanics.combination: Design a mobile vet camp choosing one daily site with limited treatment capacity.

walkthrough.setup: Four houses need a service; a central facility reaches three while an edge location reaches two.
walkthrough.action: Place the central facility first, then consider the farthest house with the remaining budget.
walkthrough.result: Coverage and unserved markers show the outcome; overlapping coverage need not add value.
walkthrough.next: Review new gaps after housing expansion before adding or relocating facilities.

prototype.firstStep: Use a bounded map, demand points and a movable coverage circle, showing coverage count and cost.
prototype.pitfall: Range, capacity and route access are different limits; distinguish them clearly and add them one at a time.
prototype.test: After new demand appears, do players reassess existing locations instead of simply adding more facilities?

mechanics.name: Road and entrance connectivity
mechanics.summary: A placed building needs reachable access for people and goods.
mechanics.rules: Players connect entrances to roads or paths. Disconnections, orientation and detours affect use; access warnings and travel routes guide redesign.
decisions: Dense plots fit more buildings but create detours.
Extra routes improve connectivity but consume productive space.

parameters.name: Travel cost
parameters.effect: Longer travel times make adjacency more valuable.

parameters.name: Entrance count
parameters.effect: Multiple entrances reduce dead zones; one entrance emphasizes orientation.

cases.implementation: Paths connect entrances and stairs link routes at different elevations.
Most buildings need road access, and network structure affects services and vehicles.

mechanics.contrast: Timberborn emphasizes walking and elevation; Cities: Skylines also carries vehicle traffic.
mechanics.combination: Require warehouses to reach docks and markets, balancing route length against capacity.

walkthrough.setup: A warehouse is close to a workshop, but its entrance faces away and forces a long detour.
walkthrough.action: Reorient the entrance and add a short road for the frequent trip.
walkthrough.result: Access becomes valid, walking distance falls and delivery waits shrink.
walkthrough.next: During expansion, keep checking entrances so new buildings do not block old routes.

prototype.firstStep: Use small-grid pathfinding, two buildings with entrances and one carrier, displaying route length.
prototype.pitfall: Large-scale avoidance and traffic can wait; first validate feedback for entrances and broken roads.
prototype.test: Can players distinguish straight-line distance from the actual route and improve delivery through entrance placement?

mechanics.name: Vertical stacking
mechanics.summary: Stack functions when land is scarce, then connect the floors.
mechanics.rules: Players build above valid platforms or structures to reuse one footprint. Stackability and vertical access constrain layouts; useful space and transport convenience provide feedback.
decisions: Building up saves land but adds movement between levels.
Reserved shafts ease expansion but use current space.

parameters.name: Height limit
parameters.effect: Low limits emphasize allocation; high limits enable vertical cities.

parameters.name: Vertical movement cost
parameters.effect: Expensive vertical movement rewards related processes sharing a floor.

cases.implementation: Platforms support building above, with paths or suitably sized structures below.
Multi-story factories use foundations, ramps and conveyor lifts for production between levels.

mechanics.contrast: Timberborn depends on valid surfaces and resident paths; Satisfactory organizes floors around machines and logistics.
mechanics.combination: Build a vertical market on a fixed footprint, arranging workshops, retail and dispatch by logistics.

walkthrough.setup: Only one ground footprint remains, but you still need storage and processing space.
walkthrough.action: Place storage below, the workshop above and a staircase between them.
walkthrough.result: The footprint supports more functions, but transport now includes vertical travel.
walkthrough.next: Review the most frequent transfers and rearrange floor functions accordingly.

prototype.firstStep: Use two fixed grids, support flags and one stair node, switching floors instead of building complex 3D navigation.
prototype.pitfall: Occlusion, support, inter-floor pathfinding and selection can interfere; start with clear floor views.
prototype.test: Do players reserve stair space and rearrange floor uses to improve transport?

mechanics.name: Modular snap construction
mechanics.summary: Align walls and floors at snap points to assemble editable structures.
mechanics.rules: Players select, rotate and snap components into structures. Dimensions and connector direction constrain joins; previews and collision feedback guide placement.
decisions: Assemble quickly with standard pieces, or adjust orientations to improve doors and passages?
Existing pieces use more space; is another module worth using to reduce awkward joints and detours?

parameters.name: Snap assistance
parameters.effect: Strong snapping is faster; weak snapping enables detail but risks misalignment.

parameters.name: Module scale
parameters.effect: Small parts support detail; large parts reduce repetition.

cases.implementation: Pieces snap to existing connectors, with an option to temporarily disable snapping.
Foundations provide grids and alignment for orderly equipment and structures.

mechanics.contrast: Valheim uses piece connectors for shape; Satisfactory often uses foundation grids for industrial layouts.
mechanics.combination: Give explorers a small kit to recombine for different crossings instead of unlocking longer bridges.

walkthrough.setup: You want to add a wall, but its doorway faces the wrong direction for the corridor.
walkthrough.action: Rotate the module, inspect the snap preview and confirm placement.
walkthrough.result: Matching interfaces connect; collisions or incompatible joints show an invalid placement.
walkthrough.next: Check that the passage remains open before selecting the next module.

prototype.firstStep: Use wall, floor and door modules with a few fixed snap points, keeping preview and placement identical.
prototype.pitfall: Arbitrary rotation, scaling and many joints multiply combinations; constrain sizes and rotation steps first.
prototype.test: Can players place a door as intended without repeated undoing and explain an invalid placement?

mechanics.name: Construction sequencing
mechanics.summary: Plan first, then build according to resources, access and urgency.
mechanics.rules: Players issue build tasks rather than instantly creating structures. Workers deliver materials and build; missing supplies or access block progress, making phases and priorities important.
decisions: Many projects divide workers and supplies.
Emergency solutions improve safety but may need rebuilding.

parameters.name: Build duration
parameters.effect: Long builds make order affect survival; short builds emphasize layout.

parameters.name: Priority granularity
parameters.effect: Fine priorities offer control but can become tedious scheduling.

cases.implementation: Colonists assigned to construction supply and build blueprints; insufficient access can prevent completion.
Task priorities and Duplicant preferences affect construction, while materials and access remain necessary.

mechanics.contrast: Both delegate plans to workers; RimWorld foregrounds assignments while ONI makes compact access planning prominent.
mechanics.combination: Expand a shelter before a storm, preserving escape routes while choosing roofs or heating first.

walkthrough.setup: You queue a wall and indoor equipment; building the wall first may block material access.
walkthrough.action: Prioritise the interior equipment and complete the enclosing wall last.
walkthrough.result: Workers deliver materials first, complete the equipment and then close the room.
walkthrough.next: Reprioritise when materials run short or emergencies arise without deleting the entire plan.

prototype.firstStep: Use one worker, a stockpile, three jobs and priorities, displaying why each job waits.
prototype.pitfall: Job competition, reservations and interrupted plans require extra state handling; make one worker reliable first.
prototype.test: When a build is blocked by enclosure, can players recover through sequencing or leaving access?

mechanics.name: Water retention and level management
mechanics.summary: Use barriers and release to manage water as a terrain resource.
mechanics.rules: Players build barriers to retain or release water. Inflow, elevation and outlet capacity determine levels; flooding and drying guide adjustments.
decisions: More storage helps dry periods but raises upstream flood risk.
Large dams centralize control; small stages are easier to validate.

parameters.name: Inflow variation
parameters.effect: Seasonal changes reward storage planning and safe overflow.

parameters.name: Response speed
parameters.effect: Slow responses reward forecasts; fast responses demand quick recovery.

cases.implementation: Height-adjustable floodgates control retention for storage and release.
Players contain liquid in pools and pump it out. Pump throughput is limited; a high overflow pump can help without guaranteeing protection against all inflow.

mechanics.contrast: Timberborn controls river retention with gates; ONI manages contained liquid through pool boundaries and active pumping.
mechanics.combination: Have villages share a river and schedule releases among irrigation, industry and flood buffers.

walkthrough.setup: Rain increases inflow and the reservoir nears capacity while downstream fields still need water.
walkthrough.action: Open the gate partly to supply downstream fields while retaining dry-season reserves.
walkthrough.result: The level shows the inflow-outflow balance: too little release floods, too much drains reserves.
walkthrough.next: During the dry period, adjust release according to remaining storage.

prototype.firstStep: Use two connected basins, fixed capacity and an adjustable gate, calculating levels from total volume rather than full fluid simulation.
prototype.pitfall: Real fluid flow, deformable terrain and gate networks greatly increase computation and debugging; test storage decisions first.
prototype.test: Across wet and dry phases, do players reserve capacity or water rather than leaving the gate fully open?

mechanics.name: Thermal zoning and control
mechanics.summary: Separate heat sources, cold storage and living areas to manage temperature through layout.
mechanics.rules: Players use walls, doors, vents and thermal equipment to control areas. Heat sources keep operating while openings and materials affect exchange; readings guide revisions.
decisions: Shared control saves equipment but may not suit every room.
Strong separation limits exchange but increases access and build costs.

parameters.name: Thermal inertia
parameters.effect: Slow change enables preconditioning; fast change needs responsive control.

parameters.name: Material differences
parameters.effect: Distinct conductivity adds material choice to layout decisions.

cases.implementation: Heaters and coolers control indoor temperature, while doors, walls and vents affect neighboring rooms.
Conductivity, insulated tiles and machine heat affect base temperature and require planned heat flow.

mechanics.contrast: RimWorld foregrounds rooms and resident needs; ONI adds material and heat-transfer detail.
mechanics.combination: Design a greenhouse using kitchen waste heat for tropical crops while protecting an adjacent cold store.

walkthrough.setup: A furnace room sits beside a cold store; an open door keeps the cooler running without reaching its target.
walkthrough.action: Separate hot and cold zones, add insulation and reduce traffic through the doorway.
walkthrough.result: Storage temperature stabilises at the cost of longer transport routes or more space.
walkthrough.next: Check temperature trends after adding heat sources or expanding rooms, then adjust equipment.

prototype.firstStep: Use temperature values for two rooms, a connecting door, a heater and a cooler with simple heat exchange.
prototype.pitfall: Per-cell conduction, gas flow and phase changes expand scope quickly; begin with room-level calculations.
prototype.test: When cooling misses its target, can players identify heat leakage instead of endlessly adding coolers?

mechanics.name: Shared attack–defense stamina
mechanics.summary: Every extra attack spends part of your escape budget.
mechanics.rules: Attacks, rolls and blocked hits draw from one regenerating pool. Deal damage while reserving enough for the next enemy response; the stamina bar makes overcommitment visible.
decisions: Finish a weakened enemy or save a roll? A quick kill competes with surviving the reply.
When raised guarding slows recovery, lowering the shield becomes an active choice.

parameters.name: Recovery delay
parameters.effect: Longer delays create a more vulnerable pause after overattacking.

parameters.name: Cost differences
parameters.effect: Expensive heavy attacks make certainty and enemy recovery more valuable.

cases.implementation: Attacks, heavy attacks, rolls and sprinting spend stamina. Heavy attacks generally cost more, while equipment load also changes rolling.
Attacks and evasive actions spend stamina in combat; stamina is not consumed outside combat, separating travel convenience from combat budgeting.

mechanics.contrast: Both constrain sustained aggression; Elden Ring explicitly relaxes the cost outside combat to reduce travel friction.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: let heavy mining tools spend combat stamina, making a surprise encounter a choice between one last extraction and a safe defense.

walkthrough.setup: You have 60 stamina; an attack costs 20 and a roll costs 25.
walkthrough.action: After the enemy finishes a swing, attack once and keep 40 stamina.
walkthrough.result: You can roll away from its reply; two attacks would have left only 20.
walkthrough.next: Back off to recover, then judge how many hits the next opening allows.

prototype.firstStep: Build one enemy with a fixed rhythm, attack and roll buttons, and a regenerating stamina bar.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid a weapon catalogue until action costs work with the enemy rhythm.
prototype.test: Watch whether players stop before exhaustion and can explain what they are saving stamina for.

mechanics.name: Timed parries
mechanics.summary: Turn defense into a risky timing decision instead of a held state.
mechanics.rules: Read the wind-up and parry inside a brief window before impact. Success changes initiative or creates retaliation; early input may become a normal block, while late input can mean damage.
decisions: A parry may win initiative while evasion is safer; is an unfamiliar attack worth the risk?
A multi-hit string asks for repeated rhythm recognition, not one successful input.

parameters.name: Timing window
parameters.effect: Narrow windows increase the skill gap and the need for readable audiovisual cues.

parameters.name: Failure fallback
parameters.effect: Allowing early input to block encourages practice; complete failure makes it more of a gamble.

cases.implementation: Pressing guard just before impact deflects the attack and pressures enemy posture; attack strings call for repeated deflections.
Raising a shield as an attack arrives can parry; melee attacks and projectiles have different responses, including reflected projectiles.

mechanics.contrast: Sekiro turns deflection into an extended exchange; Dead Cells shield parries also reflect projectiles and interact with equipment effects.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: use the parry input for harmless rhythmic machinery, teaching timing before testing recognition in combat.

walkthrough.setup: An enemy raises its blade; retreat or wait and parry as it comes down.
walkthrough.action: Read the blade movement and press defense just before contact.
walkthrough.result: Success exposes the enemy; a late input hurts you. Sound and effects distinguish the outcomes.
walkthrough.next: Counter during the opening, then check whether the next attack uses the same timing.

prototype.firstStep: Start with two readable enemy attacks, a parry check, and unmistakable success feedback.
prototype.pitfall: Align animation, contact, and input timing before adding unpredictable delays.
prototype.test: After a miss, ask whether it was early or late and see whether feedback guides the next attempt.

mechanics.name: Invulnerability-window dodging
mechanics.summary: Avoid damage by timing a brief safe window, not only by moving away.
mechanics.rules: An evasive action grants a limited window against certain damage. Its destination can still be unsafe, so the player must judge timing, direction and landing position together.
decisions: Retreating can be safer; passing through an enemy can reach a faster counterattack position.
Repeated evasions can escape one threat while moving into the next.

parameters.name: Safe-window fraction
parameters.effect: A larger fraction reduces timing difficulty while landing hazards can preserve challenge.

parameters.name: Cooldown and chains
parameters.effect: Long cooldowns demand anticipation; short ones support dense projectile patterns.

cases.implementation: Dashing provides brief invulnerability and upgrades can change the number of dashes. A dash attack is not identical in safety to a plain dash.
Rolling avoids most attacks, passes through enemies and reduces the character’s height for narrow gaps; it does not negate every hazard.

mechanics.contrast: Hades emphasizes chaining movement across a top-down arena; Dead Cells also uses the action to pass enemies and enter low passages.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: make a safe dodge landing activate a short-lived pressure plate, turning evasion into the start of an environmental chain.

walkthrough.setup: A sweeping attack approaches; a wall is behind you and space is behind the enemy.
walkthrough.action: Roll toward the attack and pass through it during the brief protected interval.
walkthrough.result: The sweep misses, but your landing position determines exposure to the next strike.
walkthrough.next: Choose whether to counter or create more distance from the new position.

prototype.firstStep: Use a simple character, one sweeping attack, and a visible dodge-protection interval.
prototype.pitfall: Resolve collision and landing before adding attacks, so successful dodges do not trap players inside enemies.
prototype.test: Check whether players adjust both timing and direction instead of repeatedly pressing dodge.

mechanics.name: Stagger buildup and punish windows
mechanics.summary: Build pressure first, then convert the opening into a valuable strike.
mechanics.rules: Alongside health, attacks or defensive interactions build a stagger state. Crossing a threshold exposes the enemy, and the player must exploit it before recovery.
loop: Cash in with a critical hit
decisions: Keeping pressure can prevent recovery, but remaining close increases exposure.
Low-damage, high-pressure moves make single-hit damage an incomplete measure of value.

parameters.name: Passive recovery
parameters.effect: Faster recovery pushes continuous close-range engagement.

parameters.name: Break reward
parameters.effect: Large rewards make setup central; smaller rewards frame breaking as brief crowd control.

cases.implementation: Attacks and deflections build posture damage. Lower enemy vitality slows posture recovery, and a break allows a deathblow.
Jumping attacks, charged attacks and guard counters can break enemy stance, opening suitable enemies to a critical hit.

mechanics.contrast: Sekiro makes its visible posture gauge a central objective; Elden Ring embeds stance breaking in weapon and attack choices.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: in co-op, one player builds stagger while another captures the target with a net, giving capture and killing different rewards.

walkthrough.setup: The enemy still has plenty of health, but its stagger meter is nearly full.
walkthrough.action: Risk one heavy attack to fill the stagger meter.
walkthrough.result: The enemy collapses and briefly offers a powerful follow-up.
walkthrough.next: Reach it to claim the follow-up; miss the window and rebuild stagger.

prototype.firstStep: Implement health and stagger meters, light and heavy attacks, and a fixed opening duration.
prototype.pitfall: A second health bar alone changes little; recovery or timing constraints must affect decisions.
prototype.test: Compare low-health and near-stagger situations and see whether players choose different attacks.

mechanics.name: Weak-point targeting
mechanics.summary: Where a hit lands changes its value against the same enemy.
mechanics.rules: Identify a vulnerable region, choose an angle and weapon, and land a valuable hit. Movement, cover or damage-type requirements complicate access; hit feedback confirms the choice.
decisions: A reliable body hit competes with a smaller, more valuable target.
Moving around to a weak region can improve damage while entering a dangerous attack arc.

parameters.name: Target size
parameters.effect: Smaller regions emphasize accuracy; faster movement emphasizes prediction.

parameters.name: Weakness visibility
parameters.effect: Scanning reduces memorization; hidden weaknesses encourage experimentation.

cases.implementation: The Focus identifies machine components and vulnerabilities; body regions and elemental responses make placement more important than simply landing a shot.
Body regions have different responses to cutting, impact, shot and elemental damage; a weak hitzone is not the same thing as a breakable part.

mechanics.contrast: Horizon emphasizes precision after scanning; Monster Hunter links target regions to weapon type and close-range positioning.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: scouting notes reveal weak regions on a later expedition without aiming for the player, separating knowledge rewards from execution.

walkthrough.setup: The enemy has a large torso and a small side core that takes extra damage.
walkthrough.action: Move to its side, wait for the core to appear, and aim.
walkthrough.result: A core hit gives distinct feedback, while repositioning exposes you to another attack.
walkthrough.next: Use remaining health and safe distance to choose another precision shot or a torso hit.

prototype.firstStep: Build one enemy with large and small hit regions and a predictable weak-point exposure.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid many weapons initially; aim assistance, occlusion, and weak-point readability need tuning first.
prototype.test: Check whether players explain when a weak-point attempt is worthwhile and abandon it under pressure.

mechanics.name: Part destruction changes the fight
mechanics.summary: Damage a local target to change enemy capabilities or earn specific rewards.
mechanics.rules: Some enemy regions have separate break conditions. Focused attacks may sever a part, detach a weapon or change rewards. Breaking every part is not always the fastest kill, and not every break weakens attacks.
decisions: Removing a dangerous weapon can be safer; attacking a damage weakness can be faster.
Pursuing a hard-to-reach part for materials can prolong the encounter.

parameters.name: Part durability
parameters.effect: Excessive durability makes dismantling impractical; too little removes the setup.

parameters.name: Capability loss
parameters.effect: Disabling a recognizable attack communicates the reward more clearly than a cosmetic break.

cases.implementation: Tear damage can detach certain machine weapons, changing their available attacks; some detached heavy weapons can be used by the player.
Breaks and tail cuts offer specific material opportunities; some also alter behavior, such as damaging Tzitzi-Ya-Ku’s flash organs.

mechanics.contrast: Horizon can turn a detached weapon into an immediate tool; Monster Hunter often extends the reward into materials and later crafting.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: removing a robot cooler makes it overheat, but the mission needs that cooler intact, creating a tradeoff between safety and delivery quality.

walkthrough.setup: An enemy has armor and a ranged turret with its own durability.
walkthrough.action: Focus on the turret first, accepting slower damage to the main body.
walkthrough.result: Destroying the turret removes that attack while the enemy remains alive.
walkthrough.next: Use the reduced threat to reposition and choose another part or finish the fight.

prototype.firstStep: Build a main body and two parts; destroying a part disables its associated attack.
prototype.pitfall: More parts multiply animation, hit, and debris states; make the first destruction result readable.
prototype.test: Give the parts different threats and see whether players change their destruction order.

mechanics.name: Cover and flanking
mechanics.summary: Safety depends on enemy firing angles, not simply occupying a spot.
mechanics.rules: Units use cover to reduce exposure, then seek angles that bypass enemy protection. Movement spends action opportunities and can expose the mover to another enemy; cover and accuracy indicators communicate the tradeoff.
decisions: Spend movement for a better angle or take a low-probability shot now?
Cover against one opponent may offer no protection from another.

parameters.name: Cover strength
parameters.effect: Stronger protection increases the value of flanking and destruction.

parameters.name: Movement cost
parameters.effect: Cheap movement encourages mobility; costly advances require stronger team support.

cases.implementation: Half and full cover offer different protection. An enemy bypassing the protected direction creates a flank, indicated by a yellow shield.
Advance between cover and create firing opportunities from the side; a unit’s action points can be allocated across movement, attacks and other actions.
cases.rights: Splash Damage / The Coalition / Xbox Game Studios

mechanics.contrast: XCOM 2 makes the move-then-shoot commitment central; Gears Tactics uses more flexible action-point allocation to encourage aggressive sequences.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: allow limited furniture placement before combat, then let enemy flanks test the plan.

walkthrough.setup: An enemy is behind a low wall; you have two actions to move or fire.
walkthrough.action: Spend one action moving to the side, then fire from an uncovered angle.
walkthrough.result: The shot is stronger, but the new position exposes you to a second enemy.
walkthrough.next: Next turn, return to cover or push forward to eliminate the threat first.

prototype.firstStep: Start with a small grid, two enemies, directional cover, and two actions per turn.
prototype.pitfall: Make flanking rules visible before adding complex terrain or multiple floors.
prototype.test: Ask players to predict safety after moving and check whether indicators explain threats from different angles.

mechanics.name: Reactive combat surfaces
mechanics.summary: An ability can transform the battlefield as well as damage a target.
mechanics.rules: Create or find surfaces such as water and oil, then change them with fire, ice or electricity. The new area affects movement and conditions on both sides, making order and coverage matter.
loop: Exploit or avoid the new area
decisions: Reactions can affect allies, so the strongest combination may be wrong for the current formation.
Setup takes extra actions; when does preparing the field pay off?

parameters.name: Reaction duration
parameters.effect: Long duration makes combat about reshaping terrain; short duration favors immediate combos.

parameters.name: Friendly exposure
parameters.effect: Affecting allies increases the importance of area planning.

cases.implementation: Oil can ignite; water and fire can produce steam, and water can become electrified. Surfaces and clouds create a transformable battlefield.
Water surfaces can freeze or electrify, and fire interacts with water. Conditions such as Wet also change how characters respond to elemental damage.

mechanics.contrast: Original Sin 2 densely integrates surface transformations; Baldur’s Gate 3 also asks players to account for movement, action economy and character conditions.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: dungeon steam both blocks sightlines and powers machinery, so extinguishing a fire changes combat and access together.

walkthrough.setup: An enemy and ally occupy nearby tiles; you can spread oil and ignite it.
walkthrough.action: Spread oil along the enemy route, then ignite a position that avoids your ally.
walkthrough.result: The ground burns, threatening the enemy and possibly blocking your ally’s shortcut.
walkthrough.next: Reposition around the changed surface and look for another useful environmental state.

prototype.firstStep: Use a grid with only water, oil, and fire, and an explicit table of state changes.
prototype.pitfall: Each element adds interactions; constrain spread and duration before expanding the set.
prototype.test: See whether players change casting order for surface effects and predict consequences for allies.

mechanics.name: Combo variety rewards
mechanics.summary: Reward expressive attack variety alongside simply winning.
mechanics.rules: Link different moves while maintaining contact and rhythm to earn ratings or points. Repeating one safe move is often less valuable than varied sequences; damage or a broken chain can lose accumulated value.
decisions: Extending a stylish chain improves the rating, while stopping early is safer.
Repeat familiar moves, or risk a failed transition to vary the chain?

parameters.name: Repetition penalty
parameters.effect: Stronger penalties encourage using the full moveset.

parameters.name: Chain grace period
parameters.effect: Longer grace allows observation; shorter grace rewards continuous aggression.

cases.implementation: Style ratings encourage varied actions; Dante expands possible sequences through weapon and combat-style switching.
Punch and kick inputs form different strings. Dodge Offset lets a held attack input preserve the string through an evasive action.

mechanics.contrast: Devil May Cry 5 emphasizes switching and variety; Bayonetta tightly links authored attack strings with dodge-based continuation.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: in a tag team, one character’s launch direction determines the next character’s follow-ups, rewarding coordination rather than alternating turns.

walkthrough.setup: Repeating one move is safe, but it is barely raising your rating.
walkthrough.action: Chain a light strike into a launch, then follow with a different move.
walkthrough.result: The rating rises, but taking a hit while extending the chain loses accumulated advantage.
walkthrough.next: Read the enemy to decide whether to extend the chain or preserve the result.

prototype.firstStep: Build three chainable moves, reduced reward for repetition, and an immediate rating meter.
prototype.pitfall: Many moves cannot replace reliable chaining; define input buffering and cancellation consistently.
prototype.test: Compare sessions with and without rating rewards and watch for voluntary variation.

mechanics.name: Combat draw–discard cycles
mechanics.summary: Playing a card solves the present while shaping the next draw cycle.
mechanics.rules: Draw a hand and play within an energy budget. Played or unretained cards enter discard; when the draw pile empties, discard is reshuffled. Draw, retain and removal effects change access to key cards.
loop: Draw or reshuffle the next hand
decisions: Defense can compete with cycling: can some damage be accepted to reach a key combination?
A strong card only matters when drawn; deck thinning and redundancy have different costs.

parameters.name: Hand-to-energy ratio
parameters.effect: Many cards with scarce energy emphasize selection; abundant energy emphasizes ordering.

parameters.name: Reshuffle frequency
parameters.effect: Small decks are more consistent; large decks need search and redundancy.

cases.implementation: Attacks, block and skills respond to enemy intent. An empty draw pile reshuffles discard, while exhausted cards enter a separate zone.
The draw cycle supports spells and unit deployment. Deployed units remain on train floors, while unplayed cards and spells continue to shape later draws.

mechanics.contrast: Slay the Spire often converts a hand directly into immediate offense and defense; Monster Train also deploys persistent units that influence many rounds.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: represent maintenance as a cycling deck where breakdowns add temporary fault cards; repairs restore machinery and improve future draws.

walkthrough.setup: You have 3 energy and attack, defense, and draw cards in hand.
walkthrough.action: Spend 1 energy drawing, then use the rest to answer the enemy’s coming attack.
walkthrough.result: Played cards enter the discard pile and return to circulation when the draw pile empties.
walkthrough.next: When the next hand arrives, reconsider immediate defense and future draw opportunities.

prototype.firstStep: Start with ten fixed cards, one enemy with visible intent, a draw pile, and a discard pile.
prototype.pitfall: Settle draw, discard, and shuffle timing before special effects obscure the core cycle.
prototype.test: See whether players sacrifice an immediate play for the next turn and understand both piles.

mechanics.name: Ability-gated backtracking
mechanics.summary: See an unreachable place, then reinterpret it with a new ability.
mechanics.rules: Traversal limits such as jump range, walls and special barriers block paths. After earning an ability, recall and revisit old obstacles; the reward is new connectivity as well as new rooms.
decisions: Continue the main route or mark a suspicious branch? Attention is allocated among uncertain rewards.
After an upgrade, advancing and revisiting become competing rhythms.

parameters.name: Gate readability
parameters.effect: Clear visual language helps players remember which ability is missing.

parameters.name: Backtrack distance
parameters.effect: Excessive distance turns revisits into chores; shortcuts preserve discovery.

cases.implementation: Mantis Claw grants wall sliding and wall jumping, turning previously inaccessible vertical spaces into routes.
Bash redirects movement using enemies, projectiles or suitable objects, turning some hazards into traversal anchors.

mechanics.contrast: Hollow Knight often gates fixed geometry; Ori’s Bash can incorporate moving enemies and projectiles into a route.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: make a crafting tool alter traversal too—a deployable loom produces cloth and creates a temporary climbing surface.

walkthrough.setup: You find a high side passage beyond your current jump height.
walkthrough.action: Remember the location, obtain a double jump elsewhere, and return.
walkthrough.result: The old obstacle becomes an entrance to a new room and a connecting route.
walkthrough.next: Revisit other remembered obstacles with the ability or continue into the new area.

prototype.firstStep: Build five linked rooms, one movement upgrade, and two visible gates it unlocks.
prototype.pitfall: Without useful connections, more abilities merely increase the burden of remembering where to return.
prototype.test: After granting the ability, remove quest guidance and see whether players remember an earlier gate.

mechanics.name: Wall-jump traversal
mechanics.summary: Turn walls from boundaries into reusable movement anchors.
mechanics.rules: Jump away from a wall, then use another wall or air control to continue rising. Plan around wall spacing, hazards and landing points; failure mainly tests timing and direction rather than key possession.
loop: Catch the next wall or platform
decisions: Waiting on a wall can reveal the route but may slide the character into danger.
Fast consecutive jumps save time; a safe platform provides a reset.

parameters.name: Horizontal push
parameters.effect: Strong push favors alternating walls; weak push supports repeated jumps up one wall.

parameters.name: Air control
parameters.effect: Generous control softens mistakes; strong inertia requires earlier planning.

cases.implementation: The character slides on walls and wall-jumps; fast movement and dense saw hazards demand precise routes from this basic action.
After acquiring Mantis Claw, pressing against a vertical surface enables sliding and repeated jumps away from it.

mechanics.contrast: Super Meat Boy makes wall jumping a baseline skill to master; Hollow Knight also uses it as a progression reward that expands world access.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: allow wall jumps only on surfaces painted by the player, combining route execution with a limited paint supply.

walkthrough.setup: Two walls lead to a ledge, with spikes above forcing a change of rhythm.
walkthrough.action: Jump from the left wall to the right, then push off again below the spikes.
walkthrough.result: You gain height, while each reversal changes the distance to the ledge.
walkthrough.next: Land to inspect the next section or keep climbing for a faster route.

prototype.firstStep: Start with a two-wall shaft, a consistent jump arc, and one safe platform.
prototype.pitfall: Unify wall contact, turning, and input forgiveness before building tight challenges.
prototype.test: See whether new players can climb repeatedly and understand failed timing or direction.

mechanics.name: Air movement and refill nodes
mechanics.summary: Chain an airborne route through a limited movement resource.
mechanics.rules: Air movement has limited charges or consumes a pickup. Reach a refill or land safely before running out; visible resource state communicates remaining corrections, while refill placement shapes the route.
decisions: Spend a charge to correct a mistake or save it for the final gap?
A straight line is shorter, but detouring through a refill can enable a longer chain.

parameters.name: Stored charges
parameters.effect: Multiple charges allow recovery; one charge makes node order central.

parameters.name: Refill placement
parameters.effect: Refills near hazards reward risk; safe refills support learning.

cases.implementation: The basic dash travels in eight directions and normally refills on landing or touching a refill crystal; hair color communicates availability.
cases.rights: Maddy Makes Games / Extremely OK Games

cases.implementation: Discarding Soul Cards triggers movement abilities such as Elevate’s jump and Godspeed’s dash; card pickups along the route determine available movement.

mechanics.contrast: Celeste primarily replenishes one core ability; Neon White supplies different functional cards and makes shooting compete with discarding.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: an aerial courier can burn parcels for movement, making arrival easier at the cost of delivery income.

walkthrough.setup: You have one air dash, two gaps ahead, and a refill point between them.
walkthrough.action: Dash diagonally into the refill, then use the restored dash across the second gap.
walkthrough.result: The refill feedback lights up, making the previously unreachable route possible.
walkthrough.next: At the next landing, check remaining charges and plan the next aerial segment.

prototype.firstStep: Build one dash, one refill object, and a room requiring two linked dashes.
prototype.pitfall: Refills must be obvious; unclear charge restoration turns route planning into guessing.
prototype.test: See whether a failed attempt changes refill order instead of merely input speed.

mechanics.name: Climbing stamina and rest routes
mechanics.summary: Break a continuous wall into climbs the character can afford.
mechanics.rules: Climbing consumes stamina, requiring choices about holds, rest points and retreat. Restoring capacity at safe positions enables another segment; overlong routes can end in a fall or a safety-rope catch.
decisions: A direct ascent is shorter but may lack intermediate rest.
A detour for a stamina upgrade can turn an impossible route into a feasible one.

parameters.name: Cost while stationary
parameters.effect: Free pauses allow observation; continuous drain adds urgency.

parameters.name: Fall protection
parameters.effect: A safety rope reduces repeated climbing and emphasizes route judgment.

cases.implementation: Players manage climbing stamina and tools; alternating hand placement and safety anchors make route execution central.
Many environmental surfaces can be climbed within a stamina limit; exchanging Chum Eggs for stamina increases expands reachable height.

mechanics.contrast: Jusant focuses on the act and safety of climbing; Sable uses stamina to limit the reach of open-world exploration.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: geological samples reduce climbing endurance through weight, forcing a choice between unloading and pursuing a rare sample higher up.

walkthrough.setup: Your stamina is limited; the direct climb is short, but a detour has a resting ledge.
walkthrough.action: Traverse to the ledge, recover, and climb the final stretch.
walkthrough.result: The total route is longer, but no segment exhausts your stamina.
walkthrough.next: From the new resting point, inspect the next holds and a retreat route.

prototype.firstStep: Use a 2D wall, fixed stamina costs, and three ledges to test route decisions.
prototype.pitfall: Free-form climbing animation, arbitrary surfaces, and rope physics rapidly expand the scope.
prototype.test: Offer two routes and check whether players plan around resting points.

mechanics.name: Grapple swings and release timing
mechanics.summary: Choose an anchor, build speed and release into a new route.
mechanics.rules: Attach to an eligible surface, swing under rope constraints and gravity, then release. The goal is useful position and speed rather than merely reaching the anchor; landing and the next anchor determine release timing.
decisions: A nearby anchor is reliable; a distant one may generate more speed.
A later release may gain height; an earlier one may preserve a better forward trajectory.

parameters.name: Anchor eligibility
parameters.effect: Broad eligibility grants freedom; authored anchors tightly control pacing.

parameters.name: Momentum retention
parameters.effect: Preserved momentum rewards chaining; forced slowdown simplifies landing.

cases.implementation: The multiplayer Grapple tactical ability attaches to terrain and allows swing steering; skilled players use slingshots to accelerate across the map.
The hook connects to structures for swinging and integrates with jumps, rooftop parkour and other traversal tools rather than only pulling directly to a destination.

mechanics.contrast: Titanfall 2 places grappling inside fast competitive movement; Dying Light 2 connects it to extended parkour routes through an open city.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: players install a few permanent anchors before timed deliveries, making early construction determine later swing routes.

walkthrough.setup: A platform lies across a ravine, with an anchor above the gap.
walkthrough.action: Attach to the anchor, swing forward, and release when your velocity points toward the platform.
walkthrough.result: Your character carries momentum into flight; releasing early or late changes the landing.
walkthrough.next: After landing, find the next anchor and decide the height and speed needed.

prototype.firstStep: Start with a 2D rope, fixed anchor, and landing target, with a predicted arc for tuning.
prototype.pitfall: Rope length, collisions, camera, and speed interact; moving anchors and rope wrapping add further complexity.
prototype.test: Check whether release timing produces repeatable landings and understandable misses.

mechanics.name: Gliding and landing choice
mechanics.summary: Convert altitude into horizontal travel and look for ways to extend it.
mechanics.rules: Deploy a glide or slow-fall ability from height, steer and predict the landing. Altitude usually decreases; some games add stamina and updrafts, making route length, destination elevation and replenishment compete.
decisions: Fly straight to the target or detour through an updraft?
A higher launch point extends range, but reaching it has a cost.

parameters.name: Descent rate
parameters.effect: Slow descent favors sightseeing and exploration; fast descent emphasizes launch planning.

parameters.name: Airborne replenishment
parameters.effect: Fixed updrafts organize routes; variable ones demand adaptation.

cases.implementation: The glide bubble allows a slow descent from height, easing the return from elevated exploration; it is distinct from the ground hoverbike.
The paraglider uses stamina; air vents provide lift and replenish stamina, creating linkable aerial routes across the city.

mechanics.contrast: Sable emphasizes safe descent and observation; Dying Light 2 adds endurance planning through stamina and vents.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: airborne collectibles add weight and increase descent speed, so collecting more changes the return landing.

walkthrough.setup: From a tower you can see the destination, but a low ridge may block your descent.
walkthrough.action: Detour toward an updraft, regain height, then head for the target.
walkthrough.result: The flight takes longer but preserves enough altitude to clear the ridge.
walkthrough.next: Use current altitude to choose between continuing and landing somewhere safe.

prototype.firstStep: Implement fixed descent, steering, one updraft, and three landing elevations.
prototype.pitfall: Make altitude loss predictable before adding strong inertia or complex wind fields.
prototype.test: Ask players to name a landing before takeoff and compare the result with their expectation.

mechanics.name: Earned map information
mechanics.summary: Make map knowledge something earned through exploration.
mechanics.rules: Move with incomplete information, then acquire a map, survey an area or update it at a base. Mapping reduces repeated confusion while preserving unknown branches; information acquisition becomes a goal.
decisions: Detour for a map, or push deeper with uncertain information?
Once the main route is known, are unmarked branches worth spending supplies on?

parameters.name: Update timing
parameters.effect: Live updates aid navigation; base-only updates emphasize memory and risk.

parameters.name: Information detail
parameters.effect: Terrain-only information preserves discovery; marking every reward creates a checklist.

cases.implementation: After buying an area map, the Quill fills in explored rooms when resting at a bench rather than continuously revealing a complete map.
Finding map fragments reveals regional map detail; nearby map-fragment markers help guide discovery along roads.

mechanics.contrast: Hollow Knight ties updates to safe rest; Elden Ring uses fragments to reveal terrain across larger areas at once.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: different NPCs provide maps with biased omissions, which the player verifies and merges into a personal route book.

walkthrough.setup: You enter a branching area; the map shows only the entrance discovered so far.
walkthrough.action: Detour to a survey point to reveal the rough connections nearby.
walkthrough.result: You discover that two routes reconnect, avoiding unnecessary repeated exploration.
walkthrough.next: Choose an unexplored branch and gather more precise information.

prototype.firstStep: Build six rooms, an unexplored overlay, and one node that reveals the area.
prototype.pitfall: Showing every reward can undermine observation; separate route information from secrets.
prototype.test: Compare routes before and after the map: do players stop looping yet still explore side paths?

mechanics.name: Unlockable fast-travel networks
mechanics.summary: Preserve the first journey, then turn repeated travel into a network choice.
mechanics.rules: Reach and activate travel nodes before selecting them as destinations. Danger or special locations may restrict use; a new node rewards the player with shorter future journeys, not merely another icon.
decisions: Risk pushing deeper to unlock a node that makes future visits much cheaper.
Return for supplies now, or reach the next node first to avoid repeating this stretch?

parameters.name: Availability conditions
parameters.effect: Disabling travel in combat prevents it from becoming a free escape button.

parameters.name: Node density
parameters.effect: Dense nodes support revisits; sparse nodes preserve the significance of journeys.

cases.implementation: The map allows travel to discovered Sites of Grace, with restrictions during combat and some special situations.
Stag Stations form a fixed transport network served by the Last Stag, with stations opened through exploration.

mechanics.contrast: Elden Ring generally permits initiating travel through the field map; Hollow Knight requires reaching a station, preserving a return route.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: repairing caravan stations unlocks fast shipping, while cargo losses still depend on route danger.

walkthrough.setup: An inactive travel station lies beyond a dangerous mountain route.
walkthrough.action: Reach and activate it on foot, then travel back through the unlocked network.
walkthrough.result: Future trips reach that station directly instead of repeating the entire mountain route.
walkthrough.next: Continue exploring from the new node or prepare supplies elsewhere first.

prototype.firstStep: Build three areas, three activatable nodes, and a menu of unlocked destinations.
prototype.pitfall: Dense nodes can erase travel experiences; check that the first journey remains meaningful.
prototype.test: See whether players detour for a strategically useful node rather than merely collecting an icon.

mechanics.name: Escalating awareness and stealth routing
mechanics.summary: Being noticed need not mean instant failure; awareness stages create response windows.
mechanics.rules: Navigate enemy sight, sound and patrol routes. Suspicious behavior escalates toward searching or combat; pause, break sight, distract or reroute in response to readable awareness feedback.
decisions: Waiting is reliable; a noise distraction is faster but changes subsequent behavior.
A discovered body or illegal act can alter the route, so plan the exit as well as entry.

parameters.name: Awareness buildup
parameters.effect: Slow buildup permits correction; rapid buildup demands reconnaissance.

parameters.name: Search persistence
parameters.effect: Persistent search reshapes the level after a mistake; brief search supports experimentation.

cases.implementation: Guards detect the protagonist through sight and sound, with escalating awareness cues; occlusion and elevated routes support bypassing combat.
Disguises permit normal behavior in some areas, but enforcers or witnesses can still become threats; breaking sight can prevent further escalation.

mechanics.contrast: Dishonored emphasizes occlusion and vertical routes; Hitman adds identity permissions, making standing openly among people a possible safe choice.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a museum restorer may enter galleries legally, but carrying the wrong tools draws attention; borrowing and returning tools changes viable routes.

walkthrough.setup: A guard turns toward the corridor and catches you at the edge of his view.
walkthrough.action: As suspicion rises, move behind a crate.
walkthrough.result: The guard loses sight and investigates your last position instead of immediately fighting.
walkthrough.next: Change route during the investigation and wait for another opening.

prototype.firstStep: Build one patrol route, a vision cone, and calm, suspicious, and pursuing states.
prototype.pitfall: Defer sound, disguises, and group alarms until every state transition has a readable cause.
prototype.test: After detection begins, can players read suspicion and successfully recover once?

mechanics.name: Route reading in procedural terrain
mechanics.summary: Read a new route each run instead of memorizing one optimal path.
mechanics.rules: Procedural layouts vary passages, hazards and rewards. Read local information and weigh detours against survival; learned rules and hazard recognition persist even when room solutions do not.
loop: Carry rule knowledge to the next level
decisions: An exit is close: is a visible reward worth one more risk?
When terrain is editable, detouring competes with making a direct route.

parameters.name: Guaranteed safe connectivity
parameters.effect: Guaranteed connectivity focuses difficulty on choices; without it, runs may feel unsolvable.

parameters.name: Visible information range
parameters.effect: Short visibility emphasizes scouting; broad visibility emphasizes route optimization.

cases.implementation: Cave layouts change between runs; traps, enemies and destructible terrain demand a fresh reading of the descent.
