Procedural caves combine with pixel-level physics; fire, liquids and destructible materials keep altering routes after generation.

mechanics.contrast: Spelunky 2 emphasizes reading recombined traps and platforms; Noita also lets material reactions continuously rewrite the generated terrain.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a procedural mine retains support pillars from prior visits, letting shifting terrain and persistent construction jointly shape future safe routes.

walkthrough.setup: This run’s exit is down-left, while a reward on the right has a new trap arrangement.
walkthrough.action: Inspect how the trap triggers before deciding whether to detour for the reward.
walkthrough.result: You judge this run using learned rules instead of following the previous route.
walkthrough.next: Enter the next area with your remaining resources and reassess the local route.

prototype.firstStep: Randomly assemble a small set of authored rooms and verify that the exit stays reachable.
prototype.pitfall: Unrestricted randomness creates impossible or dull layouts; prioritize readable choices before variety.
prototype.test: Across runs, check whether players learn reusable rules rather than a fixed path.

mechanics.name: Recipe knowledge unlocks
mechanics.summary: Acquire a recipe to turn familiar ingredients into new options.
mechanics.rules: Players learn recipes through broadcasts, relationships or exploration, then use ingredients at the appropriate station. Knowledge and material access are separate gates; an expanded recipe list makes progress visible.
loop: Cook it and unlock its use
decisions: Learn an easy recipe first, or make a special trip for a crucial benefit?
Spend today finding a new recipe, or gather ingredients for a known one before tomorrow’s departure?

parameters.name: Unlock frequency
parameters.effect: Frequent unlocks encourage experimentation; scarce recipes become expedition rewards.

parameters.name: Source visibility
parameters.effect: Clear hints reduce guide dependence; vague clues add discovery but hide content.

cases.implementation: Most recipes must be learned from sources such as cooking broadcasts, friendships and shops; learned dishes can be prepared in a farmhouse kitchen or with a Cookout Kit.
The Tales expansion adds multi-ingredient Frontier Cooking, including unique recipes found in the world. This example requires the DLC.

mechanics.contrast: Stardew spreads recipes across daily routines and relationships; The Long Dark uses unique recipes as exploration rewards.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: an inn guest recalls an incomplete family recipe; visiting their hometown reveals the missing step.

walkthrough.setup: You have fish and vegetables but have not learned the more restorative fish soup recipe.
walkthrough.action: Complete the cook’s lesson, then gather the ingredients for the newly learned recipe.
walkthrough.result: Fish soup becomes craftable, giving existing ingredients a new use.
walkthrough.next: Choose between learning another recipe and preparing this one for the next outing.

prototype.firstStep: Use three recipe cards, two learning sources and a few ingredients, distinguishing unknown recipes from missing materials.
prototype.pitfall: Large recipe lists can become collection chores; make each early recipe solve a clear activity need.
prototype.test: When a desired dish is unavailable, can players tell whether they need knowledge or ingredients?

mechanics.name: Ingredient substitution
mechanics.summary: Swap ingredients that satisfy a recipe and save scarce items for other uses.
mechanics.rules: Recipes may require exact items, categories or properties. Players choose cheap, abundant or aging ingredients while satisfying those rules; outcomes depend on constraints rather than memorizing one fixed list.
decisions: Use an expensive fish or substitute a cheap one?
Does the substitution still meet every condition, or trigger another recipe?

parameters.name: Substitution breadth
parameters.effect: Broad substitutions rescue mixed stocks; excessive freedom erases ingredient identity.

parameters.name: Conflict visibility
parameters.effect: Outcome previews support optimization; hidden priorities turn early attempts into experiments.

cases.implementation: The Crock Pot evaluates ingredient values and recipe conditions. Different combinations can yield the same dish, while exclusions or priorities may select another.
Sashimi accepts any fish, allowing low-value catches; recipe consumption makes protecting expensive fish an important consideration.

mechanics.contrast: Substitution in DST can change recipe selection; in Stardew it primarily changes opportunity cost.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: substitutions preserve a recipe but change allergens and preferences, requiring order-specific choices.

walkthrough.setup: The recipe needs one fish; you have a cheap small fish and a valuable rare fish.
walkthrough.action: Use the cheap fish and check that it meets every remaining recipe condition.
walkthrough.result: You produce the required dish while preserving the rare fish for a better use.
walkthrough.next: Choose ingredients again when your inventory changes instead of always using the same item.

prototype.firstStep: Use a fish-plus-vegetable recipe and a stricter alternative, displaying ingredient categories and expected results.
prototype.pitfall: Hidden recipe priority makes substitutions confusing; make the rule choosing the final dish explicit.
prototype.test: When an ingredient becomes valuable or nearly spoils, can players substitute deliberately?

mechanics.name: Cooking completion windows
mechanics.summary: Food must be removed after cooking but before it burns.
mechanics.rules: Food changes over time on a heat source, enters a ready window, and burns or causes trouble if left longer. Players multitask while remembering when to return, supported by sound, color or progress cues.
decisions: Guard the stove or use the waiting time productively?
Which pot should be rescued when two finish together?

parameters.name: Safe window
parameters.effect: Short windows increase attention pressure; long ones suit relaxed camp routines.

parameters.name: Burn penalty
parameters.effect: Lost ingredients reward caution; spreading fire turns one mistake into a team crisis.

cases.implementation: Meat on a cooking station can be taken when ready; leaving it over the fire turns it into coal.
Cooked food needs timely attention; ignored warnings lead to burning and possible fire, which consumes more chef time.

mechanics.contrast: Valheim uses ingredient loss; Overcooked turns overcooking into a shared disruption.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: automatic ovens prevent burning, while manual timing earns quality bonuses.

walkthrough.setup: The soup needs more time while vegetables still need chopping.
walkthrough.action: Chop while waiting, then return when the ready signal sounds.
walkthrough.result: Removing it within the ready window succeeds; waiting too long burns the ingredients.
walkthrough.next: Use the previous timing to schedule parallel work before starting the next pot.

prototype.firstStep: Start with one stove, raw/ready/burnt food states and one short competing task.
prototype.pitfall: Complex physical handling can obscure timing choices; first make readiness cues reliable and noticeable.
prototype.test: Can players leave to work elsewhere and return on cue instead of staring at the stove?

mechanics.name: Staged preparation and assembly
mechanics.summary: Split a dish into ordered steps with parallel preparation opportunities.
mechanics.rules: Players transform ingredients into intermediate states and assemble valid components. Some operations are sequential and others parallel; missing ingredients or wrong states fail the order.
decisions: Batch preparation or keep counters free of unfinished items?
Which step should be delegated to remove waiting?

parameters.name: Dependency depth
parameters.effect: Deeper chains reward planning and memory but increase novice mistakes.

parameters.name: Shared intermediates
parameters.effect: Shared ingredients enable batching but create contention.

cases.implementation: Dishes such as pizza require chopping, combination and cooking before service; recipes impose different preparation sequences.
Pizza requires dough preparation, tomato and cheese, then cooking and portioning; one batch supplies multiple servings.

mechanics.contrast: Overcooked emphasizes transport and coordination; PlateUp adds batch-size planning through multiple servings.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: shared dough branches into bread or pizza; prepare it early and commit only after orders arrive.

walkthrough.setup: A burger needs chopped vegetables and cooked meat, with space for only two intermediate items.
walkthrough.action: Start cooking the meat, then chop vegetables during the wait.
walkthrough.result: Assembly succeeds only when both ingredients are ready; a missing step blocks delivery.
walkthrough.next: Clear the counter and decide what to prepare ahead for the next order.

prototype.firstStep: Use clickable stations and state labels for two dishes to test process dependencies and counter capacity.
prototype.pitfall: Too many intermediates become inventory overhead; ensure each step creates a real sequencing or parallel-work choice.
prototype.test: Do players prepare vegetables during heating and change the sequence when counter space runs out?

mechanics.name: Timed order triage
mechanics.summary: Decide which order deserves attention first, not only how fast to cook.
mechanics.rules: Several orders wait at once with different preparation times and shrinking patience or deadlines. Players prioritize and deliver matching dishes; timely service earns rewards, while delays lose rewards or end the run.
decisions: Finish the urgent complex order or clear two quick ones?
Is preserving a service streak worth an inconvenient order?

parameters.name: Deadline variation
parameters.effect: Varied deadlines require dynamic scheduling; identical ones tend toward a simple queue.

parameters.name: Failure tolerance
parameters.effect: Score-only penalties allow risk; run-ending abandonment encourages conservative planning.

cases.implementation: Orders appear with waiting progress; players prepare specified dishes, with timely and ordered service affecting performance.
Customers have patience pressures across waiting and service stages; losing a customer ends the restaurant run, making the whole service chain relevant.

mechanics.contrast: Overcooked pressures scores and order flow; PlateUp makes the least-patient customer a run-ending bottleneck.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: customers accept one explained delay, letting limited goodwill buy scheduling flexibility.

walkthrough.setup: Two orders are nearly due: soup takes twenty seconds and salad takes five.
walkthrough.action: Deliver the salad first to clear one order, then focus on soup.
walkthrough.result: The quick order is cleared, but the soup customer now has less patience.
walkthrough.next: Reassess when a new order arrives; shortest-first is not always best.

prototype.firstStep: Use three countdown order cards and fixed preparation times, selecting work with a click.
prototype.pitfall: A large menu is unnecessary initially; varied durations and deadlines can already test scheduling choices.
prototype.test: When one deadline changes, do players reprioritise instead of following arrival order?

mechanics.name: Kitchen station handoffs
mechanics.summary: Handing off components can outperform every chef doing a whole dish.
mechanics.rules: Chefs share space and stations and can specialize in preparation, cooking or service. Components need clear handoffs; blocked counters, misplaced items and contested equipment create congestion.
loop: Pass it or use a buffer
decisions: Use fixed roles or rotate to the current bottleneck?
Take the shortest path or leave a lane open for teammates?

parameters.name: Lane width
parameters.effect: Narrow lanes intensify coordination but magnify blocking.

parameters.name: Handoff range
parameters.effect: Throwing bridges obstacles; short-range handoffs depend more on layout.

cases.implementation: Ingredient throwing sends uncooked items across distance, supporting cooperation in divided or changing kitchens.
Players arrange appliances before service and divide cooking and serving roles; counter placement defines the kitchen-to-dining handoff.

mechanics.contrast: Overcooked asks teams to adapt to authored obstacles; PlateUp lets them reshape space before dividing work.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: turbulence reverses airship-kitchen belts, requiring teams to switch handoff protocols.

walkthrough.setup: Two cooks share one chopping station; the cook by the pan keeps waiting for ingredients.
walkthrough.action: Assign one cook to chopping and the other to cooking, using a central counter for handoffs.
walkthrough.result: Ingredients flow more reliably, but a full handoff counter forces an adjustment.
walkthrough.next: Help the bottleneck when a new order changes demand, then resume roles.

prototype.firstStep: Begin with two local players, two stations and one handoff slot; test passing and blockage without networking.
prototype.pitfall: Networking, free physics and a large menu multiply scope; test role coordination separately.
prototype.test: Watch whether players establish a handoff location and redistribute work when one station backs up.

mechanics.name: Meal buff loadouts
mechanics.summary: Choose meals for the next activity rather than always eating the biggest number.
mechanics.rules: Foods provide different timed effects with limits on stacking or replacement. Players anticipate combat, travel or gathering needs, choose meals and manage duration; switching costs resources and opportunities.
decisions: Prioritize health for survival or stamina for action?
Will eating now replace a useful effect that still has time left?

parameters.name: Concurrent-effect limit
parameters.effect: Few slots force trade-offs; unlimited stacking becomes stockpiling.

parameters.name: Effect duration
parameters.effect: Short effects reward situational use; long effects emphasize preparation.

cases.implementation: Up to three different foods provide differing health, stamina and other benefits; health- or stamina-heavy combinations suit different activities.
Food buffs generally replace other food buffs, while drink buffs can stack separately; speed, luck and skill effects suit different plans.

mechanics.contrast: Valheim emphasizes configuring three food slots; Stardew emphasizes replacement rules and matching the day’s task.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: an expedition shares one stew, but each profession benefits differently from its ingredients.

walkthrough.setup: You can maintain two food effects; a long climb with enemies lies ahead.
walkthrough.action: Choose a stamina meal and a health meal, giving up a pure damage bonus.
walkthrough.result: You gain travel capacity and a safety buffer, but may not finish fights faster.
walkthrough.next: At the next rest stop, reconsider meals against the route and remaining duration.

prototype.firstStep: Use three foods, two active slots and two short encounters with different demands; display effects and duration.
prototype.pitfall: An item that wins on every stat turns meal planning into a simple tier upgrade.
prototype.test: Move a player from a long traversal to a dangerous battle and see whether the meal choice changes.

mechanics.name: Preservation through processing
mechanics.summary: Spend processing time and capacity to turn perishables into travel reserves.
mechanics.rules: Food loses value over time, and players can spend salt, fuel or processing capacity to extend its useful life. Processing takes time and space and has limits; choosing which batch to preserve matters.
decisions: Save nearly spoiled food or preserve higher-value meat?
Eat now or wait to secure future supplies?

parameters.name: Processing time
parameters.effect: Long processing demands foresight and makes sudden harvests harder to save.

parameters.name: Shelf-life gain
parameters.effect: Tiny gains discourage processing; large gains extend expedition range.

cases.implementation: Drying racks turn suitable meat into jerky, extending storage and changing food benefits; drying takes time.
Later updates add salt-curing options for meat and fish; ruined ingredients cannot be treated as endlessly recoverable cooking inputs.

mechanics.contrast: DST trades drying-rack time for shelf life; The Long Dark adds preservation supplies such as salt.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a caravan has limited smoking slots each night, competing between tomorrow’s rations and valuable cured goods.

walkthrough.setup: You have five portions of meat, two expiring tomorrow; the dryer holds two portions.
walkthrough.action: Dry the nearly expired meat first and keep today’s meal fresh.
walkthrough.result: After processing, longer-lasting rations are ready and the dryer becomes available.
walkthrough.next: Schedule the remaining food around the next journey and rotate batches.

prototype.firstStep: Use per-item shelf life, two processing slots and a fixed processing time in a small inventory prototype.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid costless, endless freshness resets; processing cost and waiting should affect scheduling.
prototype.test: If departure moves earlier, do players change processing priority and what they eat today?

mechanics.name: Measured ingredient dosing
mechanics.summary: Turn recipe quantities into amounts the player must physically control.
mechanics.rules: Players weigh, pour or divide ingredients, and actual quantities affect results. Excess may be hard to undo; measuring tools and incremental additions reduce error, while feedback distinguishes execution from recipe design.
loop: Choose a container or portioning method
decisions: Pour in one motion for speed or add gradually for precision?
Rebalance an inaccurate batch or restart?

parameters.name: Tolerance
parameters.effect: Wide tolerances suit relaxed play; narrow ones reward tool mastery.

parameters.name: Measurement feedback
parameters.effect: Live numbers support calibration; visual estimation rewards experience but reduces predictability.

cases.implementation: Recipes specify weights and seasoning amounts; players handle interactive knives, containers and seasonings, with physical actions affecting the result.
Brewing uses ingredients, equipment and recipe quantities to shape a batch; players can follow recipes or adjust their own formulations.

mechanics.contrast: Cooking Simulator ties errors to immediate physical actions; Brewmaster makes ratios part of batch experimentation and repeatability.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: medicinal-food orders have varying tolerances; calibration tools convert execution difficulty into a business decision.

walkthrough.setup: The recipe needs 100 ml of liquid and you have poured 85 ml.
walkthrough.action: Switch from continuous pouring to short taps for smaller additions.
walkthrough.result: The reading approaches the target; overshooting changes the batch outcome.
walkthrough.next: Use the error feedback to slow earlier or choose a smaller container next time.

prototype.firstStep: Use a pour button, quantity readout and target band with a fixed flow rate, not full fluid physics.
prototype.pitfall: Combining inertia, jitter and hidden tolerance complicates tuning; first make errors understandable.
prototype.test: On repeats, do players learn to make large additions first and fine adjustments near the target?

mechanics.name: Targeted flavor scoring
mechanics.summary: A valid dish still needs to satisfy a particular evaluation target.
mechanics.rules: The game presents flavor or recipe targets, and ingredients and processing affect several scoring dimensions. Serving produces feedback for the next attempt; understanding criteria matters more than maximizing quantity.
decisions: Fix a weak dimension or strengthen an existing advantage?
Is adapting to a judge worth abandoning a strong general recipe?

parameters.name: Target disclosure
parameters.effect: Visible criteria support planning; hidden tastes need readable feedback.

parameters.name: Scoring weights
parameters.effect: One dominant weight favors specialization; balanced criteria encourage ingredient combinations.

cases.implementation: Hunted ingredients feed puzzle-based cooking, where players improve dishes around competition requirements.
Career mode serves recipe-based dishes to customers, with evaluation feeding back into preparation and cooking improvements.

mechanics.contrast: Battle Chef Brigade uses puzzle manipulation; Cooking Simulator emphasizes recipe execution and physical handling.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: judges reveal two preferences; players infer a third from past reviews and decide whether to specialize.

walkthrough.setup: The judge wants a sour dish; your trial has enough salt but not enough acidity.
walkthrough.action: Spend the final ingredient on acidity rather than adding more salt.
walkthrough.result: Separate scores show which flavour matches the target and which still misses.
walkthrough.next: Adjust proportions based on the gaps and submit another attempt.

prototype.firstStep: Use sour, sweet and salty targets with four ingredients and bar feedback showing gaps after submission.
prototype.pitfall: Opaque scoring encourages exhaustive guessing; feedback should guide the next change.
prototype.test: After one evaluation, can players identify an ingredient to increase or reduce?

mechanics.name: Harvesting tool gates
mechanics.summary: Visible resources may remain inaccessible to the current tool.
mechanics.rules: Resources require a tool type or tier, and weaker tools cannot yield useful material. Players remember locations, acquire upgrades and return; successful extraction demonstrates progression.
decisions: Detour for an upgrade or gather currently accessible resources?
Which equipment or building route should the new tool unlock first?

parameters.name: Tier spacing
parameters.effect: Large gaps make upgrades dramatic but may create long stalls.

parameters.name: Failure feedback
parameters.effect: Explicit tool messages prevent wasted effort; zero-damage feedback alone can mislead.

cases.implementation: Ores require sufficient pickaxe power; Chlorophyte has a specific threshold, so tool progression opens new material tiers.
Deposits have tool-tier requirements, with later ores needing stronger pickaxes; tools also differ in durability and efficiency.

mechanics.contrast: Terraria expresses gates through pickaxe power; Valheim connects tool tiers with biome progression and upkeep.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a stronger pickaxe mines hard ore but generates more noise, opening resources while attracting creatures.

walkthrough.setup: You find iron your stone pick cannot mine, while accessible copper remains on the map.
walkthrough.action: Mark the iron deposit, gather copper and craft a suitable pick.
walkthrough.result: On returning, the previously ineffective mining action now yields resources.
walkthrough.next: Use the new material for another project and look for the next resource barrier.

prototype.firstStep: Use two tools and two deposit types, explaining incompatibility and allowing location markers.
prototype.pitfall: Too many tool tiers create repeated grinding; make each upgrade unlock a clear new use.
prototype.test: After finding an inaccessible deposit, can players identify the upgrade and plan a return?

mechanics.name: Resource detection overlays
mechanics.summary: Spend items or infrastructure to turn blind searching into localization.
mechanics.rules: Detection marks nearby resources of a selected type. It reduces search time without removing travel, terrain or danger; players still plan a route and extract the target.
decisions: Invest in detection or search using terrain knowledge?
Choose a nearby poor deposit or a distant rich one?

parameters.name: Detection range
parameters.effect: Large ranges reduce blind searching but can erase terrain discovery.

parameters.name: Activation cost
parameters.effect: Consumables encourage selective use; permanent facilities encourage gathering outposts.

cases.implementation: Spelunker Potions highlight nearby treasure and ore for a limited duration, encouraging focused mining trips.
The Scanner Room searches nearby space for a chosen resource, with a HUD chip showing targets; it requires infrastructure and power.

mechanics.contrast: Terraria makes detection a temporary mobile buff; Subnautica anchors it to infrastructure and coverage.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: scanners report only a bearing; two readings triangulate a vein before drilling.

walkthrough.setup: You need copper and have one scan left; the nearest cave is already searched.
walkthrough.action: Scan an unexplored area and inspect the highlighted deposits and routes.
walkthrough.result: Locations become known, but hazardous terrain may still block a distant deposit.
walkthrough.next: Choose a worthwhile reachable deposit, then consider replenishing scans afterward.

prototype.firstStep: Use a hidden grid, fixed scan radius and a few obstacles to compare route choices before and after scanning.
prototype.pitfall: Automatic navigation and collection attached to scanning remove decisions after discovery.
prototype.test: When scanning reveals several deposits, do players compare route costs rather than visual distance alone?

mechanics.name: Volumetric excavation
mechanics.summary: Resources occupy alterable terrain rather than a single interaction button.
mechanics.rules: Tools remove volumes of terrain to reveal or collect material. Brush shape and size affect openings, slopes and precision, while excavation changes future traversal.
loop: Collect material and keep an exit
decisions: Excavate broadly for speed or carefully to preserve routes?
Dig straight down or spend time creating a return ramp?

parameters.name: Brush size
parameters.effect: Large brushes increase throughput but reduce precision; small brushes reward spatial planning.

parameters.name: Terrain restoration
parameters.effect: Restoration encourages experimentation; irreversible edits encourage caution.

cases.implementation: The Terrain Manipulator excavates buried resources and offers terrain-editing modes, changing the landscape while gathering.
The Terrain Tool removes, adds and flattens terrain, letting players reshape space to explore planets and gather resources.

mechanics.contrast: No Man’s Sky links excavation to surveying deposits; Astroneer closely connects digging and shaping with everyday traversal.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: fragile ruins surround a vein; careful tunnels preserve clues while broad excavation risks damage.

walkthrough.setup: An ore body sits inside a slope; digging straight down is quick but may make returning difficult.
walkthrough.action: Dig a ramp from the side, then widen the opening along the deposit.
walkthrough.result: Collected material leaves a cavity that changes the traversable terrain.
walkthrough.next: Check that the exit remains usable before mining the next section.

prototype.firstStep: Start with one small voxel mass, one tool and updated collision; verify traversal after digging, without an infinite world.
prototype.pitfall: Terrain rebuilding, collision, save size and debris can each become major systems; validate them separately.
prototype.test: Can players deliberately create a return route without falling through terrain or getting stuck after repeated digging?

mechanics.name: Oxygen-budgeted gathering
mechanics.summary: Every extra pickup consumes part of the safe return window.
mechanics.rules: Gathering underwater or without breathable air consumes oxygen. Players weigh resource value against travel distance and remaining air, returning to a refill point before it runs out; equipment changes practical range.
loop: Fill oxygen and choose a route
decisions: Search one more corner or return safely with current gains?
Does extra oxygen equipment displace other useful gear?

parameters.name: Depletion rate
parameters.effect: Fast depletion creates short sorties; slow depletion permits long routes with less urgency.

parameters.name: Refill density
parameters.effect: Dense refills reduce navigation penalties; sparse ones reward route memory.

cases.implementation: Oxygen drains outside breathable environments, requiring return to the surface, a vehicle or an oxygenated facility; tanks extend dive time.
Oxygen limits dives and is affected by attacks, so Dave must return with his catch in time; upgrades extend exploration capability.

mechanics.contrast: Subnautica emphasizes 3D return navigation and mobile air sources; Dave connects oxygen with damage pressure and each dive’s haul.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: harvested seaweed restores oxygen but is also an order ingredient, forcing a mid-dive survival-versus-income choice.

walkthrough.setup: You have forty seconds of oxygen, need twenty to return and ten to mine a nearby deposit.
walkthrough.action: Take only this deposit, skip the farther resource and immediately return.
walkthrough.result: You return with materials and a small buffer for an unexpected detour.
walkthrough.next: Refill oxygen and use the known route to plan the next trip’s range.

prototype.firstStep: Use a node map, fixed oxygen costs per action and one refill point, clearly displaying the return cost.
prototype.pitfall: Hidden return costs or oxygen changes create abrupt deaths; first make the risk understandable.
prototype.test: As oxygen falls, do players voluntarily abandon loot and explain their safety margin?

mechanics.name: Gathering quotas and stopping decisions
mechanics.summary: The quantity target is met: is another swing still worthwhile?
mechanics.rules: A required quantity and progress counter define the gathering goal. Once it is met, players can stop gathering, return to hand in, or initiate extraction, but may collect extra materials; the decision is whether another haul justifies the remaining time and supplies.
loop: Keep gathering or stop and return
decisions: After meeting the quota, is a nearby extra resource worth its detour and supply cost?
Is there enough time and supply to reach one more deposit and return?

parameters.name: Quota size
parameters.effect: Small quotas create frequent stopping decisions; large quotas emphasize sustained routes and supply planning.

parameters.name: Value of surplus resources
parameters.effect: Useful surplus encourages continued gathering; low-value surplus favors returning as soon as the target is met.

cases.implementation: Mining Expeditions require a Morkite quota, after which extraction can be called; the journey back to the drop pod remains dangerous.
cases.rights: Ghost Ship Games / Coffee Stain Publishing

cases.implementation: Gathering requests count newly acquired materials such as ore after acceptance; once the count is met, players can stop and speak to the requester or continue gathering for their own needs.

mechanics.contrast: Deep Rock asks when to call extraction and then navigate back through caves; Stardew lets players stop a completed collection task and spend remaining energy on other activities.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: an expedition needs one sample of each of three ores. After completing the set, visible rich veins tempt players to spend reserve oxygen on upgrade materials rather than return safely.

walkthrough.setup: The contract needs ten ore and you have ten; a valuable deposit lies down a side path.
walkthrough.action: Compare supplies with the return distance and leave with the completed objective.
walkthrough.result: The main reward is secured while optional profit is deliberately left behind.
walkthrough.next: Bring more supplies next time before considering extra collection.

prototype.firstStep: Use a clear collection target, two optional deposits and a shrinking action budget.
prototype.pitfall: If extra collection after the target has no cost or risk, stopping is not a meaningful choice.
prototype.test: Test two return-risk levels and see whether players make different choices after meeting the same quota.

mechanics.name: Gathering to sustain gathering
mechanics.summary: Gather the supplies that keep the expedition itself running.
mechanics.rules: Some resources are not final objectives but sustain tools or the team. Players alternate between goal progress and maintaining expedition capacity; insufficient supplies can end the outing early.
decisions: Mine the nearby objective or detour for supplies first?
How much reserve is enough before stockpiling becomes wasted time?

parameters.name: Supply conversion
parameters.effect: High conversion reduces upkeep frequency; low conversion risks endless maintenance loops.

parameters.name: Resource overlap
parameters.effect: Overlapping supplies and targets smooth the loop; separate distributions force route decisions.

cases.implementation: Nitra is spent on resupply pods that restore team ammunition and condition, making it important even when it is not the mission objective.
cases.rights: Ghost Ship Games / Coffee Stain Publishing

cases.implementation: The Mining Beam needs energy and can be recharged with materials such as carbon, so gathering tools rely on resources found along the way.

mechanics.contrast: Deep Rock feeds a team’s combat endurance; No Man’s Sky closes the energy loop of the mining tool itself.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a mining vehicle burns low-grade ore as fuel; valuable cargo can be sacrificed in an emergency at a profit cost.

walkthrough.setup: Your tool is nearly empty; the target ore is ahead and recharge material lies nearby.
walkthrough.action: Detour for recharge material, refill the tool, then return to the objective.
walkthrough.result: The detour did not directly advance the objective, but extended your working time.
walkthrough.next: Check reserves along the route rather than running out at the next target.

prototype.firstStep: Use objective and energy deposits, one charge gauge and a clear mining energy cost.
prototype.pitfall: If refuelling costs more than it yields and no alternative exists, players can enter an unrecoverable loop.
prototype.test: Can players refuel proactively and budget reserves for distance rather than only reacting to an empty gauge?

mechanics.name: Clues to buried deposits
mechanics.summary: Read surface traces, then uncover what lies beneath.
mechanics.rules: Buried items leave visible surface traces such as worm-like marks, crystal fragments or light. Players recognize the clue and dig with an appropriate tool; it may pinpoint a tile or indicate a region requiring probing, with the item revealed on excavation.
loop: Dig at the mark or through nearby rock
decisions: Is the clue worth leaving the current route when time or carrying space is limited?
Does the clue pinpoint a tile, or require re-reading glow and fragments to choose a digging direction?

parameters.name: Clue precision
parameters.effect: Precise markers favor efficiency; distributed clues require spatial inference.

parameters.name: Probe cost
parameters.effect: Cheap probes encourage exploration; costly ones reward careful localization.

cases.implementation: Aquarqs in Point Extraction are buried inside rock, with blue fragments and glow helping locate them; exposed chunks must then be returned.
cases.rights: Ghost Ship Games / Coffee Stain Publishing

cases.implementation: Artifact Spots appear as worm-, stem- or twig-like surface marks. Digging with a hoe guarantees an item; possible finds depend on location and other conditions, and are not always artifacts.

mechanics.contrast: Deep Rock uses clustered fragments and glow to localize a buried region, leaving depth to infer; Stardew pinpoints one tile, shifting uncertainty toward what the dig will reveal.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: minerals change nearby plant colors, allowing learned ecological patterns to reveal underground veins.

walkthrough.setup: A patch of bright crystals appears on one wall but not on nearby rock.
walkthrough.action: Dig a layer near the densest crystals, then inspect how the clue changes.
walkthrough.result: Exposed ore or stronger light indicates whether you are moving in the right direction.
walkthrough.next: After extraction, remember the visual pattern and look for the next deposit.

prototype.firstStep: Use a two-dimensional grid with surface clues, buried targets and cell-by-cell digging; keep clues consistently related to distance.
prototype.pitfall: Without a consistent link between clues and rewards, players revert to digging everywhere.
prototype.test: After one example, can players identify a promising location in a new area and explain the clue?

mechanics.name: Dismantling for salvage
mechanics.summary: Turn useful objects into materials, gaining resources while losing infrastructure.
mechanics.rules: Players dismantle furniture, structures or abandoned equipment for partial materials. Dismantling takes time and removes the object, requiring a comparison of immediate needs and future utility.
loop: Compare materials with its current use
decisions: Strip shelter furniture for fuel at the cost of future utility?
Keep a facility for later or salvage it to meet an urgent need?

parameters.name: Recovery fraction
parameters.effect: High recovery encourages relocation; low recovery makes demolition consequential.

parameters.name: Dismantling duration
parameters.effect: Long tasks expose players to weather and enemies; instant salvage favors building convenience.

cases.implementation: Furniture, clothing and other objects can be harvested for materials such as wood or cloth; some require tools and time while survival pressures continue.
Hammers destroy many structures and recover part of their materials, removing the original function and supporting relocation or camp redesign.

mechanics.contrast: The Long Dark emphasizes finite environmental stocks and emergencies; DST integrates recovery with player construction and relocation.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: shipwreck doors yield steel, but removing one opens a monster route and changes level safety.

walkthrough.setup: A shelter has a usable bed, but you urgently need wood to repair the door.
walkthrough.action: Check other salvage first, considering the bed only if materials remain insufficient.
walkthrough.result: Salvaged material repairs the door, while the dismantled object’s function disappears.
walkthrough.next: After the emergency, restore the lost sleeping or storage function.

prototype.firstStep: Use three functional objects, fixed salvage yields and one urgent material demand; skip debris physics.
prototype.pitfall: If every salvage object is useless rubbish, the choice becomes a cleanup chore; retain some meaningful functions.
prototype.test: When short of material, do players weigh future utility instead of choosing only the highest yield?

mechanics.name: Revisiting renewable forage
mechanics.summary: Remember when resources return and turn the map into a timed harvesting route.
mechanics.rules: Wild resources regenerate under specific rules after collection, with locations or spawn areas that can be learned. Players schedule revisits around regrowth and travel costs, avoiding empty trips or missed seasonal abundance.
decisions: Follow a reliable circuit or explore for better spots?
Collect a small amount now or wait for several locations to replenish?

parameters.name: Regrowth interval
parameters.effect: Fixed cycles support planning; variable cycles require redundant routes.

parameters.name: Season dependence
parameters.effect: Strong seasonality encourages route changes and reserves; year-round respawns support steady routines.

cases.implementation: Berry bushes need time to regrow after picking, with seasonal conditions affecting production; wild or transplanted bushes can support supply routes.
Forage appears by season and area, supporting collection circuits; individual items do not all respawn at the same exact location on a fixed timer.

mechanics.contrast: DST offers persistent, memorable nodes; Stardew emphasizes checking areas and seasonal forage varieties.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: traders arrive every three days while fruit ripens every two, making route timing determine freshness at sale.

walkthrough.setup: Three forest gathering spots regenerate at different times; one was harvested yesterday.
walkthrough.action: Visit the two replenished spots and leave the third for tomorrow’s route.
walkthrough.result: You avoid an empty trip, and the log updates the next availability.
walkthrough.next: Adjust the circuit around new tasks instead of following it automatically.

prototype.firstStep: Use three map nodes with different regeneration periods and travel costs, plus a simple last-visit log.
prototype.pitfall: Identical cycles and yields become daily check-ins; introduce interacting route and timing choices.
prototype.test: When one location’s cycle changes, do players revise the visit order and avoid empty trips?

mechanics.name: Depth-targeted mining
mechanics.summary: Deeper is not always better; first decide which material you need.
mechanics.rules: Depths and strata differ in resource distribution and hazards. Players choose a target layer based on material needs, then mine within time, supply and return constraints; geological knowledge makes depth a choice rather than automatic progress.
decisions: Go deep for rare ore or finish a current upgrade in shallower layers?
Will searching for the next level distract from needed materials here?

parameters.name: Distribution overlap
parameters.effect: Low overlap rewards geological knowledge; broad overlap supports opportunistic exploration.

parameters.name: Return convenience
parameters.effect: Fast return reduces deep-mining risk; long exits require larger reserves.

cases.implementation: Mine floor bands differ in ores and enemies; unlocked elevator floors allow targeted return trips for materials such as copper, iron or gold.
Resource distributions vary across underground layers and biomes, with additional generation conditions for Hardmode ores; players choose regions suited to their target.

mechanics.contrast: Stardew uses numbered floors and elevators; Terraria asks players to learn depth and build routes through continuous terrain.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a mine elevator supports only three stops, selected around current crafting plans and costly to relocate.

walkthrough.setup: You need copper for an upgrade; shallow layers contain copper while deeper, pricier deposits are mostly iron.
walkthrough.action: Stay shallow to gather copper, postponing the search for a deeper entrance.
walkthrough.result: The trip fills the recipe gap and saves the supplies needed to return from deeper layers.
walkthrough.next: After upgrading, choose a layer based on the next material requirement.

prototype.firstStep: Use a three-layer selection screen showing resources, danger and return cost, driven by a target recipe.
prototype.pitfall: If deeper layers are superior for every goal, layer choice disappears; preserve distinct resource destinations.
prototype.test: When the recipe changes from copper to iron, do players change layers rather than always seeking maximum depth?

mechanics.name: Drafting rewards and skipping
mechanics.summary: Choose a reward card after a win, or keep the deck consistent by taking none.
mechanics.rules: After an encounter, offer a few cards and let the player take one or skip. A useful addition also occupies future draws, so its value becomes clear in the next fight.
loop: Test it in the next encounter
decisions: Do you need defense now, or are you merely tempted by another attack?
Take a speculative card, or preserve reliable draws?

parameters.name: Offer size
parameters.effect: More options improve access but can make builds converge.

parameters.name: Starting deck size
parameters.effect: An addition changes a small deck more strongly.

cases.implementation: Standard combat rewards offer one of three cards, with an option to skip.
Post-battle drafts add units or spells, whose usefulness depends on the train’s existing formation.

mechanics.contrast: Slay the Spire develops a character’s card plan; Monster Train also asks how recruits fit its floors.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: Offer three fishing-technique cards after each contest segment, with skipping allowed.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: a ten-card deck has one defense card before an aggressive encounter.
walkthrough.action: The offer contains two attacks and a shield; choose the shield.
walkthrough.result: The deck now has eleven cards, including two defenses.
walkthrough.next: Check whether defense arrives in time before adding another card.

prototype.firstStep: Build a six-card starter deck, six reward types and three fixed encounters, including a skip button.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid a hundred-card pool before the offers produce meaningful trade-offs.
prototype.test: Players can explain one pick and one skip without always choosing rarity.

mechanics.name: Investing in existing cards
mechanics.summary: Improve a card you already own instead of enlarging the deck.
mechanics.rules: Spend money, a rest opportunity or materials to improve an owned card. Limited upgrades make reliability matter: an improvement pays off each time that card is drawn.
decisions: Improve damage, or reduce a cost to make whole turns work?
Upgrade now, or spend that stop recovering health?

parameters.name: Upgrade impact
parameters.effect: Small gains accumulate; cost changes can reshape combinations.

parameters.name: Upgrade limit
parameters.effect: Per-card limits encourage investment across different roles.

cases.implementation: Smith at a rest site upgrades a card, normally competing with healing for that visit.
Shops sell unit or spell upgrades, with slots limiting investments on one card.

mechanics.contrast: The first trades improvement against immediate recovery; the second emphasizes paid upgrades and slot allocation.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: Give traveling merchants different upgrade prices so players choose between improving now and waiting.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: Fireball costs two energy out of a three-energy turn.
walkthrough.action: Spend the upgrade to reduce Fireball’s cost to one.
walkthrough.result: The next draw allows Fireball plus two other one-cost cards.
walkthrough.next: Now look for cards that exploit the freed energy.

prototype.firstStep: Use four cards with one upgrade each and compare them across two encounters.
prototype.pitfall: Random affixes and layered upgrades can hide what the investment actually changed.
prototype.test: Players predict an extra action before upgrading and see it happen afterward.

mechanics.name: Powerful cards spent for the fight
mechanics.summary: Take a powerful effect now, losing access to that card for the rest of the fight.
mechanics.rules: A marked card leaves the combat cycle when played instead of returning with the discard pile. The player decides whether the present threat warrants spending it; ordinary copies return for the next fight.
loop: Decide whether to spend the card
decisions: Survive now, or save it for the announced boss attack?
A spent utility card thins the cycle, but will you need it later?

parameters.name: One-use strength
parameters.effect: Stronger effects rescue bad turns but can overshadow reusable cards.

parameters.name: Expected fight length
parameters.effect: Longer fights make the lost reuse more costly.

cases.implementation: Exhaust removes a card from the ordinary cycle for this combat; some effects exhaust other cards too.
Spells with Consume are spent for the battle instead of cycling like ordinary discarded spells.

mechanics.contrast: Slay the Spire can build reactions around exhausting other cards; Monster Train places spent spells inside multi-wave defense.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: Save a one-use shock for the turn an enemy approaches a posture break.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: an enemy threatens ten damage; you hold three-block and one-use ten-block cards.
walkthrough.action: Play the ten-block card.
walkthrough.result: The attack is blocked and the card leaves the combat cycle.
walkthrough.next: Rely on ordinary defense or end the fight quickly.

prototype.firstStep: Implement draw, discard and exhausted piles plus one compelling emergency card.
prototype.pitfall: Do not present permanent deletion and combat exhaustion with the same label.
prototype.test: Players know when the card returns and sometimes save it for a future threat.

mechanics.name: Choosing guaranteed opening cards
mechanics.summary: Guarantee an essential setup card at the start of a fight.
mechanics.rules: Give a few cards guaranteed access in the opening hand or a special opening phase. Before battle, choose which setup step deserves certainty and pay with a hand slot, money or a scarce marker.
decisions: Guarantee safety or guarantee the engine that builds an advantage?
Will a setup-heavy opening still contain immediate answers?

parameters.name: Guaranteed-card count
parameters.effect: Too many guaranteed cards turn openings into a fixed script.

parameters.name: Opening action cost
parameters.effect: Guaranteed drawing is much weaker than guaranteed free deployment.

cases.implementation: Innate puts a card in the opening hand, occupying a normal opening draw slot.
Crowned cards appear in the opening phase and can be played before normal turns without spending a turn.

mechanics.contrast: Innate primarily fixes access; crowns also change timing by allowing deployment before normal turns.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: Guarantee one automation card at setup, then let conditions govern when it activates.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: an eight-card deck contains one generator required by other machines.
walkthrough.action: Assign the only opening marker to the generator.
walkthrough.result: The generator is available on turn one, replacing one random draw.
walkthrough.next: Choose the production plan from subsequent machine draws.

prototype.firstStep: Use eight cards and one movable opening marker across three test openings.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid adding free play, bonus draws and full ordering at once.
prototype.test: Players notice greater reliability and identify the opening option it displaced.

mechanics.name: Selective discarding and redrawing
mechanics.summary: Keep a promising combination and spend limited redraws to complete it.
mechanics.rules: Select unwanted cards, discard them and draw replacements according to the effect. Limited uses or costs prevent endless searching, and discarding may itself trigger rewards.
decisions: Chase a nearly complete combination or accept a smaller reliable result?
Use the last redraw now or save it for a worse hand?

parameters.name: Discard size
parameters.effect: Larger redraws make specific combinations easier to find.

parameters.name: Redraw budget
parameters.effect: Smaller budgets sharpen the trade-off between current gain and future insurance.

cases.implementation: Players spend discards to replace selected cards and pursue a better poker hand.
Prepared draws and then discards cards to filter the hand; discarding can interact with other card conditions.

mechanics.contrast: Balatro provides a round-level discard budget; Slay the Spire usually grants filtering through particular cards.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: Allow technique-card redraws before fishing, with each redraw advancing the fish’s departure timer.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: your hand has three red cards and two other colors, with one redraw left.
walkthrough.action: Keep the three red cards and redraw the other two.
walkthrough.result: Draw a red and a blue, creating four reds with no redraw left.
walkthrough.next: Choose a scoring target this hand can actually reach.

prototype.firstStep: Prototype three colors, a four-of-one-color target and two redraws per round.
prototype.pitfall: Hold off on discard-trigger bonuses until redraw decisions work alone.
prototype.test: Players keep useful subsets and explain why they stop chasing.

mechanics.name: Copying an invested card
mechanics.summary: A duplicate can multiply the value of upgrades already invested in a card.
mechanics.rules: At a scarce opportunity, copy an owned card with the properties the game preserves. Duplication increases access and can multiply earlier upgrades, while still adding deck size and play costs.
decisions: Copy the biggest attack or the unique card that starts the engine?
Upgrade before copying, or duplicate now to survive the next encounter?

parameters.name: Copied properties
parameters.effect: Preserving upgrades makes earlier concentrated investment more valuable.

parameters.name: Duplication frequency
parameters.effect: Frequent copying encourages repetitive decks and exposes cost or coverage problems.

cases.implementation: Dolly’s Mirror copies a chosen card on acquisition, retaining upgrades and relevant accumulated values.
A Hellvent route node duplicates an owned card, excluding the champion.

mechanics.contrast: The first is attached to a particular relic; the second is a route destination that can shape earlier investment.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: Copy an upgraded machine-card blueprint to expand production while inheriting its energy demands.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: a shield card has been upgraded from three block to five.
walkthrough.action: At a duplication node, choose the improved shield.
walkthrough.result: The deck gains a second five-block shield rather than a base copy.
walkthrough.next: Prioritize damage in later rewards to avoid too much defense.

prototype.firstStep: Use six upgradable cards and one copy node, previewing preserved properties.
prototype.pitfall: Prevent copying from recursively triggering another copy.
prototype.test: Players change an upgrade choice because of a future copy and remember its play cost.

mechanics.name: Generating cards during combat
mechanics.summary: Use a card or unit to create extra action cards within the current fight.
mechanics.rules: Some effects add cards absent from the starting deck to the hand or discard pile for this fight. Timing, hand space and play costs matter; created cards may be one-use or remain in the combat cycle.
decisions: Set up a bonus first, or generate attacks immediately to clear the threat?
Does a generator’s output justify the battlefield space it occupies?

parameters.name: Cards per trigger
parameters.effect: More output supports repeated triggers but can clog the hand.

parameters.name: Destination
parameters.effect: Hand insertion gives immediate access; discard insertion delays it.

cases.implementation: Effects such as Blade Dance create zero-cost Shivs that exhaust when played, rather than permanent reward additions.
Vinemother adds Sting spells to the hand through Resolve, turning a deployed unit into a card generator.

mechanics.contrast: Shivs emphasize immediate repeated plays; Vinemother ties ongoing supply to a unit that must survive.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: Have a temporary workshop generate support cards until it collapses, making protection compete with building.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: Prepare Materials creates two free plank cards.
walkthrough.action: Play it, then use one plank on each of two bridge gaps.
walkthrough.result: Two repairs finish this turn, and the plank cards are spent.
walkthrough.next: Next turn requires another generator draw or a different material.

prototype.firstStep: Start with one created card, one generator and a visible hand limit.
prototype.pitfall: Self-generating cards can create infinite chains; forbid them initially.
prototype.test: Players clear hand space before generating and understand that created cards do not persist after battle.

mechanics.name: Ordering effects to change the result
mechanics.summary: Add before multiplying or expose a weakness before attacking: sequence becomes a decision.
mechanics.rules: Resolve effects in a readable sequence rather than simultaneously. Players reorder modifiers or actions so earlier steps prepare later ones, with visible intermediate results.
decisions: Add before multiplying or afterward? Their resolution stage matters.
Will the remaining attacks repay the cost of applying a vulnerability first?

parameters.name: Editable order
parameters.effect: Restricting rearrangement to one stage keeps results easier to predict.

parameters.name: Intermediate feedback
parameters.effect: Showing intermediate values turns trial and error into understanding.

cases.implementation: Within a scoring stage, Jokers generally resolve left to right, so additive and multiplicative bonuses can produce different totals.
Vulnerable increases subsequent attack damage, so applying it before other attacks changes the turn’s output.

mechanics.contrast: Balatro exposes positional ordering of persistent effects; Slay the Spire uses the order of played actions.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: Build a scoring production line where cleaning adds value before a finishing multiplier.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: base multiplier is three, with add-two and multiply-by-two effects.
walkthrough.action: Place add-two before multiply-by-two.
walkthrough.result: The value becomes five, then ten; the reverse order gives eight.
walkthrough.next: When a new modifier arrives, decide where it belongs.

prototype.firstStep: Use three modifier types and a draggable queue showing each intermediate value.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid hidden priority layers whose exceptions undermine learning.
prototype.test: Players predict the difference between two orders before resolving them.

mechanics.name: Two competing uses for one card
mechanics.summary: Put two useful actions on one card so using one sacrifices the other.
mechanics.rules: Each card offers competing uses, such as shooting versus movement or attacking versus defending. Choosing one spends or defers the other, and encounters should regularly create demand for both.
loop: Cover the missing role with another card
decisions: Shoot an enemy or discard the weapon for traversal?
Is sacrificing a strong attack for movement worth the next turn’s position?

parameters.name: Power gap between uses
parameters.effect: If one use dominates, the choice becomes cosmetic.

parameters.name: Recovery after use
parameters.effect: Permanent loss, rest recovery and normal cycling create different commitment levels.

cases.implementation: Soul Cards function as guns or can be discarded for movement abilities, linking ammunition resources to traversal.
Each mercenary chooses two cards, using the top action of one and the bottom action of the other.
cases.rights: Flaming Fowl Studios / Saber Interactive / Twin Sails Interactive

mechanics.contrast: Neon White makes the trade-off during real-time traversal; Gloomhaven allocates two card halves in turn-based planning.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: Make a fire card either damage enemies or ignite route-opening mechanisms in a compact ruin.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: a wind card can shoot or be discarded to leap a gap.
walkthrough.action: Discard it to cross the gap behind a guard.
walkthrough.result: Position improves, but one shooting resource is gone.
walkthrough.next: Finish with a remaining melee card and seek another traversal resource.

prototype.firstStep: Build one grid room with two card types that each offer attack and movement; test turn-based first.
prototype.pitfall: Fast platforming, complex enemies and a large card pool can obscure the basic trade-off.
prototype.test: Players use the same card differently across layouts and explain the sacrifice.

mechanics.name: Allocating rolled outcomes
mechanics.summary: Roll first, then decide where each available result will do the most good.
mechanics.rules: Roll a pool before assigning results to eligible actions or targets. Requirements may involve numbers, parity or effect types; a limited pool makes even awkward results worth considering.
loop: Resolve and prepare the next roll
decisions: Spend a high roll on damage or reserve it for a demanding utility slot?
Reroll an awkward result or use a costly effect it enables?

parameters.name: Result manipulation budget
parameters.effect: More rerolls and conversions reduce randomness while increasing calculation.

parameters.name: Overlapping requirements
parameters.effect: Trade-offs appear when multiple actions compete for the same kind of result.

cases.implementation: Dice activate equipment slots with conditions such as even values, minimums or maximums.
Dice supply effects such as Purification and Corruption; choosing self or enemy as target changes their consequences.

mechanics.contrast: Dicey Dungeons matches numbers to equipment slots; Astrea assigns effect types to targets rather than merely valuing high rolls.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: Represent ingredient conditions with dice assigned to cutting, boiling or baking, with awkward values usable for preparation.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: roll two, four and six; a shield needs an even number and a heavy strike needs at least five.
walkthrough.action: Assign six to the strike and four to the shield.
walkthrough.result: Both actions work, leaving two for a minor heal.
walkthrough.next: The next roll requires a fresh allocation.

prototype.firstStep: Use three six-sided dice and four items with simple requirements in one encounter.
prototype.pitfall: Start with one manipulation effect; many rerolls, copies and locks can overwhelm the decision.
prototype.test: Players find uses beyond high values and reserve dice for constrained slots.

mechanics.name: Using card patterns as action requirements
mechanics.summary: The same hand can form different patterns, determining which actions become available.
mechanics.rules: Define actions or scoring through patterns such as pairs, suits or sequences. Selecting one group changes what remains for other actions, so the largest pattern is not always the best use.
loop: Assign a group to the current goal
decisions: Use a pair for a modest gain or commit more cards to a stronger effect?
One card completes two patterns: assign it to offense or defense?

parameters.name: Pattern difficulty
parameters.effect: Harder patterns reward planning but require more draw or manipulation support.

parameters.name: Fallback rewards
parameters.effect: Reliable simple patterns keep poor draws from becoming lost turns.

cases.implementation: The played poker hand sets base Chips and Mult before card and Joker effects modify the score.
Standard playing cards power equipment, with larger or stronger hands enabling stronger abilities.

mechanics.contrast: Balatro translates patterns into a score target; Poker Quest uses them as inputs for equipment actions.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: Make contracts require patterns: pairs fill small orders and flushes fill larger ones, consuming the submitted goods cards.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: two sevens and three suited cards can pay for a pair-based shield or a three-suit fireball.
walkthrough.action: One seven overlaps the suited group; spend the pair to defend.
walkthrough.result: Defense succeeds, but the fireball pattern is broken.
walkthrough.next: Check the next draw for a replacement suited card.

prototype.firstStep: Use two suits and two conditions—pair and three suited cards—for attack and defense.
prototype.pitfall: Do not implement every poker hand before legality is clearly communicated.
prototype.test: Players notice overlap and deliberately sacrifice one available pattern.

mechanics.name: Rebuilding around rule-changing passives
mechanics.summary: A passive changes which combinations are valid and which cards are worth keeping.
mechanics.rules: A few passives rewrite a base rule, such as pattern requirements or end-of-turn handling. After acquiring one, reassess the deck and future rewards around the changed rule.
loop: Build a loop around the exception
decisions: Can the new rule pay off now, or does it require several encounters of rebuilding?
Could useful draw effects become hand-clogging under a new retention rule?

parameters.name: Rule-change scope
parameters.effect: One clear exception is easier to understand than several simultaneous rewrites.

parameters.name: Support availability
parameters.effect: An interesting rule without accessible supporting cards remains an empty promise.

cases.implementation: Four Fingers permits four-card straights and flushes, changing hand evaluation and discard targets.
Runic Pyramid prevents the usual end-turn hand discard, enabling multi-turn setup while the hand limit still matters; it is not the Retain keyword.

mechanics.contrast: One relaxes pattern requirements; the other changes when cards leave the hand, reshaping draw and cost management.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: A passive lets storage items count as adjacent across one empty tile, prompting a new packing arrangement.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: an altar requires five matching colors, and the player often reaches only four.
walkthrough.action: Choose a passive reducing that requirement to four.
walkthrough.result: A previously invalid hand now activates the altar.
walkthrough.next: Future rewards can support altar payoffs instead of only adding more draw.

prototype.firstStep: Implement one base rule and one exception so the same hand can be compared before and after acquisition.
prototype.pitfall: Do not label ordinary damage bonuses rule changes; alter at least one legal action.
prototype.test: Players change the next card choice and explain what became possible.

mechanics.name: Communicating split information
mechanics.summary: One player sees the situation and another holds the clues; clear descriptions connect them.
mechanics.rules: Split essential information between players who cannot directly inspect each other’s view. One describes symbols or states, another interprets them, and the result becomes the next message.
decisions: Which description—color, shape or position—removes ambiguity first?
Try an uncertain instruction or spend time confirming it?

parameters.name: Shared information
parameters.effect: Some shared reference points aid communication; none can reduce it to guessing words.

parameters.name: Error cost
parameters.effect: Light penalties permit experiments; heavy penalties encourage confirmation.

cases.implementation: The defuser sees the bomb while experts hold its manual without seeing it, linking module features to instructions through speech.
Separated inside a castle, two players use walkie-talkies to describe their clues and solve cooperative puzzles.

mechanics.contrast: The first separates operation from rule lookup; the second joins clues from different spaces.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: one player sees inscriptions and another has a partial dictionary; each solved door expands their shared vocabulary.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: A sees three lights; B has a note saying red-blue-red means left, and they cannot look across.
walkthrough.action: A reports the order; B repeats it before asking A to press left.
walkthrough.result: The door opens; A reports success, confirming their terminology worked.
walkthrough.next: The next door uses shapes, so they agree on descriptions before trying again.

prototype.firstStep: Start with two concealed sheets and three symbol puzzles: a scene sheet and a rule sheet.
prototype.pitfall: Remove descriptions only the author understands before adding puzzles; networking and voice software are unnecessary for the first version.
prototype.test: After swapping roles, new testers can solve a puzzle by asking questions and identify where a misunderstanding occurred.

mechanics.name: Hidden roles and convincing behavior
mechanics.summary: Players with opposing goals share a space, balancing progress against looking suspicious.
mechanics.rules: Assign secret roles and goals. Some players pursue shared tasks while saboteurs blend in through similar appearances and behavior; sightings, disappearances and task changes create evidence.
decisions: Working alone is efficient but leaves no witness; should you travel with someone?
Act against the group now or first build trust by helping?

parameters.name: Role differences
parameters.effect: More abilities make behavior harder to interpret and increase learning effort.

parameters.name: Observable evidence
parameters.effect: Partial evidence supports discussion; complete visibility leaves little room for deception.

cases.implementation: Impostors can pretend to do tasks, sabotage and eliminate crewmates, who seek to complete tasks or identify the impostors.
Geese perform tasks and seek ducks, while ducks deceive and sabotage. Neutral roles have their own secret goals, so unusual behavior can have several causes.

mechanics.contrast: Among Us offers an accessible basic conflict; Goose Goose Duck adds more explanations through neutral goals.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: reveal movement logs but hide each player’s target item, making detours meaningful evidence.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: four players repair three machines, but one secretly wants the repair to fail.
walkthrough.action: The saboteur helps repair one machine, then disables another while alone.
walkthrough.result: The team sees a stopped machine but knows only who last left the room.
walkthrough.next: The saboteur explains their route while the others choose whom to watch and resume repairs.

prototype.firstStep: Use four role cards, three task tokens and a moderator who records paper turns.
prototype.pitfall: Check that deception leaves readable clues before adding many roles that can explain away every anomaly.
prototype.test: Testers can suspect someone for a specific action, while the saboteur has at least one plausible cover choice.

mechanics.name: Discussion, evidence and voting
mechanics.summary: Turn partial individual observations into a decision whose consequences affect the group.
mechanics.rules: An event opens discussion: players share observations, challenge inconsistencies and vote on a suspect or defer action. The outcome changes the group and gives remaining players a reason to reassess earlier claims.
decisions: Follow the majority with weak evidence or explain why you disagree?
Name a suspect first or give a checkable time and place?

parameters.name: Discussion duration
parameters.effect: Too short rewards interruption; too long invites repetition. Allow an account and a follow-up.

parameters.name: Outcome disclosure
parameters.effect: Revealed roles provide quick correction; concealed roles preserve uncertainty.

cases.implementation: Players report bodies or call emergency meetings, discuss suspects and vote to eject someone.
Geese report bodies and vote out ducks; varied roles and neutral goals complicate the interpretation of testimony.

mechanics.contrast: Both convert private observations into group action; larger role sets make separating observation from interpretation especially useful.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: give each player a fragment of a crime scene and vote on which evidence box to open, spending an investigation chance on mistakes.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: one of four people broke a machine. A saw B leave the room; C saw D carrying tools.
walkthrough.action: They establish the order of events: D fetched tools after the alarm, so they vote for B.
walkthrough.result: B’s role is revealed, showing which inferences held and which accounts may mislead.
walkthrough.next: Carry verified facts into the next incident rather than restarting the argument.

prototype.firstStep: Run three short cases with four different accounts, timed discussion and paper ballots.
prototype.pitfall: First ensure evidence changes votes; elaborate speaking rules, voice chat and matchmaking can hide a weak discussion loop.
prototype.test: At least one tester changes a vote because of new evidence and can name the evidence.

mechanics.name: Reviving a downed teammate
mechanics.summary: When an ally falls, trade immediate safety for restoring a teammate.
mechanics.rules: Depleted health causes a downed state before removal. A teammate must approach and spend uninterrupted time reviving while threats continue; success restores team capacity, but another casualty deepens the crisis.
decisions: Revive immediately or first remove a threat that could interrupt it?
Save a defensive resource or spend it to create a rescue window?

parameters.name: Revive duration
parameters.effect: Longer duration increases the value of cover and positioning.

parameters.name: Downed waiting limit
parameters.effect: A deadline creates urgency; no deadline allows stabilization first.

cases.implementation: A teammate must stand close to an incapacitated dwarf and hold interaction; completion restores them with part of their health.
cases.rights: Ghost Ship Games / Coffee Stain Publishing

cases.implementation: In Adventure, a fallen pirate briefly waits as a ghost for a crewmate to revive them, or offers their soul to travel to the Ferry.

mechanics.contrast: Deep Rock Galactic emphasizes reaching and completing the revive; Sea of Thieves also lets the fallen player choose waiting or the death route.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: let players drag downed allies into cover before committing time to revival.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: A falls in a doorway; B has a three-second shield and revival takes two seconds.
walkthrough.action: B shields the doorway, then stands beside A and holds revive.
walkthrough.result: A gets up, and both retreat before the shield expires.
walkthrough.next: Before the next wave, they spread out to avoid falling together in the doorway.

prototype.firstStep: Build two local players, one moving threat, a downed state and an interruptible two-second revive bar.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid a full shooter and class system initially; make failed rescues understandable first.
prototype.test: Testers create a safe window for dangerous rescues instead of always holding revive immediately.

mechanics.name: Crew a shared vehicle
mechanics.summary: A shared vessel needs steering, defense and maintenance, so the crew keeps reallocating jobs.
mechanics.rules: Players share a vehicle’s movement and damage state while operating different functions. When stations or urgent jobs outnumber the crew, they must switch roles; decisions at one station change the others’ situation.
decisions: Keep steering around danger or leave the helm to repair a leak?
Keep specialists at fixed stations or send the nearest player to an urgent job?

parameters.name: Stations per player
parameters.effect: Extra stations create trade-offs; too many overwhelm the crew.

parameters.name: Travel between stations
parameters.effect: Longer travel rewards planning and combining nearby jobs.

cases.implementation: Players run around one spaceship to operate its turrets, lasers, shields and thrusters together.
Crews divide steering, navigation, sail handling and battle readiness, then repair and bail when things go wrong.

mechanics.contrast: The first presents compact stations in a cutaway; the second spreads work across a walkable ship, with sailing and damage control competing for crew time.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: let players place submarine stations; short paths speed role changes but may concentrate hazards.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: two players crew a ship with helm, gun and repair stations; rocks lie ahead and a leak opens on the right.
walkthrough.action: A steers around the rocks while B abandons the gun to fix the leak.
walkthrough.result: The ship keeps moving and survives, but the enemy goes unchallenged.
walkthrough.next: B returns to the gun after repairs, while A announces the next turn.

prototype.firstStep: Start with a local 2D ship, two characters and three button stations: movement, defense and repair.
prototype.pitfall: Defer ocean simulation, detailed hulls and networking; first test whether the jobs depend on each other.
prototype.test: Two testers call for a role switch and can explain the consequence of leaving one station unattended.

mechanics.name: Move while physically tethered
mechanics.summary: A tether links movement: a partner can pull you upward or be dragged down with you.
mechanics.rules: A limited physical link pulls characters when stretched. Players coordinate positions, jumps and anchors to transfer motion; mistakes can propagate through the same link.
loop: Choose who anchors and who moves
Jump together or swing for momentum
decisions: Jump together or secure one player as an anchor first?
Pull a falling partner immediately or secure yourself first?

parameters.name: Tether length
parameters.effect: Short links require close coordination; long ones enable wider swings but are harder to predict.

parameters.name: Distance lost on a fall
parameters.effect: Large setbacks can turn practice into repeated travel; match them to control difficulty.

cases.implementation: The linked penguins use one partner as a ground or temporary wall anchor so the other can swing across larger gaps.
Players climb while joined by a simulated chain that can wrap around platforms, making positions and jumps interdependent.

mechanics.contrast: Bread & Fred emphasizes anchoring and swinging; Chained Together also makes 3D platform geometry affect the chain’s route.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: replace a grapple anchor with another player, beginning with a fixed-length 2D rope to test shared swinging rhythm.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: a three-meter rope joins A and B; B cannot reach the next platform and A has safe ground behind them.
walkthrough.action: A anchors behind the edge while B swings below it and jumps near the top of the arc.
walkthrough.result: B lands securely and becomes the next anchor for A.
walkthrough.next: They swap roles and apply the method to the next gap.

prototype.firstStep: Build two local 2D characters, three platforms, a fixed-length rope and an explicit anchor action.
prototype.pitfall: Defer rope wrapping and 3D collisions; unstable physics or network delay can make failure hard to understand.
prototype.test: Testers can predict who will be pulled and adjust the anchor or jump order after failure.

mechanics.name: Reach separate controls and synchronize
mechanics.summary: Two separate controls must be active together, making timing matter after everyone reaches position.
mechanics.rules: A goal requires separated conditions to overlap, preventing one player from activating everything at once. Players split up, confirm readiness and coordinate a countdown, signal or sustained hold.
decisions: Hold my control while waiting or start a countdown after both are ready?
Who takes the harder route and who gives the final signal?

parameters.name: Timing tolerance
parameters.effect: Wide tolerance supports communication puzzles; narrow tolerance tests execution.
