parameters.name: Pressure while waiting
parameters.effect: Safe waiting permits planning; ongoing danger makes arrival order matter.

cases.implementation: Co-op chambers include breakers that must be used simultaneously; timer pings help align the two actions.
Reactor Meltdown requires at least two players to hold separate hand scanners simultaneously; one player cannot complete them in sequence.

mechanics.contrast: Portal 2 uses synchronization as a puzzle step; Among Us makes it an emergency inside a group with hidden enemies.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: two players use different portals to reach opposite switches, planning their routes before a shared countdown opens the exit.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: two floor plates on opposite sides must stay pressed together for two seconds.
walkthrough.action: A reaches the left plate and reports readiness; B clears an obstacle to the right, then they count to three.
walkthrough.result: Holding both turns the door light green; if B leaves early, progress resets.
walkthrough.next: After succeeding, they swap routes for another pair at different distances.

prototype.firstStep: Build two local moving squares, two plates and a door that displays overlap time.
prototype.pitfall: Make failure visible before adding devices: distinguish wrong position, poor synchronization and insufficient hold time.
prototype.test: After one failure, testers identify the missing condition and succeed using a countdown or waiting.

mechanics.name: Combine different character abilities
mechanics.summary: Different strengths make the order of teamwork more important than individual power.
mechanics.rules: Give characters distinct tools and let one ability create conditions another can exploit. Players identify the obstacle, choose an order and combine actions; the next obstacle can give a different role the lead.
loop: Choose who sets up the situation
Let the partner use that setup
decisions: Try my tool directly or set up a safer solution for my partner?
Does the team need light, access or protection most urgently?

parameters.name: Ability dependence
parameters.effect: Fully independent tools encourage parallel solo play; total dependence can stall everyone when one player falls behind.

parameters.name: Alternating leadership
parameters.effect: Alternating which role solves the bottleneck prevents one player from remaining a permanent assistant.

cases.implementation: The Scout lights and traverses caves, the Driller reshapes terrain, and the Gunner and Engineer provide different defensive tools; the game encourages combining kits.
cases.rights: Ghost Ship Games / Coffee Stain Publishing

cases.implementation: The wizard conjures boxes and planks, the knight tackles obstacles, and the thief uses rope and arrows; players can switch alone or share roles in co-op.

mechanics.contrast: Deep Rock Galactic spreads roles across exploration, terrain and combat; Trine 2 focuses more on alternative solutions to shared platforming obstacles.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: one player builds temporary bridges and another fits through narrow gaps; a switch beyond a gap secures the bridge.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: A can place one box, B can jump two tiles, and a three-tile wall blocks the route.
walkthrough.action: A places the box beside the wall; B jumps from it and lowers a ladder.
walkthrough.result: A climbs the ladder, so both cross while the box remains below.
walkthrough.next: The next obstacle asks B to scout first and A to complete the route.

prototype.firstStep: Build two local characters with one unique ability each and three fixed obstacles that alternate who acts first.
prototype.pitfall: First verify mutual dependence with active participation; class trees and many skills can obscure why cooperation works.
prototype.test: Each player leads one solution and can explain what their partner enabled them to do.

mechanics.name: Temporary alliances and betrayal
mechanics.summary: Players need each other now but pursue their own victory, so cooperation is repeatedly renegotiated.
mechanics.rules: Players pursue separate scores while facing shared danger or a common rival. Help can yield immediate value but strengthen a competitor; promises are not binding, so actions and remaining opportunities determine whether to cooperate, leave or betray.
decisions: Will helping stop the leader merely create a new leader?
Betray for more now, or preserve help for a later danger?

parameters.name: Shared danger
parameters.effect: Weak danger removes the need to cooperate; overwhelming danger leaves little room to betray.

parameters.name: Shared versus personal reward
parameters.effect: Cooperation needs real value and betrayal needs a cost for the decision to matter.

cases.implementation: Players contest the throne through cards, schemes and actions; the developer explicitly describes betrayal, broken alliances and empty promises.
Four adventurers compete for coins, repeatedly deciding whether to continue or escape with loot and whether to cooperate or backstab.

mechanics.contrast: Armello forms temporary interests around the throne; Journey of Greed ties trust to continuing the expedition and leaving with money.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: caravan members fund a bridge together but score their own deliveries, creating room for limited deals, free riding and last-minute competition.

walkthrough.setup: Editorial example: three players each have five coins; the bridge costs three in total and rewards beyond it depend on arrival order.
walkthrough.action: A and B promise one coin each; C agrees to cover the last, while A could withhold payment and pressure the others.
walkthrough.result: All three pay this time, but B notices A’s hesitation and will not advance money next round.
walkthrough.next: At the next bridge, they renegotiate using both current funds and the history of promises kept.

prototype.firstStep: Use a three-player paper score race, three rounds of shared costs and nonbinding spoken deals to test whether alliances emerge.
prototype.pitfall: Defer negotiation AI and elaborate treaties; first make the payoffs support sensible moments for both cooperation and betrayal.
prototype.test: The same group cooperates once and later declines because circumstances changed, explaining both choices.

mechanics.name: Build a longer enemy route
mechanics.summary: Spend limited building resources to make enemies walk farther under fire.
mechanics.rules: Place obstacles or towers on buildable ground to change the route ground enemies take to their objective. Leave a legal route while increasing time spent under fire. A path preview and actual enemy movement reveal whether the layout works.
loop: Place obstacles to extend the route
Revise the layout where enemies escaped
decisions: Spend on a longer route or another weapon? Extra walking time does little without damage.
A single choke saves towers but concentrates the defense into one vulnerable location.

parameters.name: Obstacle cost
parameters.effect: Cheap obstacles encourage route experiments; expensive ones must justify every detour.

parameters.name: Required passage width
parameters.effect: Wide passages reduce extreme detours and emphasize coverage; narrow ones reward maze planning.

cases.implementation: Towers on buildable areas can redirect ground enemies. Detours increase firing time, while a viable route must remain.
Arrange tower bases into a maze, then build towers on selected bases. Players also shoot during combat, so the route affects their own fighting position.

mechanics.contrast: Defense Grid mainly stretches exposure to towers; Sanctum also needs room for the player to move and shoot.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: connect maze walls to modular construction, letting each piece rotate between two routes to repair gaps with few components.

walkthrough.setup: A straight path connects the entrance to the exit, so enemies cross quickly.
walkthrough.action: Use three walls to form a U-turn and place an arrow tower inside it.
walkthrough.result: The same enemies stay in range longer, but the walls consume money for a second tower.
walkthrough.next: Check whether travel time or damage is insufficient before the next investment.

prototype.firstStep: Use a 2D grid with one entrance, one exit and two building types; show the calculated route.
prototype.pitfall: Defer multilevel maps and flying enemies; first make blocked routes give clear feedback.
prototype.test: Can a tester explain why a wall belongs here and reroute after a leak?

mechanics.name: Set automatic target priorities
mechanics.summary: The tower fires automatically; the player decides which threat it addresses first.
mechanics.rules: Choose a target rule, such as the enemy closest to escaping or the strongest enemy. The rule persists until changed; projectiles, target markers and leaks show its effects. Range, attack type and detection still constrain eligible targets.
loop: Inspect the different threats in the line
decisions: Remove small enemies near the exit or keep heavy weapons on a durable target?
All towers focusing one threat can waste damage; splitting them may let it leave their range alive.

parameters.name: Switching cost
parameters.effect: Free switching rewards active direction; a cooldown emphasizes decisions before a wave.

parameters.name: Number of priorities
parameters.effect: Start with a few visibly different rules; many subtle rules raise reading and control costs.

cases.implementation: Many monkey towers switch among First, Last, Close and Strong targeting modes, changing which eligible bloons receive their attacks.
Tower gems offer targeting priorities. Their different effects connect the choice of target with the kind of effect applied.
cases.sourceLabel: Developer instructions — Game in a Bottle on Kongregate

mechanics.contrast: Bloons layers priorities onto tower upgrades; GemCraft also couples them to gem effects, making the recipient of control effects matter.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: let an inventory sensor switch tower priorities: intercept imminent leaks when ammunition is low, then target armored threats after resupply.

walkthrough.setup: One slow large enemy follows three small enemies nearing the exit.
walkthrough.action: Set the rapid-fire tower to the first enemy and leave the cannon on the strongest.
walkthrough.result: Small enemies are intercepted without wasting heavy shots on nearly dead targets.
walkthrough.next: Reassess the division of labor when the next wave is a swarm.

prototype.firstStep: Start with one lane, two towers and two rules: furthest along and highest health.
prototype.pitfall: Make target markers and range explicit, or players may think the tower ignored them.
prototype.test: Can a player predict which enemies escape when only the priorities change?

mechanics.name: Call the next wave early
mechanics.summary: Shorten the rest period to exchange overlapping attacks for a reward.
mechanics.rules: Start the next wave before the current interval ends. Early action grants a reward or pacing advantage, but surviving enemies, skill cooldowns and unfinished defenses remain. Remaining time and enemy counts make the added risk assessable.
loop: Inspect the next wave and remaining interval
Handle overlapping enemies and collect the benefit
decisions: Calling early with one slow enemy left looks attractive, but that enemy may still occupy a critical tower.
Can the early reward immediately buy enough reinforcement to offset the additional pressure?

parameters.name: Reward versus time saved
parameters.effect: A larger reward for earlier calls continually tests how much faster players can go; a fixed reward is easier to read.

parameters.name: Overlap limit
parameters.effect: Repeated calls allow aggressive play but require clearer warnings about the combined threat.

cases.implementation: Calling a wave early grants bonus gold, creating a trade-off between income, surviving enemies and defensive readiness.
cases.sourceLabel: Community wiki — transcription of in-game tips

cases.implementation: Wave stones allow enemies to be summoned early for rewards and a denser battle pace. Existing gem towers must still handle the combined pressure.
cases.sourceLabel: Community wiki — GemCraft Chasing Shadows talisman properties

mechanics.contrast: Kingdom Rush bonus gold can directly reinforce towers; GemCraft places wave management within a denser gem-upgrade and challenge rhythm.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: an early call provides a short-term loan repayable from that wave, creating debt pressure the player deliberately chooses.

walkthrough.setup: The next wave is 20 seconds away, with two slow enemies remaining.
walkthrough.action: Call early, collect the bonus and immediately build a cheap tower.
walkthrough.result: The waves overlap; the reinforcement either buys time or leaves the player exposed.
walkthrough.next: Use the observed spare capacity to adjust the next call.

prototype.firstStep: Implement two fixed waves, a timer and one early-call reward.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid a button that is always beneficial; overlapping pressure must be real.
prototype.test: Do testers sometimes call early and sometimes wait, with a reason for each?

mechanics.name: Invest by day, defend by night
mechanics.summary: Each safe period asks whether to earn more tomorrow or survive more safely tonight.
mechanics.rules: Separate investment and defense into recognizable phases. During safety, spend on income or protection; during danger, live with those decisions. Surviving economic structures finance the next round, while losses restrict future choices.
loop: Split spending between income and defense
Plan the next day from the result
decisions: If tonight looks barely survivable, should extra money go into tomorrow’s income?
After expansion lengthens the perimeter, can the extra income fund its guards?

parameters.name: Payback period
parameters.effect: Slow payback demands confidence in future survival; rapid payback can snowball.

parameters.name: Attack preview detail
parameters.effect: Knowing enemy routes and types supports planning; limited information encourages reserves.

cases.implementation: Build by day and defend alongside troops at night. Economic buildings such as houses and mines provide morning income if they survive.
The monarch spends coins on recruits, tools and walls. Nightly Greed attacks test the expansion and recruitment decisions made during the day.

mechanics.contrast: Thronefall makes each night a concentrated defense test; Kingdom also makes recruitment and expansion depend on travel across a side-view map.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: crops mature during daytime settlement but need workers to harvest, creating a choice between securing food and repairing walls.

walkthrough.setup: You have eight coins: wall repair costs four, a new field costs six.
walkthrough.action: Expecting a light attack, buy the field and make only a minimal repair at the weak point.
walkthrough.result: If the field survives, tomorrow’s income increases; a breached wall can destroy the investment.
walkthrough.next: Reallocate the next day’s budget after seeing the damage.

prototype.firstStep: Use one fixed map, one income building, one wall and three night attacks to test investment choices.
prototype.pitfall: Defer large-map expansion; show which surviving building generated each payment.
prototype.test: Do upcoming threats change spending, or does the same purchase order always win?

mechanics.name: Move a defender to the breach
mechanics.summary: When fixed defenses cannot cover everything, the player becomes a mobile reserve.
mechanics.rules: Automatic defenses keep working while the player controls a mobile character who can attack or intercept. Choose which entrance to reinforce, paying travel time and leaving another lane unsupported. Leaks, damaged structures and character state show the cost.
loop: Identify the lane likely to fail first
Move to the breach and intervene
Rotate elsewhere or retreat to safety
decisions: Save a collapsing tower or intercept enemies already past it?
Personal intervention saves construction costs but makes safety depend on continued attention.

parameters.name: Travel speed
parameters.effect: Slow travel makes lane changes commitments; fast travel emphasizes frequent emergency response.

parameters.name: Player versus tower contribution
parameters.effect: An overpowering character undermines layouts; an ineffective one makes intervention feel pointless.

cases.implementation: The player fights as the king and directs troops during night battles, adding a mobile layer beyond fixed towers and walls.
While towers attack automatically, players fight with first-person weapons and can temporarily cover weaknesses in their tower arrangement.

mechanics.contrast: Thronefall emphasizes top-down lane rotation and local intervention; Sanctum adds aiming and shooting, putting more weight on individual execution.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: use shared attack–defense stamina for the mobile defender; sprinting to a breach leaves less energy to block when arriving.

walkthrough.setup: Both lanes are under attack, with one nearly destroyed tower on the right.
walkthrough.action: Leave the left lane and rush right to intercept its leading enemy.
walkthrough.result: The right stabilizes, but enemies on the left begin advancing faster.
walkthrough.next: Reinforce the left with a building, or keep relying on personal rotations?

prototype.firstStep: Build two short lanes, automatic arrow towers and one movable attacking circle.
prototype.pitfall: Skip elaborate skill trees; make breach warnings readable so players need not stare at two corners.
prototype.test: Can players deliberately choose a lane to save instead of running randomly into success?

mechanics.name: Chain traps into a sequence
mechanics.summary: Slow, gather and damage enemies so several simple traps work as a sequence.
mechanics.rules: Use routes and placement to determine the order in which enemies encounter effects. Slowing increases exposure, pushing changes position and damage traps finish enemies. Budget, recharge time and trigger areas constrain layouts; actual trigger order reveals whether the sequence works.
loop: Find a narrow route enemies must cross
Adjust spacing or repair a missing link
decisions: Adjacent traps combine easily but may recharge together and let later enemies pass.
Push first or slow first? The order can move an enemy out of the intended damage zone.

parameters.name: Trigger interval
parameters.effect: Long intervals require queue management; short intervals emphasize total damage and cost.

parameters.name: Displacement strength
parameters.effect: Stronger pushes exploit the environment but may send enemies beyond the next trap.

cases.implementation: Players place varied traps and fight directly, combining slowing, displacement and damage to kill orcs; combinations depend on the effects enemies actually encounter.
Place damaging and physical traps in a dungeon, combining force, terrain and enemy routes rather than only stacking damage towers beside a path.

mechanics.contrast: Orcs Must Die! 3 lets the player intervene directly; Dungeon Warfare puts more emphasis on top-down trap placement and physical consequences.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: trigger a push mechanism only when a sensor detects a group, preventing a valuable trap from firing on one enemy.

walkthrough.setup: Enemies cross a flame trap separately, and later enemies pass while it recharges.
walkthrough.action: Add a slowing zone first so a group enters the flame area together.
walkthrough.result: One burst hits more targets, but a queue now forms behind the slow zone.
walkthrough.next: Check whether the next burst catches the queue and adjust spacing if necessary.

prototype.firstStep: Use one route and three traps—slow, push and area damage—in a repeatable short wave.
prototype.pitfall: Start with simple 2D collisions; many rigid bodies and network synchronization greatly increase debugging cost.
prototype.test: Can testers reliably change the outcome of the same wave by adjusting order or spacing?

mechanics.name: Prepare answers to enemy resistances
mechanics.summary: High damage can still be useless; first identify what kind of answer the enemy requires.
mechanics.rules: Enemies have armor, damage resistance, concealment or flight that reduces or prevents some attacks. Read the incoming threats and provide defenses that can detect, hit and meaningfully damage them. Hit feedback and leaks expose missing answers.
loop: Check the result against actual hits
decisions: Buy a dedicated tower for a few special enemies or broaden an existing tower with an upgrade?
One damage type may be efficient now but leave the entire lane ineffective against the next wave.

parameters.name: Resistance strength
parameters.effect: Immunity creates a clear gate; partial resistance allows brute force at greater cost but weakens the counter relationship.

parameters.name: Preview lead time
parameters.effect: Early previews allow preparation; surprise threats demand emergency reserves.

cases.implementation: Lead and camo bloons require different answers: some basic attacks cannot pop lead, while towers without camo detection cannot normally target camo bloons.
Armor reduces physical attacks such as arrows, while magic resistance reduces magical attacks. Players mix archers, mages and other tower roles to handle waves with different resistances.

mechanics.contrast: Bloons often uses explicit detection and popping conditions; Kingdom Rush also uses damage reduction to divide enemy roles among towers.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: apply identification to enemy resistance: use a cheap probe attack before committing to a defensive damage type.

walkthrough.setup: The next wave includes metal-shelled enemies, but both current towers fire ordinary darts.
walkthrough.action: Spend the reserve on an attack capable of breaking the shell.
walkthrough.result: The counter breaks protection while the other towers handle ordinary targets.
walkthrough.next: If the next wave is concealed, check detection instead of merely buying more shell damage.

prototype.firstStep: Start with two enemies and two attacks, using clear icons for one resistance relationship.
prototype.pitfall: Do not stack numerous colors, armors and statuses; first make one ineffective attack understandable.
prototype.test: Can players identify the missing counter instead of assuming the damage system is broken?

mechanics.name: Upgrade deeply or build wider
mechanics.summary: Spend the same money on a stronger position or on coverage somewhere else.
mechanics.rules: Tower positions, coverage and money are limited, so divide resources between construction and upgrades. Upgrading improves an existing position; a new tower adds coverage or another role. Enemy types and routes determine which investment helps, and each wave tests the choice.
loop: Check whether coverage or damage improved
decisions: A high-level tower at a good spot may fire constantly, but concentrating funds can neglect a new route.
A cheap tower may stabilize the current wave, while saving for an upgrade may serve later waves better.

parameters.name: Upgrade efficiency curve
parameters.effect: More efficient higher tiers encourage concentration; diminishing returns encourage wider layouts.

parameters.name: Number of useful positions
parameters.effect: Scarce strong positions increase the value of upgrades; abundant positions increase the importance of expansion.

cases.implementation: Towers occupy designated spots and can be upgraded into specialized forms. Changing the tower or its upgrades at one spot changes its defensive role.
cases.sourceLabel: Official press kit — Ironhide Game Studio

cases.implementation: Players can construct towers or upgrade existing ones. Buildable areas and enemy paths make each investment a choice about both damage and position.

mechanics.contrast: Kingdom Rush adds specialization to fixed tower spots; Defense Grid also connects new tower positions to the organization of ground routes.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: let players borrow to upgrade a tower early, then deduct a repayment after every wave. They must judge whether the upgrade protects enough rewards and still leaves cash to reinforce the next wave.

walkthrough.setup: One tower always has a target, while a side route occasionally leaks fast enemies.
walkthrough.action: Skip one upgrade on the main tower and add a cheap tower on the side route.
walkthrough.result: Total damage rises only slightly, but the previously uncovered segment gains an interception point.
walkthrough.next: After stabilizing the side route, invest later income in the main tower.

prototype.firstStep: Use three fixed tower spots and two upgrade tiers; send one wave down the main route and another down a branch.
prototype.pitfall: Do not begin with dozens of towers; make both spending options useful in different situations.
prototype.test: Can two enemy schedules make upgrading and building each a reasonable answer?

mechanics.name: Keep defensive guns supplied
mechanics.summary: A built turret is not a finished defense: it stops firing when ammunition runs out.
mechanics.rules: Ammo-fed turrets turn stored supplies into attacks. Manufacture, transport and refill those supplies. Dense attacks increase demand, making delivery routes and buffer stocks determine endurance. Ammo counts, congestion and silence reveal bottlenecks.
loop: Refill buffers or repair delivery bottlenecks
decisions: Add another turret or keep existing ones fed? More barrels also empty reserves faster.
A large frontline reserve survives surges but ties up materials that could expand production or improve technology.

parameters.name: Ammo per attack
parameters.effect: High consumption makes sustained defense a logistics problem; low consumption can make supply a one-time setup.

parameters.name: Turret buffer capacity
parameters.effect: Large buffers tolerate brief interruptions; small buffers demand steadier delivery.

cases.implementation: Gun turrets require magazines, supplied manually or continuously through belts and inserters. An empty turret cannot keep shooting.
Some turrets use materials such as copper or graphite as ammunition. Conveyors connect production to the front, and available ammo types can alter attack behavior.

mechanics.contrast: Factorio commonly processes materials into magazines before delivery; some Mindustry turrets consume production materials directly, adding ammo choice to resource allocation.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: route production by-products to emergency ammunition with lower damage, connecting factory blockage and defensive shortages.

walkthrough.setup: Two turrets consume four ammo units per second, but delivery supplies only three.
walkthrough.action: Stock a reserve for the short wave and then improve a delivery segment.
walkthrough.result: The buffer covers the temporary deficit, but a longer attack still drains it.
walkthrough.next: Before adding more turrets, check whether total supply can support them.

prototype.firstStep: Start with one abstract supply line, an inventory counter and one ammo-fed turret; a full factory is unnecessary.
prototype.pitfall: Show the cause of a stoppage before adding ammo types, or players may confuse supply and range problems.
prototype.test: Can players detect a sustained deficit from the inventory trend and fix it before firing stops?

mechanics.name: Exclusive specialization branches
mechanics.summary: At a milestone, commit to one branch of expertise.
mechanics.rules: At a milestone, choose between mutually exclusive paths, such as a higher sale price or more output. The choice changes which later actions pay off; the alternative remains unavailable under the current choice.
decisions: Take an immediate benefit or prepare for a later plan that needs supporting resources?
Deepen an existing strength or use a second specialty to cover a weakness?

parameters.name: Branch exclusivity
parameters.effect: Fewer simultaneous paths make choices more consequential and demand clearer previews.

parameters.name: Milestone timing
parameters.effect: Early choices may be uninformed; late choices delay a distinct identity.

cases.implementation: At skill levels 5 and 10, choose one of two profession bonuses; the earlier choice determines the level-10 branches. These are skill specialties, not a new character identity.
Choose a first mastery at level 2 and optionally a second at level 10. Their combination determines the class and which skill trees are available.

mechanics.contrast: Stardew Valley branches the rewards within a work skill; Grim Dawn combines two combat skill trees to change available tools.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: specialize a shop in premium small batches or cheap volume, then use customer reactions to judge the choice.

walkthrough.setup: Your shop reaches level 3: gain 2 coins per item or make 3 extra items daily.
walkthrough.action: With only 4 daily customers, choose the higher margin.
walkthrough.result: Selling 4 items earns 8 extra coins; capacity is unchanged.
walkthrough.next: Next choose between better products and more customers to exploit the specialty.

prototype.firstStep: Build two exclusive bonuses and one fixed-demand selling round, with a one-round benefit preview.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid a full skill tree while both branches merely grant equivalent money.
prototype.test: Change customer demand and see whether players change their choice for a clear reason.

mechanics.name: Practice-based skill growth
mechanics.summary: Repeated actions build the corresponding skill.
mechanics.rules: Successful actions grant experience to the skill used. Reaching a threshold improves efficiency or unlocks options. Experience cannot simply be assigned elsewhere, so time spent solving the current problem competes with practicing a weak skill.
loop: Use the gain or train elsewhere
decisions: Finish quickly with your strongest skill or practice a weaker approach?
Specialize for efficiency or spread practice to handle more tasks?

parameters.name: Experience trigger
parameters.effect: Rewarding meaningful results discourages empty repetition, but the trigger must be clear.

parameters.name: Skill benefit
parameters.effect: Tiny numeric gains can be obscure; lower costs or new actions are easier to notice.

cases.implementation: Farming, mining, fishing and other activities accumulate their own skill experience, with benefits such as tool proficiency and recipes.

cases.game: The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim Special Edition
cases.implementation: Using a skill develops it, and skill increases also advance character level. Actual choices in combat, stealth or crafting shape the character.

mechanics.contrast: Stardew Valley develops daily work skills; Skyrim also feeds skill increases into character level, linking practice to overall progression.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: workshop orders grant payment and matching craft experience, trading reliable income against practicing a new craft.

walkthrough.setup: Carpentry is at 8/10 experience and sewing at 1/10; you can finish two jobs today.
walkthrough.action: Make a box and gain 2 carpentry experience.
walkthrough.result: Carpentry improves; later wooden items use one less plank.
walkthrough.next: Spend the remaining job on profitable carpentry or sewing practice?

prototype.firstStep: Build two job types, separate experience bars and one visible cost-reduction threshold.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid dozens of skills before each one has an activity worth repeating.
prototype.test: Can players connect an action to a gain and deliberately switch jobs to train?

mechanics.name: Refund and reassign upgrades
mechanics.summary: Keep earned progress but pay to change its allocation.
mechanics.rules: Refund invested points and allocate them to other abilities. A fee, location requirement or limit on what can change makes failed plans recoverable while retaining a cost for switching.
decisions: Pay to switch now or save resources with the current setup?
Fix one weakness or rebuild everything and relearn how the parts work?

parameters.name: Refund cost
parameters.effect: High cost discourages experiments; no cost encourages a tailored setup for every encounter.

parameters.name: Editable choices
parameters.effect: Changing abilities while keeping identity preserves some long-term commitment.

cases.implementation: Pay Withers 100 gold at camp to choose a class again and reassign earned level-up choices; race and background do not change through this service.
A Spirit Guide refunds skill investments for iron bits, letting points be reassigned. Dependent skills must be removed in the required order.

mechanics.contrast: Baldur’s Gate 3 rebuilds class and level choices; Grim Dawn’s skill refunds operate on individual investments and their dependencies.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a craftsperson can pay to change specialties while a loan payment is due, making adaptation compete with cash safety.

walkthrough.setup: All 6 points boost fire; the next enemy is weak to ice, and you have 30 coins.
walkthrough.action: Pay 10 coins to move 3 points into freezing.
walkthrough.result: You now have another damage option but only 20 coins left.
walkthrough.next: Test the new setup before paying for more changes.

prototype.firstStep: Build two three-rank abilities, a fixed enemy and a refund screen that previews the fee.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid rebuilding every identity choice before refunds and dependencies behave clearly.
prototype.test: After failure, can players identify an adjustment and predict the refund and new ability?

mechanics.name: Persistent currency between attempts
mechanics.summary: An unsuccessful attempt can still fund the next one.
mechanics.rules: Attempts award a resource that persists between runs and buys lasting improvements. Alongside winning this run, players pursue a smaller goal: funding a better next start. Temporary and persistent rewards need distinct identities.
decisions: Pursue a win or take the route that funds future attempts?
Buy a small benefit now or save for a more transformative upgrade?

parameters.name: Retention on failure
parameters.effect: Higher retention softens failure but may make deliberately short runs efficient.

parameters.name: Starting advantage
parameters.effect: Large gains trivialize early sections; tiny gains make progress hard to feel.

cases.implementation: Darkness earned during attempts returns to the House and funds lasting Mirror of Night abilities, unlike resources confined to the current escape.
A predecessor’s wealth develops the manor, whose lasting upgrades support subsequent heirs. The playable person changes while family investment continues to matter.

mechanics.contrast: Hades organizes lasting abilities through the Mirror; Rogue Legacy 2 connects successive characters through manor investment. Both turn a failed attempt into longer-term progress.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: random routes offer a shortcut to the finish or a detour with persistent resources, supporting different goals for an attempt.

walkthrough.setup: You have 8 badges; an extra starting heal costs 12.
walkthrough.action: You lose to the boss but retain 4 badges earned on the way.
walkthrough.result: Spend 12 at the hub to start the next attempt with one extra heal.
walkthrough.next: Retry the boss or gather resources for the next upgrade.

prototype.firstStep: Build one short challenge, one persistent currency and two lasting upgrades, with purchases after failure.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid endless upgrade ranks or requiring many runs before the core controls become enjoyable.
prototype.test: After failure, can players name what they retained and choose a goal for the next attempt?

mechanics.name: Choose the next heir
mechanics.summary: Start the next attempt with a different mix of strengths and quirks.
mechanics.rules: When a character’s attempt ends, choose from successors with different classes and traits. Persistent investment remains useful, but each new person changes the immediate approach. The loop selects among candidates rather than breeding traits.
decisions: Choose a familiar class or adapt to an unfamiliar trait?
Select for the current obstacle or for exploring a different route?

parameters.name: Candidate count
parameters.effect: More candidates make unwanted traits easier to avoid but reduce adaptation.

parameters.name: Trait impact
parameters.effect: Stat-only traits can feel similar; movement or perception changes are distinct but need clear explanations.

cases.implementation: After death, a descendant continues, with traits that alter the experience of the castle. This candidate system should not be read as controlled genetic breeding.
After death, the next heir brings a combination of class and traits to the new attempt, supported by the family’s lasting investments.

mechanics.contrast: Both use death as a transition to another person; the sequel further combines distinct class actions with traits, changing how the next attempt plays.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: heirs trade high stamina and slow recovery against a smaller fast-recovering pool; choose for the next enemy’s rhythm.

walkthrough.setup: The last adventurer failed; candidate A has 80 stamina with slow recovery, B has 50 with fast recovery.
walkthrough.action: Choose B to face a guard with frequent attacks.
walkthrough.result: You can only strike once, but a short retreat restores enough stamina to dodge.
walkthrough.next: Afterward, judge whether the next room also suits short exchanges.

prototype.firstStep: Build three fixed candidates, each with one strength and one constraint, followed by the same short level.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid dozens of random traits until combinations that make the level impossible are excluded.
prototype.test: Does changing the character produce a visible change in play rather than just a new name?

mechanics.name: Reset progress for lasting acceleration
mechanics.summary: Trade this cycle’s progress for a faster next cycle.
mechanics.rules: When growth slows, voluntarily reset ordinary resources and facilities in exchange for a lasting reward based on progress. The next cycle starts earlier but grows faster. Decide whether to reset now or push further for a better return.
loop: Replay early stages with a bonus
decisions: Reset for a quick payback or wait to reach a larger reward threshold?
Spend the lasting reward on broad speed or a specialized production route?

parameters.name: Reset reward curve
parameters.effect: Wider reward thresholds make the decision to wait more consequential.

parameters.name: Replay time
parameters.effect: Slow recovery feels punitive; instant recovery makes early purchases irrelevant.

cases.implementation: Ascension resets a production cycle for prestige and heavenly chips, which fund upgrades for later cycles. Players choose when to cash out their current accumulation.
Ascension exchanges current advancement for lasting resources such as Hero Souls while resetting cycle progress such as hero levels; retained benefits accelerate later cycles.

mechanics.contrast: Cookie Clicker repeats a production curve; Clicker Heroes repeats hero upgrades and combat stages. Both exchange a voluntary reset for lasting acceleration.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: reset ordinary shop shelves after a season for a lasting display bonus, encouraging a different layout next season.

walkthrough.setup: The workshop earns 10 coins per minute; resetting grants 1 emblem, or 2 after another 100 coins.
walkthrough.action: Reset now and spend 1 emblem on a permanent production bonus.
walkthrough.result: Machines are cleared, but the first repurchased machine now makes 2 per minute instead of 1.
walkthrough.next: Reach a new threshold faster, then decide when to reset again.

prototype.firstStep: Build three production tiers, one permanent multiplier and a reset preview listing what is lost and retained.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid enormous numbers before the first minutes after reset offer choices beyond repurchasing.
prototype.test: Ask why the player resets now and watch whether the second cycle changes their purchase order.

mechanics.name: Escalating challenge conditions
mechanics.summary: Add another constraint after mastering the base challenge.
mechanics.rules: After completing the base challenge, unlock tougher tiers or choose added restrictions such as less healing or stronger enemies. Familiar content now demands a revised strategy, and the interface states exactly what changed.
decisions: Raise difficulty for a new goal or practice a weakness at a familiar level?
When restrictions are selectable, can the current setup handle fewer supplies or stronger enemies better?

parameters.name: Cumulative restrictions
parameters.effect: Stacked restrictions test overall mastery; independent ones isolate a skill.

parameters.name: Modifier visibility
parameters.effect: A clear start-of-run list makes losses attributable to specific changes.

cases.implementation: Ascension increases difficulty through successive restrictions on the same climbing rules, requiring adaptation to accumulating conditions.
The Pact of Punishment lets players select added conditions and raise Heat, changing enemies or resource constraints through different combinations.

mechanics.contrast: Slay the Spire largely follows fixed cumulative tiers; Hades lets players compose conditions and choose the kind of pressure.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: unlock a half-lighting-fuel challenge for a familiar cave, requiring different supplies and turnaround timing.

walkthrough.setup: You cleared three rooms; the next tier reduces healing from 3 health to 1.
walkthrough.action: Replace a healing-focused item with a shield that blocks one hit.
walkthrough.result: The enemy keeps its familiar rhythm, but mistakes are harder to repair.
walkthrough.next: After winning, add another condition or practice consistency here.

prototype.firstStep: Build a beatable short challenge, then two clearly stated modifiers that can be toggled separately.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid only increasing health; modifiers should change decisions instead of prolonging repetition.
prototype.test: Does enabling a modifier change a preparation or action instead of merely adding repetitions?

mechanics.name: Random choices at level-up
mechanics.summary: Each level offers a small random set that shapes the current build.
mechanics.rules: At an experience threshold, choose one upgrade from a small random set. Offers can strengthen an existing ability or add a new one. The desired option is not guaranteed, creating a tradeoff between immediate relief and a future combination.
decisions: Take defense to survive now or an attack that could complete a later combination?
Strengthen a reliable ability or use a slot for something new?

parameters.name: Number of offers
parameters.effect: More offers support planned growth; fewer require adaptation.

parameters.name: Reroll cost
parameters.effect: Limited rerolls offer recovery while creating a save-or-spend decision.

cases.implementation: Leveling pauses the action and offers weapons or passive abilities to acquire or improve, gradually forming a combination during the run.
Experience earns levels, whose four stat-upgrade offers are resolved after the wave; paid rerolls are available. Growth decisions are concentrated between battles.

mechanics.contrast: Vampire Survivors interrupts combat at level-up; Brotato resolves stat choices between waves, preserving each wave’s continuity.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: offer new tools and upgrades together while allowing only three equipped tools, making existing slots part of the decision.

walkthrough.setup: You have two weapons and one open slot; choose a shield, a new bow or +2 damage to the current sword.
walkthrough.action: Take the bow to handle distant enemies in the next wave.
walkthrough.result: You gain range, but no slot remains for the next new tool.
walkthrough.next: Now favor existing upgrades or seek a way to replace a tool.

prototype.firstStep: Build six upgrade cards, random three-option offers and a short wave that makes effects visible.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid hundreds of upgrades before random sets consistently include useful choices.
prototype.test: Do players choose for the next wave or current weakness rather than always taking the largest number?

mechanics.name: Complete a weapon evolution recipe
mechanics.summary: Keep the required pieces until a weapon can transform.
mechanics.rules: A weapon must reach its required state, be paired with specified items and trigger a fusion to transform. Reserve space for the future combination while surviving with pieces that may be weak alone. Completion should visibly change the attack.
decisions: Take a stronger immediate item or reserve the slot for a recipe component?
Wait for the missing piece or abandon the investment to survive now?

parameters.name: Recipe visibility
parameters.effect: Visible recipes support planning; clues add discovery but can make failed attempts feel wasted.

parameters.name: Value before fusion
parameters.effect: Weak standalone components increase risk before completion and need a clear payoff.

cases.implementation: Many standard evolutions require a fully leveled base weapon, its matching passive item and an eligible chest. Weapon and stage exceptions mean no single recipe rule covers every evolution.
Collaboration weapons combine two compatible max-level weapons at a Golden Anvil, requiring investment in two weapon lines beforehand.

mechanics.contrast: Many Vampire Survivors recipes pair a weapon with a passive and use a chest trigger; HoloCure collaborations fuse two max-level weapons at a Golden Anvil.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: two ordinary weapons fuse into one within a three-slot loadout, freeing space and changing later equipment choices.

walkthrough.setup: You hold a level-3 fire rod; the recipe needs level 4 plus a wind wheel, and one slot remains.
walkthrough.action: Take the wind wheel, then upgrade the rod to level 4.
walkthrough.result: At the forge, they become a fire cyclone whose attack circles instead of traveling straight.
walkthrough.next: Use the freed slot for another recipe after checking the new attack’s blind spots.

prototype.firstStep: Build four components, two fixed recipes and a forge, with a distinct attack path for each result.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid a large recipe catalogue while every result is only a numeric upgrade.
prototype.test: Do players reserve a slot for an incomplete recipe and change positioning after fusion?

mechanics.name: Research prerequisite chains
mechanics.summary: Research is a route through prerequisites, not just a timer.
mechanics.rules: A technology requires specific earlier research plus resources or researcher time. Choose the next worthwhile unlock among competing goals, then use it to improve the economy or settlement and support further research.
loop: Use it to support later research
decisions: Solve today’s problem or work on prerequisites for a long-term goal?
Allocate materials and labor to research or keep current production running?

parameters.name: Prerequisite depth
parameters.effect: Deeper chains reward planning but need a clearly understood payoff.

parameters.name: Shared research costs
parameters.effect: When research and production share inputs, research speed becomes an explicit economic tradeoff.

cases.implementation: Technologies require prerequisites and labs consuming the appropriate science packs. Later research adds pack-production requirements, connecting the research route to factory construction.
Many projects have prerequisites, and colonists working at research benches generate progress. Research competes for time that could go to care, construction or other work.

mechanics.contrast: Factorio emphasizes a continuing material supply; RimWorld emphasizes allocating limited workers. Both gate important unlocks behind earlier research.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: an order due in three days requires dyes before printing; choose immediate paid jobs or invest in the research chain.

walkthrough.setup: You want a cooler, but metalworking is required first; the researcher completes one project daily.
walkthrough.action: Research metalworking today and schedule the cooler for tomorrow.
walkthrough.result: Metal recipes become available now, but food storage still waits a day.
walkthrough.next: Continue toward the cooler or interrupt the plan for urgent defense research?

prototype.firstStep: Build six research nodes, two resources and one researcher; each completion opens a usable production action.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid hundreds of nodes before prerequisites, spending and new output form meaningful interactions.
prototype.test: Can players explain the next missing prerequisite and alter research order because of production pressure?

mechanics.name: Death costs trained abilities
mechanics.summary: Death can cost training as well as possessions.
mechanics.rules: Death reduces trained proficiency, or a successor does not inherit the previous character’s training. Compare the benefit of pushing farther with the cost of retraining. Recovering equipment and recovering abilities are separate concerns.
decisions: Risk a well-trained character or retreat to protect that investment?
Rebuild the former specialty or develop a different way to survive?

parameters.name: Training loss
parameters.effect: Large losses make retreat meaningful but encourage repetitive safe training.

parameters.name: Recovery options
parameters.effect: Recovery offers more agency when retraining can use another route rather than repeat identical actions.

cases.implementation: Death normally reduces skill proficiency; recovering equipment does not restore all training. The penalty’s strength depends on world settings.
cases.rights: Iron Gate AB / Coffee Stain Publishing

cases.implementation: After death, a new character can enter the retained world but does not inherit the previous character’s earned skill experience. Occupation and traits still provide starting skills.

mechanics.contrast: Valheim normally reduces the same character’s proficiency; Project Zomboid ends that character and starts another person’s training.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: tools remain recoverable after death while tool proficiency drops; decide between immediate retrieval and training with a spare.

walkthrough.setup: Climbing proficiency is 10, and a reward lies farther ahead, but stamina is half full.
walkthrough.action: You push on and fall; this example removes 2 proficiency on death.
walkthrough.result: Your gear can be recovered, but climbing proficiency is now 8.
walkthrough.next: Retrain on a safer route or face the challenge with lower proficiency.

prototype.firstStep: Build a safe training route, a risky route and one proficiency value with an explicit death deduction.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid reducing many skills at once; unclear losses create frustration without a useful decision.
prototype.test: Do players sometimes retreat near danger and accurately explain what needs rebuilding after death?

mechanics.name: Progress through learned knowledge
mechanics.summary: The character is unchanged; the player learns an action that was already possible.
mechanics.rules: An obstacle checks no new level or item; it requires knowledge of a rule, timing or action. Explore for clues, form an understanding and return to test it. Once understood, the same route can be completed more directly.
decisions: Keep experimenting here or search elsewhere for an explanation?
Test the current idea now or gather more evidence before a costly attempt?

parameters.name: Distance to clues
parameters.effect: Distant clues require better records and landmarks to connect them to an obstacle.

parameters.name: Cost of testing
parameters.effect: Fast tests encourage hypotheses; long repeats discourage experiments.

cases.implementation: Explore a solar system within a time loop, learning locations, rules and secrets. Understanding persists across loops and makes previously baffling routes actionable.
Collected manual pages teach hidden techniques and secrets that make earlier clues usable. This case concerns those knowledge gates; the game also has equipment and other progression.

mechanics.contrast: Outer Wilds ties understanding to time-loop exploration; some TUNIC secrets tie it to collecting manual pages. Their knowledge gates can be remembered rather than repurchased as abilities.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a map door appears to need a key, but translated writing teaches a knocking rhythm; players who remember it can pass directly next time.

walkthrough.setup: A door has three lights; you have no key or new ability.
walkthrough.action: Elsewhere, decode “one knock for each flash,” then follow the lights at the door.
walkthrough.result: The door opens with no change to inventory or character stats.
walkthrough.next: Remember the rule and look for other mechanisms using the same signals.

prototype.firstStep: Build a three-input mechanism, a distant clue and a return shortcut; all controls are available from the start.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid an arbitrary secret code; the clue should let players explain why the solution works.
prototype.test: Can players return and solve it after reading the clue, then pass directly after a restart?

mechanics.name: Disguise permissions
mechanics.summary: Changing clothes changes where you are allowed to go.
mechanics.rules: Areas decide access and permitted equipment by role. Acquire an outfit and use its permissions to approach a goal; recognizers and forbidden actions can still expose you, with clear feedback explaining why.
loop: Use access to reach the goal
decisions: Detour for a more useful outfit, or use a narrower route with your current role?
If a role grants access but forbids your weapon, leave it behind or find another entrance?

parameters.name: Permission coverage
parameters.effect: Broader access reduces outfit changes; overlapping permissions create route choices.

parameters.name: Recognizer density
parameters.effect: A few consistent recognizers clarify the rule; too many make disguises ineffective.

cases.implementation: Outfits determine access and legal equipment, while specific NPCs recognize impostors; these rules carry over from the trilogy’s first game.
cases.sourceLabel: Official HITMAN (2016) manual; shared trilogy mechanics

cases.game: Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun
cases.implementation: Aiko uses a geisha disguise and conversation to distract enemies; the ability belongs to a specific squad member.

mechanics.contrast: HITMAN lets one character collect permissions; Shadow Tactics makes disguise one squad member’s specialty.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: outfits use equipment slots, so carrying two uniforms means one fewer tool; access plans and loadouts become one decision.

walkthrough.setup: The warehouse admits porters; the office admits clerks.
walkthrough.action: Wear the porter outfit to retrieve an office key, then return to change.
walkthrough.result: You have the key, but the porter outfit still cannot safely cross the office.
walkthrough.next: Decide whether another trip for the clerk outfit is worth it.

prototype.firstStep: Build two rooms, two outfits and one guard; color-code the areas your current role can enter.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid complex NPC memory first; make unlocking a door distinct from being permitted inside.
prototype.test: Ask why the same doorway reacts differently after changing clothes, and watch whether players plan outfit order.

mechanics.name: Sound lures
mechanics.summary: Send a guard toward a sound to open the route you actually want.
mechanics.rules: A thrown object or ability creates a sound that draws nearby guards off patrol. Use the opening to pass, collect something or ambush; make hearing range, responders and investigation duration readable.
decisions: A distant lure may be safer, but will it attract a second guard?
Recover the reusable lure now, or use the brief open route first?

parameters.name: Hearing radius
parameters.effect: A wider radius reaches targets easily but makes selective distraction harder.

parameters.name: Investigation duration
parameters.effect: Duration sets the length of the available action sequence; excessive time removes urgency.

cases.implementation: Coins and remote audio distractions draw nearby NPCs to investigate, moving attention away from a route.
cases.sourceLabel: Official HITMAN (2016) manual; shared trilogy mechanics

cases.implementation: Hector’s whistle draws nearby guards toward him, making his position both the lure location and a source of risk.

mechanics.contrast: Coins place sound elsewhere; a whistle anchors it to the character, requiring an escape or ambush position.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: borrow cast-placement decisions; stones make different sounds on metal, mud and water, so players read surfaces before throwing.

walkthrough.setup: A guard watches the door; an empty room sits to the right.
walkthrough.action: Throw a pebble into the empty room while staying left of the door.
walkthrough.result: The guard turns to investigate, briefly leaving the doorway unwatched.
walkthrough.next: Pass through and decide whether recovering the pebble is worth the risk.

prototype.firstStep: Build one patrolling guard, one throwable pebble and patrol–investigate–return states.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid unexplained random refusal to investigate; first make responder selection and duration consistent.
prototype.test: Can players predict which guard will move and use the opening to get past?

mechanics.name: Moving and hiding bodies
mechanics.summary: Taking down a guard is only half the task; the body still needs a destination.
mechanics.rules: Downed characters remain in the level and can change alert behavior when found. Moving or concealing them costs time and makes escape harder; choosing a destination before a takedown matters.
loop: Move the body out of sight
decisions: Leave the body and save time, or move it before a later patrol arrives?
A nearby hiding spot may pull you away from the exit; is a longer carry worthwhile?

parameters.name: Carry speed
parameters.effect: A larger speed penalty makes takedown location and other guards’ sightlines more important.

parameters.name: Hiding capacity
parameters.effect: Limited capacity spreads takedowns across the level instead of encouraging one dumping spot.

cases.implementation: Incapacitated people can be dragged and placed in suitable containers to prevent passers-by finding them.
cases.sourceLabel: Official HITMAN (2016) manual; shared trilogy mechanics

cases.implementation: Characters can move downed guards into hiding places such as bushes, adding a body-disposal route to the plan.

mechanics.contrast: HITMAN uses explicit containers; Desperados III integrates carrying with overhead sightlines and squad positioning.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: in a rescue mission, carrying a wounded ally fills the weight budget; abandon loot to bring the ally home.

walkthrough.setup: A patrol circles past a staircase beside a bush.
walkthrough.action: Down another guard by the stairs and drag him into the bush.
walkthrough.result: The patrol returns without seeing the body, but carrying made you miss the door opening.
walkthrough.next: Next time lure the target closer to concealment before acting.

prototype.firstStep: Build two guards, one patrol route, a draggable body and one concealment zone.
prototype.pitfall: Do not start with complex body physics and animation; a draggable token can test route costs.
prototype.test: On the second attempt, do players check hiding locations before choosing the takedown spot?

mechanics.name: Queued synchronized actions
mechanics.summary: Queue several characters, then act together against guards watching one another.
mechanics.rules: Assign targets and actions to several characters before one release command. Resolve mutually watching guards together before one can raise an alarm; approach and execution times still matter.
decisions: Release everyone now, or let the distant character get closer first?
Assign the third character to another patrol, or reserve them for a failed plan?

parameters.name: Execution-time difference
parameters.effect: Larger duration differences increase the value of positioning and staggered starts.

parameters.name: Pause while queuing
parameters.effect: Pausing reduces execution pressure; live queuing retains patrol-reading and speed demands.

cases.implementation: Showdown queues actions for coordinated release; it pauses by default, but not on Desperado difficulty.

cases.game: Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun
cases.implementation: Actions for the team can be planned in advance and executed together to resolve situations one character cannot handle alone.

mechanics.contrast: Both compress squad execution into one release; Desperados III also makes planning-time pause a difficulty choice.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: during a kitchen infiltration, one character hands over a tray as another swaps a document; success depends on the handoff timing.

walkthrough.setup: Two guards watch one another; each has an agent hidden behind them.
walkthrough.action: Queue one knockout per agent and release both.
walkthrough.result: Both guards fall before either can react to the other’s takedown.
walkthrough.next: Assign one agent to bodies and another to watch the next patrol.

prototype.firstStep: Start with two agents, two stationary guards, one queued action each and a shared release button.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid long command chains initially; distinguish moving into place from being ready to execute.
prototype.test: Can players explain failure in terms of position, action duration or release timing rather than unresponsive agents?

mechanics.name: Moving through light and shadow
mechanics.summary: Light and shadow tell you where to wait and where to cross quickly.
mechanics.rules: Light changes how easily the character is seen. Wait and observe in darkness, then cross exposed areas; interactive lights can change the safe route. Show clearly whether the character is currently in shadow.
decisions: Take the short exposed route or the longer dark one?
A light can be disabled, but is reaching it riskier than crossing normally?

parameters.name: Detection effect of light
parameters.effect: Too little difference makes lighting cosmetic; too much may make darkness completely safe.

parameters.name: Distance between safe patches
parameters.effect: Larger gaps require better patrol timing and fallback plans.

cases.implementation: The Light Gem reports whether Garrett is in shadow, where he is less likely to be spotted.
The ninja becomes a dark silhouette with red details in shadow and changes appearance in light, making the character the visibility indicator.

mechanics.contrast: Thief uses a dedicated meter; Mark of the Ninja places feedback on the character the player is already watching.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a lamp reveals route markings but exposes the player, creating a switch between reading the route and moving unseen.

walkthrough.setup: Two shadows are separated by a lit corridor that takes two seconds to cross.
walkthrough.action: Wait for the guard to turn, then move between the shadows.
walkthrough.result: Reach darkness before the guard looks back and regain the hidden indicator.
walkthrough.next: The next exposed stretch is longer; look for a light switch first.

prototype.firstStep: Use a 2D map with two dark zones, one lit zone and a turning guard; calculate visibility from zone tags first.
prototype.pitfall: Do not start with realistic lighting; a dark-looking area that counts as lit undermines trust.
prototype.test: With the indicator briefly hidden, can players predict safer positions from the scene?

mechanics.name: Peeking before committing
mechanics.summary: Spend a little time seeing the other side before stepping into it.
mechanics.rules: Doors and corners hide information. Peeking reveals a limited view without fully entering the danger area; it may cost time or action points and does not necessarily reveal every enemy. Check before committing to movement.
decisions: Spend an action to check, or save it and cross immediately?
Is seeing one guard enough, or should you check the blind spot from another angle?

parameters.name: Observation cost
parameters.effect: Low cost helps learning, but cheap complete information can become a routine click at every door.

parameters.name: Reveal coverage
parameters.effect: Partial room coverage preserves the value of a second viewpoint.

cases.implementation: Garrett can look through keyholes and peepholes to inspect the other side before entering.
Peeking costs action points and reveals information before an agent commits to moving into dangerous tiles.

mechanics.contrast: Thief limits a first-person view through an aperture; Invisible, Inc. makes information part of the action-point budget.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: map rooms only after peeking inside, and timestamp observations to remind players patrols may have changed.

walkthrough.setup: You stand beside a closed door with three action points left.
walkthrough.action: Spend one point to peek and see a guard walking away.
walkthrough.result: Entry is safe now, but the remaining two points cannot reach the distant cabinet.
walkthrough.next: Move into cover beyond the door and collect the item next turn.

prototype.firstStep: Build one hidden room and a peek button that reveals a limited area for one action point.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid making peeking mandatory busywork; offer useful alternatives such as waiting, detouring or entering directly.
prototype.test: Do remaining action points change the decision to peek, rather than producing the same click at every door?

mechanics.name: Surveillance control
mechanics.summary: A camera can expose you—or become your own lookout.
mechanics.rules: Security devices watch areas and may record evidence or raise alarms. Bypass, disable or take control at a cost in resources or travel; distinguish new information from the separate benefit of erasing evidence.
loop: Locate the device or control point
Use the new safety or information
decisions: Disable a camera for passage, or invest more to use it for ongoing reconnaissance?
After being recorded, leave with the objective or detour to erase the evidence?

parameters.name: Control coverage
parameters.effect: Controlling more devices per terminal raises its value but can make it the only sensible solution.

parameters.name: Capture cost
parameters.effect: Higher costs make players judge the value of information along the whole route.

cases.implementation: After being recorded, the player can erase surveillance evidence at security equipment; recording affects stealth evaluation.
cases.sourceLabel: Official HITMAN (2016) manual; shared trilogy mechanics

cases.implementation: Cameras are hackable mainframe devices; gaining control turns their coverage into information for the player.

mechanics.contrast: HITMAN emphasizes erasing evidence after exposure; Invisible, Inc. emphasizes converting hostile surveillance into vision.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: connect a captured camera to a conditional switch that turns off a lamp when someone passes, creating a small automated cover system.

walkthrough.setup: A camera watches the safe; a distant terminal can capture it for two power units.
walkthrough.action: Capture it at the terminal, then use its feed to check the guard beyond the door.
walkthrough.result: The safe is no longer under hostile surveillance, and you know when the guard leaves.
walkthrough.next: Save remaining power for the next room instead of capturing irrelevant devices.

prototype.firstStep: Build one camera, one terminal and hostile/player ownership; reuse the same visibility data under either owner.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid a full hacking minigame initially; make ownership visibly change what the player can see.
prototype.test: Can players identify the new information from a captured camera and use it to change their next move?

mechanics.name: Hiding spots and exit timing
mechanics.summary: A hiding spot offers safety in exchange for waiting for a safe exit.
mechanics.rules: Enter a designated cabinet or container to leave ordinary sight, then observe before exiting. Clearly define witnessed entry, occupied spots and available visibility; hiding should not automatically erase a pursuer’s knowledge.
decisions: Hide and wait now, or keep moving through the patrol opening?
With an incomplete view outside, wait another cycle or emerge to scout?

parameters.name: Entry and exit time
parameters.effect: Longer transitions reward planned stops instead of instant escape.

parameters.name: View from inside
parameters.effect: A narrower view makes exiting uncertain; sound or a viewing slit should offer clues.

cases.implementation: Some containers hold bodies and allow 47 to hide; existing occupancy limits the available space.
Hiding spots have separate enter, exit and barge-out controls, allowing a choice of when and how to emerge.

mechanics.contrast: HITMAN connects hiding to container occupancy; Thief offers different ways to leave a hiding spot.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a hiding cabinet has two spaces and a rescued companion occupies one, turning safe stops into limited capacity.

walkthrough.setup: A patrol is about to turn the corner beside an empty cabinet.
walkthrough.action: Enter unseen and watch through the slit as the guard passes.
walkthrough.result: You are safe for now, but have only a brief exit window before the return pass.
walkthrough.next: Exit when the footsteps recede and reach the next obstruction.

prototype.firstStep: Build a cabinet and a back-and-forth patrol; entry disables movement but leaves a small observation window.
prototype.pitfall: Define witnessed entry explicitly so players understand why hiding succeeds or fails.
prototype.test: Do players check patrol timing before exiting rather than treating the cabinet as an unlimited pause button?

mechanics.name: Knockout timers and pinning
mechanics.summary: An unconscious guard may recover: assign someone to hold them, or leave quickly?
mechanics.rules: A nonlethal takedown buys time rather than permanent removal. Guard, restrain or escape before recovery; compare temporary control with the agent time and tools needed to maintain it.
decisions: Pinning extends safety, but does losing an active agent slow the objective?
Spend a limited restraint or accept the risk of recovery in a few turns?

parameters.name: Recovery duration
parameters.effect: Short timers reward momentum; long timers resemble permanent removal and weaken pinning choices.

parameters.name: Cost of maintaining control
parameters.effect: Requiring an agent versus a consumable creates different staffing and supply decisions.

cases.implementation: Dragging or ending a turn pinning a guard prevents the knockout timer from decreasing, tying up an agent’s position.
cases.sourceLabel: Community guide — revised for released game

cases.implementation: Kate can knock enemies out but has no rope, so another character must restrain them to prevent recovery.

mechanics.contrast: Invisible, Inc. uses ongoing positional commitment; Desperados III uses complementary character abilities for restraint.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: allow a lockpicker and watcher to hand off duties, making the timer determine who finishes first and who takes over.

walkthrough.setup: A guard will recover in two turns; opening the safe takes three.
walkthrough.action: Leave one agent pinning the guard while another works on the safe.
walkthrough.result: The timer stops, but the watcher cannot collect the extra loot in the corridor.
walkthrough.next: After opening the safe, withdraw together and decide whether extra loot is worth another risk.

prototype.firstStep: Build two agents, one knockout counter and a multi-turn objective; nearby pinning pauses the counter.
prototype.pitfall: Keep recovery timing predictable; do not advance the counter on unexplained actions.
prototype.test: Do players compare objective duration with recovery time and assign someone to pin the guard?

mechanics.name: Staging environmental accidents
mechanics.summary: Read props and patrol routes, then let the environment deliver the final action.
mechanics.rules: Hazardous props affect an area that a target may enter. Observe the route, prepare the interaction and wait for the right moment; position and event order matter as much as aiming.
loop: Read when the target will pass
decisions: Wait for the target’s natural route, or lure them in to save time?
If bystanders share the danger zone, skip this opening or choose another method?

parameters.name: Trigger window
parameters.effect: Narrow windows emphasize timing; wider ones emphasize route planning and setup.

parameters.name: Hazard readability
parameters.effect: A clear affected area makes failure an understandable miscalculation rather than a physics guess.

cases.implementation: Environmental actions such as ledge pushes can produce accident kills and require the target to be in a valid position.
Hazards of the Trade offers environmental accident opportunities involving horses and fire along targets’ routes.

mechanics.contrast: HITMAN connects accident types to stealth evaluation; the Desperados III mission arranges several hazards into a route puzzle.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: use box pushing to change where a weight lands, then wait for the target; the result could be a nonlethal obstruction.

walkthrough.setup: A suspended crate hangs above a patrol route; its lever is behind a wall.
walkthrough.action: Reach the lever and wait for the target to enter the marked area alone.
walkthrough.result: The crate drops and blocks the passage, trapping the target before other guards arrive.
walkthrough.next: Use the newly open route to take the document and leave.

prototype.firstStep: Build one patrol, one lever and a marked falling-object zone with deterministic outcomes.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid unpredictable physics deciding success; identical setups should produce identical outcomes.
prototype.test: After one attempt, can players predict who will be affected by changing the trigger timing?

mechanics.name: Competing survival needs
mechanics.summary: While fixing hunger, thirst and fatigue keep building.
mechanics.rules: Read several changing needs and decide which deserves attention now. Gathering, eating and resting all take time; helping one need can let another worsen, so preserve enough capacity to keep acting.
loop: Spend time to restore one need
decisions: Fix the lowest meter or the fastest falling one? Both level and rate matter.
Detour for more food or return while enough energy remains?

parameters.name: Different drain rates
parameters.effect: Different rates change priorities; identical rates encourage a fixed refill routine.

parameters.name: Threshold penalties
parameters.effect: Losing efficiency before health gives players a chance to change plans.

cases.implementation: Warmth, fatigue, thirst and hunger are tracked separately; empty needs threaten condition, while meeting needs supports recovery.
Hunger, health and sanity are separate. Food gathering competes with darkness and sanity pressures; thirst is not part of the same basic meter set.

mechanics.contrast: The Long Dark schedules physical needs; Don’t Starve adds sanity, changing the pressures around a food route.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: reorder renewable foraging routes around hunger, fatigue and sunset so today’s best route differs from yesterday’s.

walkthrough.setup: Example: food lasts two turns; energy lasts one.
walkthrough.action: Rest at camp for one turn instead of picking fruit.
walkthrough.result: Energy returns, but food now lasts only one turn.
walkthrough.next: The next turn must secure food rather than more rest.

prototype.firstStep: Start with two need meters and Gather/Rest buttons; each action advances one turn.
prototype.pitfall: Too many meters turn decisions into dashboard checking; start with two clear conflicts.
prototype.test: Swap the drain rates and observe whether players change action order.

mechanics.name: Collecting and purifying water
mechanics.summary: Available water is not always worth drinking immediately.
mechanics.rules: After finding water, drink immediately or spend fuel, a container and time making it safe. Safe water supports travel but carrying capacity is limited; quality labels and thirst show readiness.
loop: Find water and check its quality
Consume and replenish along the route
decisions: When already thirsty, accept unsafe water or wait for treatment?
Extra water improves safety but displaces loot or fuel.

parameters.name: Treatment time
parameters.effect: Long treatment favors preparation; short treatment supports quick stops.

parameters.name: Quality information
parameters.effect: Clear labels make risk legible; uncertainty needs clues.

cases.implementation: Snow can be melted into unsafe water and then boiled; purification tablets offer another treatment route.
Unsafe water can cause parasites; boiling water in a vessel over a fire makes it safe.

mechanics.contrast: The Long Dark separates melting from boiling; Green Hell emphasizes source safety and vessel preparation.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: put water and purification equipment in one weight budget, trading carried water for on-route treatment.

walkthrough.setup: Example: one fuel unit, two dirty bottles, and a route requiring one bottle.
walkthrough.action: Purify one bottle and leave the other at camp.
walkthrough.result: You gain safe water but have no fuel left.
walkthrough.next: Collect fuel on return before purifying again.

prototype.firstStep: Build one round trip with three items, a Purify button and two water qualities.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid a full fluid simulation; first test whether preparation changes routes.
prototype.test: Offer a light long route and a loaded short route; observe water-based choices.

mechanics.name: Fatigue and sleep planning
mechanics.summary: Schedule sleep before exhaustion chooses for you.
mechanics.rules: Activity and time awake build fatigue and weaken later performance. Choose when, how long and where to sleep; restored energy, elapsed time and changed surroundings shape the next outing.
loop: Return or find a resting place
decisions: One more task may pay, but cost the safe return window.
A short sleep preserves daylight; a long sleep delays the next interruption.

parameters.name: Fatigue penalties
parameters.effect: Early carrying or combat penalties encourage planning; zero-only penalties invite delay.

parameters.name: Recovery curve
parameters.effect: Fast early recovery favors naps; increasing returns favor full rests.

cases.implementation: Wakefulness and activity drain the fatigue meter; tiredness reduces carrying capacity, while sleeping restores energy.
