In single-player, fatigue creates sleep pressure and affects combat. Players sleep in suitable places; multiplayer sleep requirements depend on server settings.

mechanics.contrast: The Long Dark changes carrying capacity; Project Zomboid also makes the resting location and nearby threats important.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: allow staged contract deliveries, making players schedule two trips around work and sleep.

walkthrough.setup: Example: three turns until dark, a two-turn delivery, one turn of energy.
walkthrough.action: Sleep for one turn to recover.
walkthrough.result: Delivery is now possible, with no detour margin.
walkthrough.next: Compare distance and rest needs before the next contract.

prototype.firstStep: Use a daylight clock, energy meter and three locations, with turn-based sleep.
prototype.pitfall: Long idle waits interrupt play; allow fast-forward.
prototype.test: Observe whether players return before reaching exhaustion.

mechanics.name: Bleeding and urgent bandaging
mechanics.summary: Stop ongoing damage before trying to refill health.
mechanics.rules: An injury may cause both immediate damage and ongoing blood loss. Choose when to move, fight or bandage. Treatment stops further loss without instantly healing the original wound.
decisions: Bandaging now risks interruption; running first costs more blood.
With limited supplies, prioritize the fastest bleeding wound.

parameters.name: Bleed rate
parameters.effect: Fast bleeding demands immediate shelter; slow bleeding permits difficult retreats.

parameters.name: Treatment interruption
parameters.effect: Partial progress permits staged treatment; resets demand a full safe window.

cases.implementation: Open wounds can bleed and be bandaged with strips or bandages. Neck wounds are especially dangerous; stopping bleeding does not cure infection or fractures.
Injuries differ in bleeding rate. Medical tending stops bleeding, while recovering function remains a separate process.

mechanics.contrast: Project Zomboid asks for direct body-part treatment; RimWorld turns care into doctor and bed scheduling.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: bandages consume carrying capacity, so extra aid supplies compete with loot space; dropping weight on retreat reduces the time spent exposed while injured.

walkthrough.setup: Example: six health, one lost per turn, four turns to the exit.
walkthrough.action: Spend a turn bandaging in a room.
walkthrough.result: Health drops to five, then stops draining.
walkthrough.next: Escape injured and heal afterward.

prototype.firstStep: Test one bleeding state, an interruptible bandage action and a retreat route.
prototype.pitfall: Many wound types obscure the decision; begin with two bleed severities.
prototype.test: Check whether players can explain treating first versus moving first.

mechanics.name: Wound hygiene and infection prevention
mechanics.summary: Skipped care today can become tomorrow’s complication.
mechanics.rules: Wounds keep changing during recovery. Clean them, select dressings and check replacements. The immediate goal is risk control; wound labels and later complications provide feedback.
decisions: Use the last clean supply now or reserve it for another injury?
Interrupt work to recheck the wound or wait until the current task ends?

parameters.name: Complication delay
parameters.effect: Delayed consequences make prevention matter but need causal logs.

parameters.name: Dressing wear
parameters.effect: Excessive wear becomes busywork; moderate wear supports departure checks.

cases.implementation: Clean or sterilized dressings reduce ordinary wound infection risk; dirty ones need replacing. Wound infection is distinct from fatal Knox infection.
An infected wound needs different care from a simple dressing. Inspect the body to see the affected area and apply the appropriate treatment.

mechanics.contrast: Project Zomboid emphasizes dressing condition during recovery; Green Hell emphasizes recognizing and matching wound care.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a slot-limited medical kit trades spare clean dressings against other supplies.

walkthrough.setup: Example: an old dressing is dirty and only one clean spare remains.
walkthrough.action: Replace it and shorten the outing.
walkthrough.result: The old wound is safer, but there is no spare for a new injury.
walkthrough.next: Restock before the next long expedition.

prototype.firstStep: Use visible clean, dirty and infected states, one wound type and two supplies.
prototype.pitfall: Do not require real medical knowledge; item text should explain in-game use.
prototype.test: Have players handle two wounds without a guide and explain state changes.

mechanics.name: Inspecting the body to find problems
mechanics.summary: Find what is wrong before choosing treatment.
mechanics.rules: A warning signals pain or trouble. Open a body view, inspect regions and choose tools for the issue found. Location and appearance guide action instead of one all-purpose heal button.
loop: Identify the issue and choose a tool
decisions: Inspect the likeliest region first or check everything?
After finding one wound, should you keep checking?

parameters.name: Clue precision
parameters.effect: Vague warnings emphasize observation but need legible visual or location clues.

parameters.name: Inspection cost
parameters.effect: Timed inspection creates urgency; free inspection supports slower diagnosis.

cases.implementation: Players rotate and inspect limbs for leeches or wounds, then apply items to the affected location.
The health panel separates body regions, lists their injuries and offers treatment actions; diagnosis is more list-based than 3D inspection.

mechanics.contrast: Green Hell makes players visually find issues; Project Zomboid centralizes locations in a readable body-part list.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: combine wound location with scene clues to infer the hazard and revise the next route.

walkthrough.setup: Example: a warning appears after walking without stating its cause.
walkthrough.action: Inspect the left leg and find a parasite.
walkthrough.result: Removing it clears the warning and stops deterioration.
walkthrough.next: Remember the water crossing and inspect after using it again.

prototype.firstStep: Use one 2D body diagram, four inspection regions and two conditions.
prototype.pitfall: A rotating 3D body is unnecessary; match clues, locations and treatments clearly.
prototype.test: Without answer hints, see whether inspection leads to the correct treatment.

mechanics.name: Food balance and nutrition
mechanics.summary: Beyond fullness, consider what food restores and the cost of relying on one source.
mechanics.rules: Foods supply different nutrients or calories, and condition responds to intake over time. Players adjust their diet rather than always choosing the largest refill; the UI must explain the consequences.
loop: Adjust the next meal from the result
decisions: With one slot left, fill a nutritional gap or stock a common food?
Eat a calorie-rich meal now or save it for a long trip?

parameters.name: Deficiency consequence
parameters.effect: Effects on stamina, condition caps or long-term weight create different rhythms; avoid stacking them all.

parameters.name: Food complementarity
parameters.effect: If every food covers every need, composition stops being a decision.

cases.implementation: The watch tracks protein, fat, carbohydrates and hydration; deficiencies reduce the health ceiling, so one food cannot solve every need.
The game distinguishes hunger from calorie balance; sustained intake changes weight, which affects physical performance.

mechanics.contrast: Green Hell exposes several immediate deficits; Project Zomboid emphasizes accumulated dietary effects on weight.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: prepare a travel meal covering two deficiencies while weighing portability, shelf life and nutrition.

walkthrough.setup: Example: the character is full but low on protein, with fruit and fish available.
walkthrough.action: Save the fruit for travel and cook the fish.
walkthrough.result: The deficit is filled and the condition ceiling recovers.
walkthrough.next: Seek a fat source on the next outing instead of collecting only fruit.

prototype.firstStep: Start with three nutrients, six foods and a clear deficiency panel.
prototype.pitfall: Do not begin with a human metabolism simulation; keep consequences that support understandable food choices.
prototype.test: Give two inventories and see whether players can explain why they would swap a meal.

mechanics.name: Stress buildup and crisis
mechanics.summary: Accumulated hardship can disrupt control, giving rest and reassurance practical value.
mechanics.rules: Events and surroundings change stress or mood. Near the danger zone, extra work or exploration must be weighed against a crisis; relief costs time, resources or a party slot.
loop: Continue the task or seek relief
decisions: Ask a stressed character for one more shift or replace them now?
Spend a scarce relief resource or accept downtime?

parameters.name: Risk visibility
parameters.effect: Show the danger zone and leading causes so crises feel manageable.

parameters.name: Crisis duration and impact
parameters.effect: Brief refusal and harm to allies require very different warnings and recovery room.

cases.implementation: Low mood can trigger a mental break that interrupts normal work; needs, surroundings and traits affect the risk.
Expeditions build stress; at a threshold a resolve check can produce an affliction or a virtuous state.

mechanics.contrast: RimWorld ties crises to ongoing life and work; Darkest Dungeon concentrates stress in expeditions and threshold checks.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a trusted companion can provide reassurance at the cost of an exploration slot.

walkthrough.setup: Example: a miner nears the stress danger zone with one ore batch remaining.
walkthrough.action: Stop mining, assign rest and let another worker haul.
walkthrough.result: Output falls this round, but the miner returns to a manageable state.
walkthrough.next: Reserve a relief worker before the next run of night shifts.

prototype.firstStep: Use one character, three stress sources, two relief actions and one brief refusal crisis.
prototype.pitfall: Do not obscure causes with many unpredictable punishments; make stress sources understandable first.
prototype.test: After one crisis, observe whether players proactively change the next schedule.

mechanics.name: Wetness, cold and warming up
mechanics.summary: Weather alters physical condition, forcing choices between travel, shelter and drying off.
mechanics.rules: Rain, snow or cold create adverse conditions; clothing, shelter and heat alter exposure and recovery. Route quality depends on recovery stops as well as distance.
decisions: Take a short exposed route or detour past a safe fire?
Wait until clothing dries or use the remaining daylight?

parameters.name: Exposure rate
parameters.effect: Fast accumulation emphasizes emergency shelter; slow accumulation emphasizes preparation.

parameters.name: Shelter recovery
parameters.effect: Faster recovery makes shelter locations more influential route choices.

cases.implementation: Clothing supplies warmth and wind protection, with wetness, freezing and damage affecting protection; players manage clothing and warming opportunities.
Wet and cold conditions impair recovery; fire helps remove wetness and counters cold, creating a travel-and-warm-up loop.
cases.rights: Iron Gate AB / Coffee Stain Publishing

mechanics.contrast: The Long Dark emphasizes clothing and sustained exposure; Valheim uses status effects and fire for a more immediate rhythm.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: reaching a camp and repairing its stove unlocks a fast-travel node. It closes when the fire dies, making fuel provision a return-route decision.

walkthrough.setup: Example: the exposed shore takes two turns; a route through a fire hut takes three.
walkthrough.action: Choose the hut route while clothing is wet.
walkthrough.result: Spend an extra turn but arrive with enough stamina.
walkthrough.next: Restock the hut so it remains useful on the return trip.

prototype.firstStep: Start with wet and cold states, three route nodes and one lightable fire.
prototype.pitfall: Skip dynamic climate and cloth simulation initially; make exposure predictable before moving.
prototype.test: Introduce rain and see whether players reconsider their route.

mechanics.name: Injured limbs change capabilities
mechanics.summary: A leg injury affects escape and an arm injury affects work or combat, changing treatment priorities.
mechanics.rules: Damage affects specific body regions and their associated actions. Beyond staying alive, players prioritize which capability to restore and adapt through substitutions, protection or route changes.
loop: Read the injury and affected function
decisions: Treat the slow scout or the guard struggling with a weapon first?
Keep the plan while injured or choose a route allowing a slow retreat?

parameters.name: Number of regions
parameters.effect: A few meaningful regions are more readable than many nearly identical ones.

parameters.name: Impairment strength
parameters.effect: Total loss forces replacement; partial impairment allows a decision to push on.

cases.implementation: Damage is tracked by body part, with leg injuries reducing movement speed; severe injuries force evacuation and rescue decisions.
Injuries lower body-part efficiency and related capacities such as movement and manipulation, requiring work reassignment.

mechanics.contrast: Kenshi makes impaired movement an expedition problem; RimWorld connects body capacities to colony work allocation.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: an injured character supports from cover while a mobile teammate handles the flank.

walkthrough.setup: Example: an archer injures an arm while a carrier injures a leg.
walkthrough.action: Let the archer lead with a light load; treat and unload the carrier.
walkthrough.result: The party gives up ranged combat temporarily but can retreat together.
walkthrough.next: Restore the archer’s combat ability after reaching camp.

prototype.firstStep: Link legs to movement and arms to attacks, with one treatment and one replacement character.
prototype.pitfall: Body parts affect animation, equipment and AI; prototype with icons and values first.
prototype.test: Swap the injuries and see whether players change roles rather than just repeat treatment clicks.

mechanics.name: Temporary symptom relief
mechanics.summary: Relieving symptoms buys a window to act without necessarily repairing the injury.
mechanics.rules: Symptoms and underlying injuries are tracked separately. Temporary relief reduces a penalty, while the cause may remain afterward; players use the window to reach safety or complete recovery.
decisions: Use relief to return now or save it for a worse stretch?
Explore while able or prioritize recovery?

parameters.name: Relief duration
parameters.effect: The window should enable a meaningful action; too short becomes repeated maintenance.

parameters.name: Symptom versus cause feedback
parameters.effect: Keep both the injury and relief timer visible so relief is not mistaken for a cure.

cases.implementation: Painkillers reduce pain without replacing wound treatment; after relief fades, the actual injury still determines care and rest.
Pain caused by sprains is treated separately from the sprain itself; relief does not mean the injury has healed.

mechanics.contrast: Project Zomboid treats pain as a separate impairment; The Long Dark distinguishes sprain treatment from pain relief.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a small aid kit holds relief plus one treatment material, defining which setbacks it can handle.

walkthrough.setup: Example: a leg injury adds a turn to each move, with camp three steps away.
walkthrough.action: Use an item that relieves the penalty for three moves.
walkthrough.result: Reach camp at normal speed while the injury icon remains.
walkthrough.next: Begin proper recovery before relief expires.

prototype.firstStep: Build one evacuation with an injury, a separate symptom and a visible timer.
prototype.pitfall: Identical feedback for relief and healing misleads players; change the symptom icon while retaining the injury icon.
prototype.test: Check whether players distinguish being able to act from being healed.

mechanics.name: Interrupt disease transmission
mechanics.summary: Beyond treating a sick character, trace transmission through contact, food or air.
mechanics.rules: Disease follows defined routes, and isolation or cleaning works only on relevant routes. Players identify the chain, change contact or infrastructure, then watch later cases to judge success.
loop: Separate contacts or clean the chain
decisions: Pause production to trace the source or maintain supply while protecting key workers?
Use scarce space for isolation or rebuild shared facilities?

parameters.name: Route count
parameters.effect: One understandable route is enough; extra routes require traceable evidence.

parameters.name: Symptom delay
parameters.effect: Delay makes tracing harder, but long delays without logs obscure cause and effect.

cases.implementation: Germs travel on materials and cause disease through specific routes; food poisoning requires ingestion, making sanitation and logistics relevant.
Sick creatures can infect nearby members; separation reduces contact transmission while disrupting group positioning.

mechanics.contrast: Oxygen Not Included traces germs through infrastructure and supplies; Niche focuses on spatial contact among creatures.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: give clean and isolation areas separate entrances so layout affects exposure.

walkthrough.setup: Example: three characters share a table and one shows symptoms.
walkthrough.action: A log links the cases to one food batch; withdraw that stock.
walkthrough.result: Later meals produce no new cases while existing patients still need recovery.
walkthrough.next: Add a cleaning step at food preparation before restoring service.

prototype.firstStep: Start with five characters, one foodborne route and an exposure log.
prototype.pitfall: Do not begin with airborne, contact, latency and mutation systems at once; prove one traceable chain.
prototype.test: Introduce one contamination event and see whether players identify its source and verify control through later cases.

mechanics.name: Arrange neighbors to breed plants
mechanics.summary: To obtain new plants, decide which should grow together and which must stay apart.
mechanics.rules: Plant layout affects crossing or pollination. Select parents or neighboring varieties, wait for growth or pollination, then inspect and retain useful results; production plots and experimental plots may need separation.
loop: Choose a target variety or trait
Arrange plants that influence one another
Keep the result and revise the next group
decisions: Use limited plots for reliable harvests or reserve one for an experiment?
Keep a useful plant or cross it again for a better trait mix?

parameters.name: Interaction range
parameters.effect: Adjacency, radius or hive range creates different separation layouts.

parameters.name: Result predictability
parameters.effect: Visible parents and outcomes favor planning; hidden outcomes need persistent experiment records.

cases.implementation: Plant genes affect growth, and neighboring plants influence crossing; cloning preserves a desirable genetic combination.
Working bees visit nearby flowers; visited combinations participate in cross-pollination, letting players discover flowers by arranging varieties.

mechanics.contrast: Rust optimizes and clones plant gene combinations; APICO discovers flower species through bee visits, making layout the experiment condition.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: reserve enough seed for another production cycle so breeding experiments compete with current income for space.

walkthrough.setup: Example: a three-slot nursery holds two red flowers and one yellow; the target is orange.
walkthrough.action: Place red and yellow within one hive’s range and move the spare red outside as reserve stock.
walkthrough.result: One pollination round yields a candidate variety while preserving the originals.
walkthrough.next: Record the arrangement, then expand the new variety or test another pair.

prototype.firstStep: Use four flowers, three nursery slots and a fixed crossing table instead of a full genetics simulation.
prototype.pitfall: If every neighbor mixes randomly with no way to isolate plants, experiments lose controllability.
prototype.test: Provide production and experiment plots; see whether players preserve parents and repeat a successful cross.

mechanics.name: Select parents for offspring traits
mechanics.summary: Inspect both parents before breeding and check which traits the offspring inherits.
mechanics.rules: Choose a pair for a target, then generate offspring under visible or learnable inheritance rules. Uncertain results require choosing which offspring to retain for further breeding, not simply increasing numbers.
loop: Retain suitable offspring for another generation
decisions: Choose the two strongest individuals or a complementary pair?
Stop at a useful offspring or keep trying for a rare combination?

parameters.name: Inheritance visibility
parameters.effect: Visible appearance encourages trials; hidden-gene information supports more deliberate pairing.

parameters.name: Breeding capacity cost
parameters.effect: Offspring must occupy space or care resources for another attempt to be a meaningful choice.

cases.implementation: Creatures inherit genes from both parents, including dominant, recessive and codominant patterns; mating choices pass useful adaptations onward.
Fertile animals of the same species produce offspring inheriting parental genes; genetic information supports mate selection.

mechanics.contrast: Niche ties inherited traits to survival in the wild; Planet Zoo embeds mate selection in long-term care and zoo management.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: reveal hidden parental traits through inspection before allocating a limited breeding slot.

walkthrough.setup: Example: the next map is cold; three candidates favor cold resistance, speed and gathering.
walkthrough.action: Pair the cold-resistant creature with the gatherer.
walkthrough.result: The offspring retains cold resistance but has ordinary gathering ability.
walkthrough.next: Keep it for migration, then decide whether a second breeding slot should improve gathering.

prototype.firstStep: Build a three-generation experiment with two traits, three parents and an explainable inheritance table.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid dozens of appearances and a complex pedigree initially; first make pairings change offspring decisions.
prototype.test: Watch two generations of choices and see whether offspring results change the next pairing.

mechanics.name: Preserve genetic diversity
mechanics.summary: Keeping only one successful family can make future pairings harder.
mechanics.rules: A population needs compatible future pairings as well as strong current individuals. Inspect lineage or key genes, retain members from different sources and balance immediate performance against future breeding options.
decisions: Introduce an ordinary unrelated individual or keep breeding the strong existing family?
When space is tight, keep a rare gene or the strongest current contributor?

parameters.name: Cost of repeated genes
parameters.effect: Consequences should be predictable before birth rather than unavoidable surprises.

parameters.name: Newcomer cost
parameters.effect: Harder access to newcomers makes existing diversity more valuable.

cases.implementation: Matching immunity alleles cause genetic sickness; comparing mates’ immunity genes helps avoid harmful offspring combinations.
The official genealogy feature traces family relationships to help manage breeding and avoid inbreeding.

mechanics.contrast: Niche exposes specific immunity alleles; Planet Zoo organizes family relationships through genealogy.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: an underrepresented lineage can be valuable to your population even when its market price is low.

walkthrough.setup: Example: four animals share one lineage, with only one slot remaining.
walkthrough.action: Keep an ordinary newcomer instead of a fifth high-scoring descendant.
walkthrough.result: Average current ability falls slightly, but another future pairing becomes available.
walkthrough.next: Pair it with the established line and inspect the next generation.

prototype.firstStep: Start with three visible gene markers and limited slots, clearly showing risky pairings.
prototype.pitfall: Pedigrees quickly become an information burden; begin with two generations and direct pairing guidance.
prototype.test: Offer a weaker newcomer and see whether players keep it for future breeding value.

mechanics.name: Gradually tame wild animals
mechanics.summary: To gain a lasting animal companion, provide food and manage its wariness.
mechanics.rules: Taming requires repeated approaches, feeding or safe conditions. Wildness, alarm and handler skill affect progress or success; players invest resources and choose when to approach or back away.
loop: Choose a target and prepare food and space
Attempt taming and read the response
Continue investing or choose another target
decisions: Tame an easy, modestly useful animal or risk a more valuable target?
Approach again for progress or withdraw so it can settle?

parameters.name: Predictability
parameters.effect: Accumulating progress supports planning; chance-based attempts emphasize budgeting, with clear failure feedback.

parameters.name: Interruption conditions
parameters.effect: Hunger, alarm and handler skill require different preparation.

cases.implementation: Handlers attempt taming using animal skill; wildness affects required skill and success, linking targets to worker assignments.
Tameable animals need food and calm conditions; prepare an enclosure and supplies, then allow progress from a safe distance.
cases.rights: Iron Gate AB / Coffee Stain Publishing

mechanics.contrast: RimWorld emphasizes handler skill and attempts; Valheim emphasizes preparation and sustained calm.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: include a safe feeding route in enclosure design so access supports taming.

walkthrough.setup: Example: a creature is enclosed but alarms when approached, with no food on the ground.
walkthrough.action: Place food from outside and move out of sight.
walkthrough.result: It settles, eats and begins gaining taming progress.
walkthrough.next: Refill food when it moves to the far side to avoid another disturbance.

prototype.firstStep: Use one animal, calm and alarmed states, one food and a visible progress bar.
prototype.pitfall: Skip elaborate animal AI initially; make interruptions understandable first.
prototype.test: Without explicit action prompts, see whether players learn to withdraw and wait from the animal’s response.

mechanics.name: Control breeding and population size
mechanics.summary: Births are welcome, but the next generation also consumes food, space and care.
mechanics.rules: Populations grow through breeding while resources remain limited. Set retention targets, pause breeding or move surplus animals to balance ongoing production with a manageable population.
loop: Set retention targets or breeding controls
decisions: Keep more young for expansion or stay within current food capacity?
Which pair should stop breeding without losing useful future options?

parameters.name: Reproduction rate
parameters.effect: Births faster than players can react become cleanup; forecasts should leave time to act.

parameters.name: Control granularity
parameters.effect: Species, age or sex controls reduce repetition while allowing exceptions for important individuals.

cases.implementation: Growing herds increase feed demand; auto-slaughter rules manage counts by species, replacing repeated cleanup with retention policies.
Animal management provides contraception controls to pause breeding while planning space and population composition.

mechanics.contrast: RimWorld emphasizes retention policies after births; Planet Zoo can pause breeding beforehand, shifting the point of intervention.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: warn when feed falls below three rounds, while letting players choose breeding exceptions.

walkthrough.setup: Example: capacity is six, with four adults and two births expected.
walkthrough.action: Pause the other pair while keeping the expected births.
walkthrough.result: The next round reaches six without an additional space shortfall.
walkthrough.next: Resume the paused pair after expansion.

prototype.firstStep: Use one species, six slots, turn-based births and a breeding switch.
prototype.pitfall: Skip a full economy and policy editor; start with a two-round population forecast.
prototype.test: Run five rounds and see whether players manage growth before births rather than repeatedly clear overflow.

mechanics.name: Check habitat capacity before adding animals
mechanics.summary: A habitat that fits one animal may not support five more.
mechanics.rules: Meet both species requirements and population-level capacity. Added or growing animals change space, equipment or care demand, so expansion requires reassessment rather than one permanent terrain match.
loop: Read condition feedback and retain headroom
decisions: Add a valuable animal or reserve capacity for existing young to grow?
Upgrade shared support or build a separate habitat?

parameters.name: Demand scaling
parameters.effect: Fixed demand per animal emphasizes counts; size-dependent demand emphasizes growth forecasts.

parameters.name: Warning headroom
parameters.effect: Warnings only after overload force crisis response; visible headroom supports planning.

cases.implementation: Animals need appropriate terrain, water and habitat arrangements; managing groups also requires checking space and social needs beyond appearance.
Tank inhabitants have distinct care and water-quality requirements; tanks, filtration and staff must support the combined collection.

mechanics.contrast: Planet Zoo combines environment, activity space and group structure; Megaquarium connects stocking decisions to tanks and supporting equipment.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: share environmental equipment by habitat zone while reserving expansion space to avoid rebuilding after every birth.

walkthrough.setup: Example: a tank holds ten capacity points; three young fish use six now and nine when grown.
walkthrough.action: Decline a new fish needing three points and upgrade the tank first.
walkthrough.result: Income stays unchanged, but the grown population retains headroom.
walkthrough.next: After the upgrade, compare the new fish’s value with added maintenance.

prototype.firstStep: Use one tank, two species, current and adult demand columns, and one upgrade.
prototype.pitfall: Do not begin with full water chemistry; one capacity meter and one condition can test expansion decisions.
prototype.test: Show adult-demand forecasts and see whether players reserve capacity before it is exhausted.

mechanics.name: Plan which species can share a home
mechanics.summary: Sharing environmental needs does not guarantee compatible neighbors.
mechanics.rules: Assign species to limited habitats while checking threats, social preferences or cohabitation benefits. A newcomer can change existing residents’ safety or value, so evaluate combinations rather than independent scores.
decisions: Is shared infrastructure worth a predation risk that may change with size?
Add a species for cohabitation benefits or keep a simpler single-species group?

parameters.name: Relationship visibility
parameters.effect: Show clear conflicts before placement so losses follow decisions rather than hidden knowledge.

parameters.name: Growth-dependent relationships
parameters.effect: Compatibility that changes with growth requires advance relocation planning.

cases.implementation: Predators have size-based prey limits, and growth changes what they can eat; mixed tanks must account for future size.
Some species combinations gain interspecies enrichment; players check relationships alongside habitat requirements. No bonus does not automatically mean cohabitation is impossible.

mechanics.contrast: Megaquarium ties cohabitation to prey-size risk; Planet Zoo also offers positive bonuses for particular combinations.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: treat habitat slots as a limited loadout where compatible combinations reduce separate infrastructure.

walkthrough.setup: Example: two tanks house three fish species; the largest will eventually prey on the smallest.
walkthrough.action: Separate large and small fish, placing medium fish with the large species.
walkthrough.result: The arrangement saves a separate tank while avoiding the known future conflict.
walkthrough.next: Before adding a new species, compare it with every resident in the tank.

prototype.firstStep: Use four species, two habitats and a visible relationship table, with one conflict and one bonus.
prototype.pitfall: Pairwise relationships grow quadratically; do not rely on a large species catalog for depth.
prototype.test: Introduce a species that changes the best grouping and see whether players reorganize current residents.

mechanics.name: Prepare conditions that enable breeding
mechanics.summary: The right parents are only a start; timing, surroundings and nursery conditions matter too.
mechanics.rules: Breeding requires conditions beyond the parents. Read clues, adjust the environment and test, then use feedback to diagnose missing requirements; successful births also need appropriate care.
loop: Care for the young and record conditions
decisions: Change conditions for this pair or choose another pair suited to the current setup?
Wait for a natural time or weather window or spend resources to create it?

parameters.name: Conditions and clues
parameters.effect: More conditions require clearer feedback; a bare failure message cannot support informed experiments.

parameters.name: Nursery burden
parameters.effect: Extra care after success creates a next step but should be forecast rather than punish success unexpectedly.

cases.implementation: Some bee crosses depend on time, weather or nearby conditions as well as parent species; adjusting conditions reveals new bees.
The Freshwater Frenzy expansion adds breeding with species-specific requirements and ongoing juvenile care; this does not apply to every base-game animal.

mechanics.contrast: APICO uses environmental clues to discover bees; Megaquarium’s expansion connects breeding requirements to juvenile care.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: growing plants changes conditions around a hive, connecting cultivation to breeding experiments.

walkthrough.setup: Example: notes say a pair needs night and shelter; only the night condition is met.
walkthrough.action: Move the hive under a roof while keeping the same parents.
walkthrough.result: The next attempt produces a new species and marks the conditions in the journal.
walkthrough.next: Prepare a separate hive and choose whether the next experiment changes weather or flowers.

prototype.firstStep: Use two parent pairs, day/night and shelter conditions, and separate feedback for each requirement.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid realistic weather and many hidden recipes initially; first test whether players can change one variable at a time.
prototype.test: Cause a failure missing one condition and see whether players change that condition and reproduce success.

mechanics.name: Previewing enemy intent
mechanics.summary: Read the threat, then spend limited actions to change what happens.
mechanics.rules: Before an enemy acts, reveal its target, area or damage. Players defend, kill, move or interrupt, then check the resolution. Visible information must be reliable, with any remaining uncertainty clearly indicated.
loop: Spend actions to change the situation
Resolve and read the next threat
decisions: Block the damage or eliminate the most dangerous enemy?
Protect yourself or an objective threatened this turn?

parameters.name: Preview detail
parameters.effect: Showing only attack type preserves uncertainty; exact targets and values support precise planning.

parameters.name: Response budget
parameters.effect: Fewer actions force the player to choose which threats deserve intervention.

cases.implementation: Enemy attacks are telegraphed before the player acts, allowing attacks to be redirected or prevented to protect buildings.
Intent icons reveal upcoming attacks, defense or other actions, usually including damage for attacks.

mechanics.contrast: Into the Breach makes intent spatial; Slay the Spire turns it into an attack-versus-block budget.
mechanics.combination: Combine intent previews with box pushing: a crate blocks a shot but may obstruct retreat.

walkthrough.setup: Two enemies will deal 3 damage to you and 5 to a villager; you have two actions.
walkthrough.action: Push the enemy off the villager’s firing line, then defend yourself.
walkthrough.result: The villager is safe and your shield absorbs 3 damage.
walkthrough.next: Targets change next turn, so reassess the most urgent threat.

prototype.firstStep: Build three turns on a small grid with two enemy types and move, attack and defend.
prototype.pitfall: A preview that disagrees with resolution breaks trust.
prototype.test: Check whether testers can explain safety before resolution and the cause of failure afterward.

mechanics.name: Forced movement
mechanics.summary: Moving an enemy somewhere dangerous can matter more than damage.
mechanics.rules: An attack can push or pull a target as well as deal damage. Its new position changes targeting, obstacles and hazards. Predict the landing point, choose a direction, then plan from the altered board.
decisions: Deal direct damage or displace the enemy so its attack misses?
Will pushing an enemy out of reach also lose recoverable loot?

parameters.name: Displacement distance
parameters.effect: Distance changes reachable positions; excessive range weakens positioning.

parameters.name: Collision rules
parameters.effect: Wall, unit and pit collisions need distinct, readable outcomes.

cases.implementation: Many mech weapons push enemies; displacement can redirect their attacks, and chasms destroy pushed ground enemies.
Shove previews success and landing position; strength and target weight affect distance, while a chasm may kill a target and lose its loot.

mechanics.contrast: Into the Breach emphasizes deterministic grid displacement; Baldur’s Gate 3 adds success checks, elevation and possible loot loss.
mechanics.combination: Let displacement also alter a beam puzzle: enemies block beams or land on switches.

walkthrough.setup: A tough monster stands one tile from a pit, while you are beside it.
walkthrough.action: Move in front of it, then use a push dealing only 1 damage.
walkthrough.result: The push drops it into the pit, solving a high-health threat with little damage.
walkthrough.next: The next monster stands against a wall, requiring a different direction.

prototype.firstStep: Start with one-tile cardinal pushes, walls and pits, without full physics.
prototype.pitfall: Hidden landing positions or ambiguous collision order turn planning into guessing.
prototype.test: Give testers three positions for the same enemy and look for different solutions.

mechanics.name: Shared action points
mechanics.summary: A limited turn budget makes movement compete with attacks.
mechanics.rules: At turn start, grant a fixed action budget shared by movement, attacks and support. Players sequence actions before the budget runs out; it refreshes next turn. Explicitly show actions that end a turn rather than implying everything through point cost.
decisions: Spend movement for a better angle or attack again from here?
Reload for the next round or spend the last point attacking now?

parameters.name: Points per turn
parameters.effect: Small budgets sharpen trade-offs; larger budgets add combinations and planning time.

parameters.name: Turn-ending actions
parameters.effect: Uniform costs are easier to learn; exceptions that end a turn need clear labels.

cases.implementation: Units normally have two actions; blue movement uses one and a yellow dash uses two, while a standard shot normally ends that unit’s turn.
cases.rights: Firaxis Games, Feral Interactive (Mac), Feral Interactive (Linux)

cases.implementation: Units start with three actions, freely divided among movement, shooting, reloads and other abilities, including repeated moves or shots.

mechanics.contrast: XCOM 2 emphasizes order and turn-ending actions; Gears Tactics permits freer repetition.
mechanics.combination: Let equipment weight affect movement cost, connecting loadout to each turn’s action combinations.

walkthrough.setup: You have 3 points; cover costs 1 move, a shot costs 1, and only one bullet remains.
walkthrough.action: Move, shoot, then spend the last point reloading.
walkthrough.result: You attack once but finish in cover with a full magazine.
walkthrough.next: Next turn you can attack repeatedly or budget for retreat.

prototype.firstStep: Start with one unit, three actions and three points; preview the remaining balance.
prototype.pitfall: Unsignaled turn-ending effects cause accidental commitments.
prototype.test: Check whether players can predict their remaining actions before clicking.

mechanics.name: Overwatch and reaction fire
mechanics.summary: Reserve an opportunity for enemy movement and threaten an area.
mechanics.rules: A unit forgoes immediate attack to enter overwatch. Enemy movement or entry into range triggers a reaction; if nothing triggers it, the opportunity may be wasted. Choose a position, resource commitment and possible lure.
decisions: Take a low-probability shot now or guard a likely route?
Focus on a narrow entrance or cover more possible routes?

parameters.name: Trigger conditions
parameters.effect: Movement, entry or firing triggers encourage different ways to bait enemies.

parameters.name: Reaction count and accuracy
parameters.effect: Reaction count and accuracy determine denial strength; excessive power punishes all aggression.

cases.implementation: Overwatch reserves a shot for enemy movement into line of sight, normally with an aim penalty.
cases.rights: Firaxis Games, Feral Interactive (Mac), Feral Interactive (Linux)

cases.implementation: Players set a cone; remaining actions affect reaction shots, and a narrower cone improves accuracy.

mechanics.contrast: XCOM 2 focuses on line of sight and movement; Gears Tactics adds explicit cone placement and action investment.
mechanics.combination: Make elevation or shortcuts bypass overwatch, so route discovery changes the fight.

walkthrough.setup: An enemy hides behind a wall and may leave through the left doorway.
walkthrough.action: Skip an immediate shot and watch the doorway.
walkthrough.result: Crossing the door triggers a shot; staying put instead wastes your attack opportunity.
walkthrough.next: Use its choice to decide whether to guard another exit or advance next turn.

prototype.firstStep: Prototype one doorway and a single movement-triggered shot, then add a second unit.
prototype.pitfall: Multiple simultaneous reactions need a clear order and rules for targets that die early.
prototype.test: Check that attackers understand the danger and find a bypass or bait.

mechanics.name: Simultaneous planned orders
mechanics.summary: Plan a few seconds of action, then watch both plans collide.
mechanics.rules: Combat alternates planning and execution. Queue movement, aim or attacks, then commit both sides to the same time interval without continuous intervention. Reassess afterward. Enemy plans may be hidden or partly revealed, changing the central challenge.
decisions: Stop to aim or cross a firing line early?
Bet on the likeliest enemy plan or trade efficiency for robustness?

parameters.name: Execution interval
parameters.effect: Longer intervals increase commitment and make mistakes harder to diagnose.

parameters.name: Enemy plan visibility
parameters.effect: Hidden plans favor prediction; visible plans favor temporal and spatial scheduling.

cases.implementation: Both sides plan and simulate orders before simultaneous resolution; a simulation tests assumptions rather than revealing the opponent’s real plan.
The timeline exposes upcoming enemy actions so players can schedule movement and attacks before execution and the next planning phase.

mechanics.contrast: Frozen Synapse emphasizes prediction under hidden plans; Phantom Brigade turns visible future actions into scheduling and counters.
mechanics.combination: Add limited rewinds that revise one plan while preserving the consequences for other units.

walkthrough.setup: Two allies must cross one firing line; the enemy fires at second 2.
walkthrough.action: Schedule the first crossing at second 1 and the second at second 3.
walkthrough.result: Both avoid the firing window; waiting proves useful.
walkthrough.next: The enemy turns in the next interval, requiring a new schedule.

prototype.firstStep: Start with two units, discrete time slots and fixed enemy plans in one room, without free physics or networking.
prototype.pitfall: If preview and execution use different rules, players cannot trust the timeline.
prototype.test: Check whether players can locate a mistaken second in replay and revise that interval.

mechanics.name: Pausing to issue orders
mechanics.summary: Pause simultaneous problems long enough to organize the team.
mechanics.rules: Combat runs in real time, but players can pause to inspect and order several units or systems. Orders execute after resuming; new injuries, targets or failures prompt another pause. Pausing supports parallel decisions rather than solving them automatically.
decisions: Rescue a threatened ally or interrupt the next enemy attack?
Are the orders ready to test, or does another unit need attention?

parameters.name: Auto-pause events
parameters.effect: Auto-pausing on key events prevents missed threats; too many interruptions fragment pacing.

parameters.name: Order queue depth
parameters.effect: Single orders are clear; longer queues enable planning but are harder to revise.

cases.implementation: Players can pause ship combat to inspect rooms, order crew, redistribute power and choose weapon targets.
The PC version lets players pause, assign targets and abilities to party members, then resume real-time combat; higher difficulty relies more on tactical management.

mechanics.contrast: FTL coordinates crew and ship systems; Dragon Age: Origins coordinates party positions and abilities.
mechanics.combination: Connect power allocation to tactical pause: shut down production briefly to power shields.

walkthrough.setup: A room is burning while an enemy weapon nears a full charge.
walkthrough.action: Pause: send one crew member to extinguish the fire, another to repair shields, and aim at the enemy weapon room.
walkthrough.result: After resuming, tasks proceed together and you inspect what remains unresolved.
walkthrough.next: Pause again when someone is injured and move them somewhere safer.

prototype.firstStep: Use three rooms, two characters, fires and repairs to test pause-order-resume.
prototype.pitfall: Unclear target changes or order replacement can look like ignored commands.
prototype.test: Give testers two simultaneous events and ask what each unit will do after resuming.

mechanics.name: Area attacks with friendly fire
mechanics.summary: Powerful area attacks require safe positions for allies.
mechanics.rules: Some area attacks also affect allies inside the area. Weigh enemy damage against friendly losses, or reposition allies first. Damage and positions shape the next action. Clearly state which skills, difficulties or talents prevent friendly fire.
loop: Move allies or accept the cost
decisions: Miss one enemy to protect an ally or accept friendly damage to end the fight?
Is an ally’s repositioning action worth the better area attack?

parameters.name: Friendly damage ratio
parameters.effect: Reduced damage eases learning; full damage increases positional importance and punishes mistakes.

parameters.name: Area preview accuracy
parameters.effect: Highlight affected allies so players choose a risk instead of guessing collision rules.

cases.implementation: Fireball affects the blast area rather than filtering only enemies, so placement depends on ally positions and any class-based protections.
On PC, several area spells can harm allies; the manual specifies immunity on Easy, half damage on Normal, and no reduction on Hard.

mechanics.contrast: Baldur’s Gate 3 ties risk to spell areas, positioning and class abilities; Dragon Age: Origins also scales the penalty through difficulty.
mechanics.combination: Combine with surface reactions: move allies out of water before electrifying clustered enemies.

walkthrough.setup: Three enemies surround your fighter; a fireball would hit all four.
walkthrough.action: Move the fighter one tile away, then place the blast behind the enemies.
walkthrough.result: Two enemies are hit and the ally is safe; you deliberately sacrifice the third target.
walkthrough.next: When the survivor approaches, choose a single-target attack or regroup the enemies.

prototype.firstStep: Use a circular or tiled area, two allies and three enemies; implement an accurate preview before effects.
prototype.pitfall: Mismatch between the shown and actual area turns deliberate risk into frustration.
prototype.test: Ask players who will be hit before casting and whether they would ever deliberately accept friendly damage.

mechanics.name: Destroying cover to reshape a fight
mechanics.summary: Remove protection or obstructions to change which positions are safe.
mechanics.rules: Walls and cover are not permanent boundaries: certain attacks destroy them. Spend a limited resource to open a route or remove protection, then exploit new sightlines. The same destruction may expose allies, requiring plans for the changed map.
decisions: Spend an explosive to remove cover now or save it for later?
Will the new sightline expose your rear units as well?

parameters.name: Destructible scope
parameters.effect: Specific destructible tiles are predictable; complex collapse raises production and comprehension costs.

parameters.name: Destruction scarcity
parameters.effect: Limited uses make the chosen opening matter; unlimited destruction can invalidate cover.

cases.implementation: Frag grenades can destroy cover and walls so teammates can attack exposed targets; tougher terrain may survive one grenade.
cases.rights: Firaxis Games, Feral Interactive (Mac), Feral Interactive (Linux)

cases.implementation: Rockets can destroy walls and change routes and sightlines; grenade blasts do not destroy walls in the same way.

mechanics.contrast: XCOM 2 uses cover removal to prepare follow-up shots; Frozen Synapse wall destruction also changes routes for planned simultaneous orders.
mechanics.combination: Connect pre-battle construction to destructible cover so player-built defenses can develop breaches during combat.

walkthrough.setup: An enemy hides behind a low wall; you have one bomb and a shooter who has not acted.
walkthrough.action: Destroy the wall, then fire at the exposed enemy.
walkthrough.result: The shot improves, but the area can no longer protect your own units.
walkthrough.next: Choose the next turn’s position away from the newly exposed ground.

prototype.firstStep: Use tiled walls that switch between intact and destroyed, updating paths and sightlines without debris simulation.
prototype.pitfall: Destroyed visuals with old pathing, or intact-looking walls that no longer block fire, undermine clarity.
prototype.test: Before and after breaking a wall, ask testers to identify new routes, exposed targets and lost protection.

mechanics.name: Take one option from a shared pool
mechanics.summary: Your pick disappears from everyone else’s options.
mechanics.rules: Players choose from one public pool. A taken item is unavailable to others, so each choice considers personal needs and opponents’ priorities. Pick order, remaining items and replenishment timing change an option’s value.
loop: Take one and update the pool
decisions: Take your best fit or deny the one piece an opponent needs?
Can a common option safely wait until your next pick?

parameters.name: Replenishment frequency
parameters.effect: Immediate replacement softens competition; round-end replacement emphasizes order.

parameters.name: Pick constraints
parameters.effect: Placement or use requirements give the same item different values for different players.

cases.implementation: On a turn, draft a public die into a legal window space respecting color, value and adjacency restrictions; that die leaves the shared pool.
Shared draft rounds let players take a champion from a common selection, considering its attached item as well; a claimed option is gone for later pickers.
cases.sourceLabel: Official developer design article — Riot Games

mechanics.contrast: Sagrada resolves individual die-picking turns with immediate placement; TFT’s shared draft uses release order and packages a champion with an item.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: draft battle rewards from a shared pool into personal decks, anticipating which cards teammates take and keeping a backup choice.

walkthrough.setup: Three players see two swords and one shield; you lack defense and an opponent has only weapons.
walkthrough.action: Take the only shield.
walkthrough.result: You gain protection and the opponent must choose between swords.
walkthrough.next: The opponent may prioritize defense next round, so inspect the new pool.

prototype.firstStep: Use three local players, six public cards and two collection goals for one draft.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid a universal ranking that dictates every pick.
prototype.test: Do players change their picks after checking others’ needs?

mechanics.name: Commit a worker to occupy an action
mechanics.summary: An occupied action serves you and temporarily blocks others.
mechanics.rules: Place limited workers on public action spaces, pay requirements and gain the effect. Most spaces become unavailable for the round. Sequence actions around urgent needs and likely competition, then retrieve workers for the next round.
loop: Commit a worker to an action
Retrieve workers for the next round
decisions: Gather first to build later, or secure a contested action now?
Is taking a low-value space worthwhile just to deny an opponent?

parameters.name: Workers per round
parameters.effect: Fewer workers make each placement a stronger commitment.

parameters.name: Space capacity
parameters.effect: Multiple slots with increasing costs can soften total exclusion.

cases.implementation: The played card determines eligible agent locations, which normally cannot already contain an agent; card access and occupied spaces jointly shape sequencing.
Agents occupy building action spaces for benefits; occupied spaces normally block placement, with explicit exceptions from certain quests or cards.
cases.sourceLabel: Official rules FAQ — Wizards of the Coast

mechanics.contrast: Dune gates destinations through cards; Waterdeep’s buildings and special effects alter available spaces and exceptions.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: materials and construction permits require separate action spaces, linking build order to backup projects when a space is taken.

walkthrough.setup: You have two workers; a bridge needs wood, and logging and bridge construction each have one free space.
walkthrough.action: Take the logging space first.
walkthrough.result: You gain wood, but an opponent then takes bridge construction.
walkthrough.next: Build storage instead or save the wood for an early bridge next round.

prototype.firstStep: Give three local players two workers and five fixed action spaces for one round.
prototype.pitfall: Too many access conditions and exceptions obscure the core conflict.
prototype.test: Can players explain a blocked space and find an alternative immediately?

mechanics.name: Control an area by having more presence
mechanics.summary: One extra unit can change who controls an area.
mechanics.rules: Players commit countable units or markers to areas. At a defined time, compare totals to award control or rewards. Divide limited strength between areas, avoid excess investment and protect narrow leads, with explicit tie rules.
decisions: Extend a one-unit lead or contest another area?
Chase a deficit or concede it to preserve other rewards?

parameters.name: Scoring time
parameters.effect: Continuous control rewards immediate presence; timed scoring rewards late reversals.

parameters.name: Tie rules
parameters.effect: No control, shared rewards and faction advantages create different thresholds.

cases.implementation: A clearing is normally ruled by the faction with the most warriors and buildings combined; ties normally mean no ruler, with explicit exceptions such as the Eyrie.
Cities occupied separately can merge as tiles connect; completed features award points by follower majority, with tied leaders each scoring the full feature value.
cases.rights: Artefacts Studio / Twin Sails Interactive / Hans im Glück

mechanics.contrast: Root uses rule to affect movement and action eligibility; Carcassonne links majorities to merging features and completion scoring.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: facility coverage generates influence, with service rights going to the strongest local coverage; compare reinforcing a district with opening a new one.

walkthrough.setup: The north is tied at two each; you have one marker in the south and the opponent none.
walkthrough.action: Put the new marker in the north.
walkthrough.result: You lead the north three to two.
walkthrough.next: The opponent can reinforce; choose whether the next marker protects the north or expands south.

prototype.firstStep: Use three areas, six markers per player and a fixed scoring round.
prototype.pitfall: Keep counts, leaders and scoring time visible together.
prototype.test: Do players stop overcommitting to secure areas and contest new ones?

mechanics.name: Claim routes to alter an opponent’s path
mechanics.summary: A route can connect your network and force an opponent to detour.
mechanics.rules: Routes or junctions have exclusive occupancy. Claiming a connection or site prevents others from extending through the same position. Balance personal connectivity against denial, with detours, remaining entrances and building costs showing the consequences.
loop: Pay to claim an edge or junction
Detour or contest the next gap
decisions: Build the shortest path first or secure a bottleneck both sides need?
Is the original goal still worthwhile after an expensive detour?

parameters.name: Alternative routes
parameters.effect: A single route magnifies first access; alternatives create recovery options.

parameters.name: Occupancy duration
parameters.effect: Permanent claims reward anticipation; temporary blocks emphasize timing.

cases.implementation: Each individual route can be claimed by only one player, denying that edge to other networks; parallel routes have separate player-count restrictions.
cases.sourceLabel: Primary research — formal model of Ticket to Ride route rules

cases.implementation: Each edge holds one road, and an opponent’s settlement blocks road extension through its junction, so claimed positions change expansion possibilities.

mechanics.contrast: Ticket to Ride primarily claims edges; Catan also blocks junctions with settlements, giving nodes and edges different strategic value.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: automated trade follows owned connections; a contested link forces rerouting and a comparison between longer transport and a new port.

walkthrough.setup: A mine and port are linked by a two-edge shortcut and a four-edge detour.
walkthrough.action: Spend resources to secure the shortcut’s bridge.
walkthrough.result: Your short route is secured and the opponent must detour.
walkthrough.next: With fewer resources left, choose whether to finish the route or save.

prototype.firstStep: Draw six nodes and eight exclusive edges; two local players spend tokens to connect them.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid a single opening claim eliminating meaningful participation.
prototype.test: Can players identify a detour and its extra cost after a route is taken?

mechanics.name: Race for a public objective reward
mechanics.summary: Meeting the requirement matters only if the reward is still available.
mechanics.rules: Several players pursue a public objective with limited reward slots or an initial holder. Watch relative progress and decide how much to spend on speed. Once claimed, rivals must switch goals or continue pursuing a reward that can be taken back.
loop: Claim the reward or lose the opportunity
decisions: Pay extra to finish now or risk a rival getting there first?
Chase while behind or pursue a less contested goal?

parameters.name: Reward slots
parameters.effect: Fewer slots increase attention to rivals, but too few can leave late players without goals.

parameters.name: Reclaimability
parameters.effect: Permanent claims encourage sprints; transferable rewards require upkeep.

cases.implementation: Milestones require meeting a condition and paying to claim it; the base game allows only a limited number to be claimed, and a claimed milestone cannot be claimed again.
cases.rights: Artefacts Studio / Twin Sails Interactive / FryxGames

cases.implementation: Reaching a faction’s alliance requirement first can claim its alliance token; a rival with greater influence can later take it, so the initial winner must monitor challengers.
cases.sourceLabel: Official designer diary — Dire Wolf Digital

mechanics.contrast: Terraforming Mars milestones remain claimed; Dune alliances can transfer, separating the initial race from defending the lead.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: public delivery contracts pay only the first arrival, making stock and travel time determine whether to race for a nearby order or pursue a quieter distant one.

walkthrough.setup: Three players can claim a first-delivery reward for five goods; you and one rival each have four.
walkthrough.action: Pay a premium for the last item and deliver now.
walkthrough.result: You secure the reward but lose cash.
walkthrough.next: The next goal needs different goods; choose between switching production and rebuilding cash.

prototype.firstStep: Give two local players three public goals with one-time rewards removed when claimed.
prototype.pitfall: Distinguish eligibility from claiming so lost rewards feel understandable.
prototype.test: Do rivals’ progress cause players to accelerate, switch goals or cut losses?

mechanics.name: Keep savings to earn next-round interest
mechanics.summary: Skipping an upgrade can increase income in later rounds.
mechanics.rules: Round-end savings generate extra income, often in capped thresholds. Balance immediate upgrades against future growth, checking whether a purchase crosses an interest threshold and whether the current force can survive the delay.
loop: Check savings and the next threshold
decisions: Can you afford another loss to preserve an interest threshold?
Keep saving near elimination or spend the reserve for immediate strength?

parameters.name: Interest thresholds
parameters.effect: Thresholds make each coin near a breakpoint matter more.

parameters.name: Interest cap
parameters.effect: A cap creates a clear spending point and limits compounding advantage.

cases.implementation: Banked gold grants interest, encouraging delayed purchases, rerolls or leveling for economic growth; thresholds and caps depend on the rules version.
Savings add round income; official updates changed the interest cap, illustrating how delayed investment must stay balanced against immediate spending.

mechanics.contrast: Both reward banked gold, but income sources, timing and version-specific caps differ; one patch’s numbers are not a universal rule.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a shop earns savings interest while a loan approaches repayment; retaining cash raises income but may leave too little stock to repay on time.

walkthrough.setup: In this example, each ten saved coins earns one interest; you have twenty and need an upgrade.
walkthrough.action: Spend two coins on a small upgrade.
walkthrough.result: Savings fall to eighteen, reducing next interest from two to one.
walkthrough.next: Decide whether the upgrade is enough; otherwise consider spending further for a meaningful improvement.

prototype.firstStep: Build three numerical rounds, two upgrades and a visible interest preview.
prototype.pitfall: Unclear timing feels unfair; preview the income change before spending.
prototype.test: Can players explain the interest lost on a purchase and why it is worthwhile?

mechanics.name: Recruit from a shared stock
mechanics.summary: Opponents buying the same unit reduce your remaining supply.
mechanics.rules: Copies of each unit come from a finite pool shared by all players, and shops draw from what remains. Observe opponents’ holdings before chasing more copies or switching to less contested choices. Rules such as selling can return stock.
loop: Inspect your roster and rivals’ holdings
Buy or pass on a contested unit
Let the shared remainder affect future offers
decisions: Keep rerolling after investing heavily if several opponents want the same unit?
Is denying a needed copy worth tying up cash and bench space?

parameters.name: Copies per unit
parameters.effect: Smaller pools make scouting more important and force more pivots.

parameters.name: Return rules
parameters.effect: Returns after selling or elimination can reopen scarce options and create timing windows.

cases.implementation: All players recruit from a shared champion pool, so others’ choices affect availability and give scouting economic value.
Hero copies likewise come from a common pool; opponents’ purchases reduce copies available to shops, with stock differing by cost tier.

mechanics.contrast: Both turn recruitment into indirect resource competition, but unit tiers, pool sizes and roster rules prevent transferring the same recruitment odds.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: limited inventory slots constrain stockpiling, forcing a choice between holding scarce recruits to deny rivals and keeping useful tools.

walkthrough.setup: A unit has six shared copies; you hold two and rivals hold three.
walkthrough.action: After scouting, stop repeatedly rerolling for the final copy.
walkthrough.result: You preserve cash but leave the intended combination incomplete.
walkthrough.next: Buy an abundant alternative or wait for a rival to sell.

prototype.firstStep: Use two local players and three shared unit pools, updating counts on each purchase.
prototype.pitfall: Without explaining the shared source, changing odds feel like pure luck.
prototype.test: Do opponents’ holdings change reroll and pivot decisions?

mechanics.name: Reserve a shop item for a later purchase
mechanics.summary: Keep a useful offer even when you cannot afford it yet.
mechanics.rules: Mark an offer to persist through rerolls or restocking while unmarked slots refresh. Reservation buys time for money or a combination, but occupies space that could reveal new options. Releasing it restores that slot.
loop: Find an offer you cannot use yet
Reserve it and refresh other slots
Gain resources or revise your needs
Buy it or release the slot
decisions: Will reserving a future combo piece hide more useful immediate offers?
Once you can afford it, should changed needs make you release it anyway?

parameters.name: Reservation capacity
parameters.effect: More reserved slots reduce fear of missing out; fewer make shop space costly.

parameters.name: Persistence
parameters.effect: One-reroll persistence supports short choices; multi-round persistence supports longer plans.

cases.implementation: The documented demo rules allow shop items to be reserved across rerolls or the next round, letting players wait for coins or inventory space.
Shop pets and food can be frozen, keeping them from being replaced on a reroll while the player waits for money or a useful upgrade.

mechanics.contrast: Backpack Battles adds physical inventory fit; Super Auto Pets emphasizes the team, pet upgrades and food effects.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: reserving an oddly shaped item creates a packing goal for the next round, with the option to release it when making room costs too much.

walkthrough.setup: A six-coin sword appears while you have four coins and expect three next round.
walkthrough.action: Reserve the sword and reroll only the other slots.
walkthrough.result: The sword remains, but one fewer slot reveals new items.
walkthrough.next: Next round, compare buying the sword with releasing it to seek alternatives.

prototype.firstStep: Build a four-slot shop, reroll button, coins and reservation markers across two rounds.
prototype.pitfall: Visually distinguish reservation from ownership.
prototype.test: Do players release obsolete reservations rather than hold every slot forever?

mechanics.name: Reverse the next pass to compensate late picks
mechanics.summary: Early players pick first; late players may pair consecutive picks.
mechanics.rules: For repeated picks, proceed in order and then reverse the next pass. This reduces repeated first access while making the gap until the next pick important. Players at the turn-around can take consecutive picks and secure a pair.
loop: Pick again after the order reverses
Build a plan from the pair
decisions: Take the strongest standalone item first or start a combination that needs another piece?
Use consecutive picks for a pair or two broadly strong options?

parameters.name: Number of passes
parameters.effect: One out-and-back pass is easy to read; repeated reversals need persistent order cues.

parameters.name: Pair strength
parameters.effect: Stronger pair rewards make consecutive picks more valuable.

cases.implementation: Each round drafts once in player order and then once in reverse, giving the last player adjacent picks.
In standard variable setup, players place one settlement-road pair in order, then place the second pair in reverse from the last player; normal turns do not use this order.

mechanics.contrast: Sagrada repeats the pattern for each dice draft; Catan primarily uses it for initial placement before normal turn order resumes.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: snake-draft dual-use cards, letting early players secure versatile cards while the last player takes a production-and-action pair together.

walkthrough.setup: Three players draft six tools in the order A, B, C, C, B, A.
walkthrough.action: C takes a saw and clamp consecutively.
walkthrough.result: C completes a pair while A’s strong first pick lacks support.
walkthrough.next: A must take a general tool last or plan to find support later.

prototype.firstStep: Use three local players, six tool cards and two pair bonuses with the full order visible.
prototype.pitfall: Snake order offsets some first-pick advantage but cannot balance every reward structure.
prototype.test: Do early and late pickers use different strategies and explain why?

mechanics.name: Choose a phase that others can also use
mechanics.summary: Opening your action can also advance an opponent’s plan.
mechanics.rules: Players choose phases, then only selected phases occur. Eligible rivals may participate as well. Predict others’ choices to use phases they open, while choosing a phase yourself guarantees it or earns a selector benefit.
loop: Choose a phase you must guarantee
Use the result to predict the next round
decisions: Trust someone else to select production and choose selling, or guarantee production yourself?
Open a useful phase if it advances an opponent’s score even more?

parameters.name: Hidden selection
parameters.effect: Simultaneous hidden picks emphasize prediction; visible sequential picks emphasize response.

parameters.name: Selector benefit
parameters.effect: A benefit compensates for opening a public opportunity without making following pointless.

cases.implementation: Players choose action cards simultaneously; selected phases occur for everyone, with a matching bonus for the player who selected each phase.
cases.rights: Temple Gates Games / Rio Grande Games

cases.implementation: A die selects a guaranteed phase while worker dice are assigned across phases; phases selected by others also occur, but a player needs assigned workers to act in them.
cases.rights: Temple Gates Games / Rio Grande Games

mechanics.contrast: Race uses action cards and selector bonuses; Roll additionally requires advance worker allocation, so predicting a phase is insufficient without assigned workers.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: factories each choose a public production step; only selected steps run, allowing one player to rely on a rival’s processing phase and choose transport instead.

walkthrough.setup: You have raw material and the opponent has material ready to process; both may choose processing.
walkthrough.action: Expect the opponent to process and choose transport.
walkthrough.result: The opponent selects processing, so both phases occur and you process before shipping.
walkthrough.next: The opponent’s stock is now empty, so the same prediction may fail next round.

prototype.firstStep: Use two local players choosing among three phases privately; resolve production, processing and selling in fixed order.
prototype.pitfall: Distinguish selecting a phase from eligibility to act in it.
prototype.test: Do players predict phases from rivals’ stock and explain failed predictions?

mechanics.name: Drift to charge a release boost
mechanics.summary: Hold a drift through a corner to earn a longer burst on the exit.
mechanics.rules: Maintain a drift through a corner while steering and building a boost. Releasing the drift converts the stored reward into a short burst. Judge how much longer the line is safe and whether the exit has enough room to use the speed.
loop: Adjust the line and watch charge
decisions: Keep charging or release now to stay on the road?
Is a full boost useful with another corner so close?

parameters.name: Charge thresholds
parameters.effect: The spacing between thresholds shapes the temptation to hold a little longer.

parameters.name: Steering during a drift
parameters.effect: Limited correction makes entry position matter; too much can remove the line choice.

cases.implementation: Sustained drifting produces colored tire sparks. Releasing the drift activates a Mini-Turbo whose duration depends on the reached tier.
A continuous drift builds a boost that releases when the drift button is let go, with limited steering corrections during the drift.

mechanics.contrast: Mario Kart communicates tiers through spark colors; the Sonic manual emphasizes sustaining a drift with limited correction. Both connect the cornering line to exit speed.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: give deliveries a deadline, with unloading just after a tight bend. A boost saves time but makes stopping harder.

walkthrough.setup: In the teaching prototype, a long bend leads to a straight. The drift has reached its first tier.
walkthrough.action: Hold for another half-second and steer slightly inward.
walkthrough.result: Tier two lights up. Releasing gives a longer boost, but the vehicle is now near the road edge.
walkthrough.next: Return to a safe line, then decide whether to enter the next turn earlier.

prototype.firstStep: Use a top-down rectangle vehicle, one bend and two charge tiers to test release timing.
prototype.pitfall: Establish predictable steering first; more vehicles and tracks amplify unclear drift feedback.
prototype.test: Can players explain why they released early in one corner and held longer in another?

mechanics.name: Follow a lead vehicle to gain speed
mechanics.summary: Hold a following position to gain speed, then move aside to pass.
mechanics.rules: A favorable zone behind a lead vehicle reduces drag or grants a timed boost to a follower that stays in position. The follower then chooses between staying behind and moving out to pass. Implementations can use continuous drag reduction or a boost awarded after following for a while.
loop: Read the speed gap and road ahead
Pull out to pass or keep following
decisions: Keep following for an advantage or pass before the road narrows?
Is staying close worth it when the lead car is about to brake?

parameters.name: Following zone
parameters.effect: A narrow zone demands alignment; a very wide zone requires little input.

parameters.name: How the gain develops
parameters.effect: Continuous drag reduction rewards positioning; a delayed boost creates a clear moment to pass.

cases.implementation: Stay close behind a rival through the airflow effect to gain a temporary speed increase for catching up.
The official competition guide explains that following closely reduces drag, building a speed advantage for overtaking on a straight.

mechanics.contrast: Mario Kart turns following into an explicit temporary boost; Gran Turismo explains the passing opportunity through reduced drag and a speed difference.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: in a two-person delivery vehicle, one player drives while another watches the road and nearby traffic, coordinating when to follow and pass on a shared screen.

walkthrough.setup: In the teaching prototype, a slightly slower follower approaches a lead car on a straight before a bend.
walkthrough.action: Align behind the lead car and hold a short following distance.
walkthrough.result: The follower gains speed, but staying directly behind would cause contact.
walkthrough.next: Pull aside to pass or slow down and give up the opportunity.

prototype.firstStep: Use two lanes, one fixed-speed lead car and a following zone before building racing opponents.
prototype.pitfall: Make lead-car slowing and collision distance legible so failures do not feel random.
prototype.test: Do players deliberately leave the best following position when choosing a passing moment?

mechanics.name: Time the throttle during the countdown
mechanics.summary: One or several timed throttle inputs determine the speed gained at the start.
mechanics.rules: A countdown supplies predictable audio or visual cues. Throttle inputs within a valid window charge or trigger a start boost; early, missed or mistimed inputs can lose the reward. Read the cue, act, see the launch result and adjust the next attempt in a short practice loop.
loop: Read the boost or failure feedback
Adjust timing on the next attempt
decisions: Choose a safer timing window or aim for a more precise, stronger launch?
During repeated charges, chase the next cue or stick to a rhythm you can reliably execute?

parameters.name: Valid input window
parameters.effect: A wide window is approachable; a narrow one needs clearer cues and failure explanations.

parameters.name: Failure cost
parameters.effect: Losing only the bonus supports learning; an extra delay makes early input riskier.
