cases.implementation: Holding acceleration at the countdown’s two can trigger a Rocket Start. Better timing extends the boost; starting too early causes failure.
In typical races, pressing and releasing the throttle with countdown cues builds successive start-boost levels. Some time-trial and challenge starts differ.

mechanics.contrast: Mario Kart focuses on when to begin holding the throttle; Sonic typically asks for repeated inputs across the countdown.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: preheat a food truck’s pan into a useful window, then launch accurately to deliver hot food. Overlapping timing windows create an attention tradeoff.

walkthrough.setup: The teaching prototype changes its cue light once a second, with a short input window after the final light.
walkthrough.action: Hold the throttle after noticing the final cue.
walkthrough.result: The car launches with a boost; feedback shows the input was slightly late.
walkthrough.next: Try slightly earlier on the next attempt and compare launch distance.

prototype.firstStep: Build a countdown, one button and a three-second straight sprint, then show timing error after each attempt.
prototype.pitfall: Handle input latency and cue synchronization before interpreting player errors.
prototype.test: Can players use feedback to consistently adjust their next input in the right direction?

mechanics.name: Perform an airborne trick for a boost
mechanics.summary: Turn a ramp’s brief airtime into an extra action and a speed reward.
mechanics.rules: A ramp or drop creates a trick window at takeoff or during airtime. Successful input awards a boost. The rules determine the timing window and how many actions can be chained, so players read the terrain and judge whether enough time remains.
loop: Use the reward for the next section
decisions: Take the smooth route or a drop that offers a trick?
Is there time for another trick, or should you prepare to land?

parameters.name: Where the window occurs
parameters.effect: A takeoff input rewards anticipation; midair input rewards judging remaining airtime.

parameters.name: Chained-trick reward
parameters.effect: Increasing rewards tempt one more trick, but the reason for a failed attempt must be legible.

cases.implementation: A correctly timed trick input at a ramp or drop earns a Jump Boost that activates on landing.
A jumping car or boat can perform directional rolls, with successful chains earning a boost. Plane mode also supports close-call rolls near obstacles.

mechanics.contrast: Mario Kart emphasizes timing at takeoff; Sonic permits a sequence of directional actions during a jump, adding an airtime-allocation decision.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: random routes change ramps and exits, forcing players to decide which jumps are worth a trick and which need full attention on landing.

walkthrough.setup: The teaching prototype has long and short jumps, with each trick taking a fixed amount of time.
walkthrough.action: Complete one trick on the long jump, then attempt a second.
walkthrough.result: The second finishes just in time, earning two rewards on landing; the short jump cannot fit both.
walkthrough.next: On the next short jump, the player chooses only one trick.

prototype.firstStep: Start with fixed jump arcs, two airtimes and one trick button; vehicle physics is unnecessary for this timing test.
prototype.pitfall: Match animation and completion timing so a visibly finished trick does not fail.
prototype.test: Do players change the number of tricks according to jump length?

mechanics.name: Adjust vehicle pitch before landing
mechanics.summary: Change pitch while airborne so the wheels meet the next surface at a useful angle.
mechanics.rules: After leaving the ground, lean or throttle/brake inputs affect vehicle rotation. Read the landing slope, adjust toward a viable angle and touch down to continue. Overcorrection creates a new tilt, making when to stop input as important as when to begin.
loop: Take off and read the landing slope
Correct the pitch and stop in time
Land and prepare for the next rise
decisions: Correct strongly now or wait until the landing is clearer?
With the pitch near its target, should the input continue?

parameters.name: Pitch response and inertia
parameters.effect: Fast response enables late correction; greater inertia requires releasing earlier.

parameters.name: Landing tolerance
parameters.effect: A wide tolerance supports learning; a narrow one makes slope reading and small corrections matter.

cases.implementation: Airborne movement and landing require balancing the bike. The official tandem-bike example asks both players to coordinate leaning and right the bike during a long fall.
Throttle and brake also influence rotation while airborne. Players use these inputs to correct the landing angle over uneven terrain.

mechanics.contrast: Trials emphasizes rider lean and bike balance, with coordination added in tandem mode; Hill Climb Racing maps airborne rotation to the existing throttle and brake controls.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: cargo weight changes pitch response. Before leaving, choose more cargo or easier handling, starting with just light and heavy settings.

walkthrough.setup: In the teaching prototype, the nose is raised while the landing surface slopes downward.
walkthrough.action: Briefly apply forward pitch to rotate the nose toward the slope.
walkthrough.result: The vehicle approaches the slope angle, with a little rotation remaining after release.
walkthrough.next: Releasing early allows a safe landing and informs the next jump’s correction.

prototype.firstStep: Use a rotating rectangle, a fixed jump arc and two landing slopes to test input against landing angle.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid complex suspension, damage and multiple wheel contacts until pitch changes are predictable.
prototype.test: After failing, can players identify late input versus holding too long and improve the next attempt?

mechanics.name: Earn by hand, then buy passive output
mechanics.summary: Turn the first manual earnings into a continuing income, then reconsider where to spend attention.
mechanics.rules: Earn resources through a direct action such as clicking, then buy units that keep producing. Manual input can still supplement automatic income. Decide whether to act, buy another producer or save for a different purchase. The focus is the handoff from manual to passive output, not a production chain.
decisions: Buy a cheap producer now or keep acting until a more efficient one is affordable?
Once passive income grows, is the extra manual gain worth the attention?

parameters.name: Producer payback time
parameters.effect: Short payback shifts attention toward investment sooner; long payback keeps manual input relevant.

parameters.name: Manual scaling
parameters.effect: Flat manual rewards soon become irrelevant; scaling them preserves a reason to intervene.

cases.implementation: Click the big cookie for cookies, then spend them on buildings such as cursors that supply continuing production.
Initially click monsters for damage and gold, then hire heroes that attack automatically. Manual clicks and hero damage can both advance a run.

mechanics.contrast: Cookie Clicker converts investment directly into production per second; Clicker Heroes converts it into damage, then gold from defeated enemies.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: finance the first producer with a loan that requires a fixed payment each round, making early automation a solvency decision.

walkthrough.setup: Each manual craft earns one coin. You have ten; a machine costs ten and yields two each round.
walkthrough.action: Buy the machine, then craft twice by hand.
walkthrough.result: The next round combines two machine coins with two manual coins, totaling four.
walkthrough.next: The next machine costs more; decide whether to craft or wait for income.

prototype.firstStep: Build one manual button, one currency and one purchasable income timer.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid dozens of upgrades before players can distinguish manual rewards from income per second.
prototype.test: Does buying a passive producer change how often players choose to act?

mechanics.name: Set up earnings before leaving
mechanics.summary: Offline rewards depend on the setup left behind and may have a time limit.
mechanics.rules: Before leaving, choose a continuing action or production setup. On return, the game settles eligible offline time; consumables, capacity or time limits may stop equivalent gains. The reason progress stopped informs the next preparation.
loop: Fix the limiting factor for next time
decisions: For a long absence, choose high output that soon exhausts materials or lower sustainable output?
Improve production speed or extend the useful offline window first?

parameters.name: Eligible offline time
parameters.effect: Shorter caps create more mismatch with time away; clearly show when settlement stops.

parameters.name: Offline efficiency
parameters.effect: Matching online efficiency is easier to read; if it differs, show both the rate and reason.

cases.implementation: The selected activity can continue earning experience and items under offline-progression rules. Eligible time is capped, and activity requirements still matter.
The PC version unlocks and improves offline production through heavenly upgrades, affecting efficiency and the optimal production window. Mobile rules differ.

mechanics.contrast: Melvor carries over the chosen activity and its requirements; PC Cookie Clicker makes offline efficiency and duration upgradeable capabilities.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: offline gathering fills a limited-slot store. Before leaving, reserve slots or gather an already stacked resource; explain what filled the storage first.

walkthrough.setup: Mining yields ten ore an hour with a four-hour eligible window; the player expects six hours away.
walkthrough.action: Extend the window to six hours before starting mining.
walkthrough.result: Return to sixty ore and a report that all six hours counted.
walkthrough.next: A longer absence creates a new choice between duration and speed.

prototype.firstStep: Save an exit time and one task; settle a capped elapsed duration on return with a visible breakdown.
prototype.pitfall: Define behavior for clock changes, duplicate settlement and exhausted materials.
prototype.test: Can players explain a shortfall from the settlement report?

mechanics.name: Allocate capacity across ongoing projects
mechanics.summary: Assigned capacity is not immediately consumed, but one project cannot use capacity committed elsewhere.
mechanics.rules: Assign a limited pool of capacity to ongoing projects. More allocation usually speeds progress, but individual projects may have a speed cap. Capacity can be withdrawn and reassigned. Compare progress and rewards to choose focused completion or parallel growth.
decisions: Concentrate on an urgent project or keep long-term projects progressing?
If a project is already at maximum speed, is leaving capacity there convenient or wasteful?

parameters.name: Allocation-to-speed curve
parameters.effect: A linear relationship is easy to estimate; caps or diminishing returns encourage reassignment.

parameters.name: Reassignment cost
parameters.effect: Free reassignment supports continuous optimization; cooldowns or lost progress make commitment matter.

cases.implementation: Energy and Magic can be assigned to training, augments, NGUs and other features to advance their progress; assigned resources are unavailable elsewhere.
Shadow clones can train physical and skill exercises. Each training has a clone requirement for its fastest rate, and the Cap control helps allocate that amount.

mechanics.contrast: NGU distributes capacity across many long-term features; Idling to Rule the Gods represents it as clones and exposes training caps that reveal excess allocation.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: let players set a condition that moves capacity to the next project on completion, after they first understand manual allocation.

walkthrough.setup: Ten capacity points are available. A needs twenty progress; B has just begun. Each point adds one progress per round.
walkthrough.action: Assign all ten points to A.
walkthrough.result: A completes after two rounds, releasing all ten points.
walkthrough.next: Move capacity to B or reserve some for newly unlocked C.

prototype.firstStep: Build two progress bars, one fixed capacity pool and allocation controls.
prototype.pitfall: Clearly distinguish spent resources from temporarily assigned capacity so players feel able to reallocate.
prototype.test: Do players reclaim excess capacity near a cap or completion?

mechanics.name: Spend a resource that also grants a held bonus
mechanics.summary: The same resource funds purchases and contributes to current output.
mechanics.rules: Holding a resource grants an ongoing bonus, but it can also purchase specific upgrades. Spending reduces the balance and its existing bonus. An upgrade must outweigh that loss to be worthwhile, so compare the total before and after rather than the upgrade text alone.
loop: Check the bonus from the held balance
Compare the upgrade with the lost bonus
Choose an amount to spend or retain
Judge the result by total output
decisions: Is a strong upgrade worth spending most of the reserve and lowering its existing bonus?
Make small purchases and observe the result, or save for a pivotal one?

parameters.name: Held-bonus curve
parameters.effect: A sensitive low-balance curve encourages a reserve; a flatter curve makes spending easier.

parameters.name: Before-and-after preview
parameters.effect: Showing the net change makes this a strategy decision rather than a calculation trap.

cases.implementation: Unspent Hero Souls grant damage and can also summon or level Ancients. Spending changes both the remaining balance bonus and the purchased ability.
Angel Investors boost profits and can be sacrificed for angel upgrades. Spent angels stop contributing their previous profit bonus.

mechanics.contrast: Clicker Heroes weighs balance-based damage against Ancient abilities; AdVenture Capitalist weighs the general profit bonus against angel upgrades.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: unequipped energy shards grant a small global bonus; slotting them into abilities trades that bonus for a stronger local effect.

walkthrough.setup: Ten gems yield twenty per round. Spending four lowers balance-adjusted output to sixteen before a new 1.5× upgrade.
walkthrough.action: Inspect the net-output preview and buy.
walkthrough.result: Final output becomes twenty-four, four more than before.
walkthrough.next: A more expensive next upgrade requires a fresh comparison.

prototype.firstStep: Use one currency with a held bonus, two upgrades and a before-and-after preview.
prototype.pitfall: Do not show only the upgrade percentage while hiding the lost balance bonus.
prototype.test: Can players explain why buying a particular upgrade now could make them weaker?

mechanics.name: Reach a quantity threshold for a production jump
mechanics.summary: The final investments before a threshold may matter more than ordinary ones.
mechanics.rules: Purchases or levels increase a count. Reaching a visible threshold grants an extra speed or output bonus. Ordinary gains between thresholds are smoother, while crossing one creates a jump. Compare distance to the next threshold as well as immediate return.
loop: Estimate the cost to reach it
Complete one set or spread investment
decisions: Buy the best current return or complete another item that is close to a multiplier?
Is improving the weakest item worthwhile to earn an all-items threshold reward?

parameters.name: Threshold spacing
parameters.effect: Short intervals create frequent goals; long intervals need clear progress and reward previews.

parameters.name: Local versus global reward
parameters.effect: Local rewards encourage focus; all-items rewards give a reason to improve lagging projects.

cases.implementation: Many heroes gain additional damage multipliers at level thresholds, changing the value of further levels near those points. Heroes and late-game ranges have exceptions.
Business-count unlocks grant speed or profit rewards, including goals that require multiple businesses to reach a count, changing purchase priorities.

mechanics.contrast: Clicker Heroes mainly changes a particular hero’s damage at thresholds; AdVenture Capitalist also uses counts to create goals across businesses.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: unlock a global speed reward when all three lines reach five items per round, encouraging material redistribution to lagging lines.

walkthrough.setup: Producer A has nine units and doubles at ten; B currently offers a slightly better per-unit return.
walkthrough.action: Buy the tenth A first.
walkthrough.result: The whole A group doubles, outperforming the immediate B purchase.
walkthrough.next: A’s next threshold is distant, so reconsider buying B.

prototype.firstStep: Build two producer types with one count threshold each; show purchases remaining to the reward.
prototype.pitfall: Do not bury threshold rewards in long lists or purchases become blind clicking.
prototype.test: Do players switch their purchase target as different thresholds approach?

mechanics.name: Each additional copy costs more
mechanics.summary: An earlier choice grows more expensive, forcing each next investment to be reconsidered.
mechanics.rules: Every copy of a producer raises the price of the next, while its base output can stay constant. Compare additional income and payback time, switching among producer types. This decision comes from rising marginal cost, independently of threshold rewards.
loop: Buy or save for another type
decisions: Keep buying the familiar cheaper producer or wait for a larger, better-returning one?
Does buying in bulk save effort but pass the point where another producer becomes better?

parameters.name: Price growth per copy
parameters.effect: Fast growth encourages earlier switching; slow growth keeps one choice attractive longer.

parameters.name: Return display
parameters.effect: Showing added output alongside the next price supports comparison better than total output alone.

cases.implementation: The next base price of a building type rises with the number owned, encouraging repeated comparison of marginal production from buildings and upgrades.
Each added business investment raises subsequent cost using that business’s growth coefficient. Different coefficients mean a previously cheap option need not remain efficient.

mechanics.contrast: Cookie Clicker uses a broadly shared base price-growth rule; AdVenture Capitalist gives businesses differing cost-growth rates.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: hire increasingly expensive workers to meet a contract deadline, buying only enough capacity to finish without leaving an unpayable investment afterward.

walkthrough.setup: A adds one output: the next costs ten, the one after fifteen. B adds two for twenty-four.
walkthrough.action: Buy the ten-coin A.
walkthrough.result: The next A now costs fifteen, changing the comparison for further purchases.
walkthrough.next: Reconsider B rather than repeatedly clicking the same button.

prototype.firstStep: Use two producer types and one currency; show the rising next price, not the historical average.
prototype.pitfall: Prevent overflow or rounding that makes distinct prices appear identical.
prototype.test: Can players notice that the best next purchase changes with ownership counts?

mechanics.name: Overlap temporary income boosts
mechanics.summary: A short overlap of two boosts can be worth more than using each separately.
mechanics.rules: Temporary output boosts may be activated deliberately or appear as opportunities. Compatible simultaneous effects can multiply returns or amplify particular actions. Choose between waiting for overlap and using a boost immediately, then rebuild the conditions for another window.
loop: Inspect active boosts and time remaining
Set up the next window afterward
decisions: Take a certain gain now or wait for a combination that may not arrive?
With little time left, keep setting up or perform the action that benefits now?

parameters.name: Stacking rule
parameters.effect: Multiplication emphasizes timing; addition is gentler; incompatible effects need explicit feedback.

parameters.name: Overlap duration
parameters.effect: Short windows emphasize preparation and execution; long windows emphasize resource planning.

cases.implementation: Compatible golden-cookie effects such as Frenzy and Click Frenzy can overlap for a large earning window; not every effect stacks freely.
Production spells last for a duration, while Tax Collection grants an immediate amount based on production, allowing it to be cast during production boosts.

mechanics.contrast: Cookie Clicker often responds to golden-cookie opportunities; Realm Grinder more directly schedules spells around mana reserves.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: overlap a double-order-reward window with a faster oven, encouraging advance preparation and targeted order priority.

walkthrough.setup: One boost doubles output for three rounds; another becomes ready next round and triples output for one round.
walkthrough.action: Start the longer boost now and the short boost next round.
walkthrough.result: With multiplicative rules, the overlapping round yields sixfold output.
walkthrough.next: Afterward, rebuild the resources needed to trigger another window.

prototype.firstStep: Build two timed boosts and one output action; display how simultaneous effects are calculated.
prototype.pitfall: Do not require an external calculator to discover incompatible effects.
prototype.test: Do players wait for an understandable overlap rather than activate every ready button?

mechanics.name: Spend an item to bring future earnings forward
mechanics.summary: The same time token can produce different results after improving the setup.
mechanics.rules: A limited time-advance item immediately settles a duration under eligible current production or progress rules. Upgrading first can change the reward, but waiting has an opportunity cost. The game must clarify which systems advance and whether temporary effects count.
loop: Decide whether to improve the setup first
Spend it to advance eligible progress
Invest the proceeds into the next loop
decisions: Use the item to pass a bottleneck now or wait for an upgrade that makes it more valuable?
Spend several at once or reinvest between uses?

parameters.name: Settlement basis
parameters.effect: Using current rates is easy to predict; simulation must explain mid-period stoppages and unlocks.

parameters.name: Affected systems
parameters.effect: A local effect creates a targeting choice; global advancement needs clear consistent boundaries.

cases.implementation: Time Warps grant a duration’s profits immediately and display the amount in advance; official help specifies that they affect the planet where purchased.
Timelapse exchanges rubies for time advancement and associated gold. It follows its own settlement rules, not a simulation of every possible manual click.

mechanics.contrast: AdVenture Capitalist emphasizes a planet’s immediate profit preview; Clicker Heroes places time advancement within hero, skill and quest progression.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a limited time token advances workshop output and debt payments due in that interval, requiring a net-income check.

walkthrough.setup: Output is five coins per round. A token advances ten rounds; a twenty-coin upgrade raises output to eight.
walkthrough.action: Buy the upgrade before using the token.
walkthrough.result: The token yields eighty instead of fifty, while the upgrade has cost twenty.
walkthrough.next: Reevaluate when to use the next token with the new balance.

prototype.firstStep: Advance one resource only, previewing duration, expected income and exclusions.
prototype.pitfall: Prototype with tokens earned through play rather than requiring real purchases.
prototype.test: Do players inspect production before choosing to use or save a token?

mechanics.name: Dispatch limited teams for delayed rewards
mechanics.summary: A long task occupies a team, so its reward must be weighed against missed alternatives.
mechanics.rules: Assign limited teams or characters to tasks with durations and rewards. Dispatched units are unavailable for other tasks; suitability and risk affect outcomes. On completion, recover the team and rewards. The key cost is how long a team remains committed, not personally fulfilling an order.
loop: Wait and bear the commitment cost
decisions: Commit the strongest team to a long high-reward task or keep it for new opportunities?
Risk a poorly matched team or leave a slot idle?

parameters.name: Concurrent assignments
parameters.effect: Few slots emphasize priority; too many can reduce the choice to dispatching everyone.

parameters.name: Duration-risk relationship
parameters.effect: Long tasks can change risk, rare rewards or preparation requirements rather than only scaling payout.

cases.implementation: Mercenaries undertake quests of differing durations and reward types, occupying that mercenary; death and revival add further trade-offs.
Players assemble frigates for fleet expeditions, matching the fleet to the task and waiting for returns; expeditions can also send events requiring a response.

mechanics.contrast: Clicker Heroes centers on individual mercenary duration and rewards; No Man’s Sky adds fleet composition, suitability and expedition events.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: equip each team with one meal; stamina food shortens the task while protective food reduces damage risk, competing for shared ingredients.

walkthrough.setup: Two teams face one three-round task and two one-round tasks.
walkthrough.action: Send the strong team on the long task and the other on one short task.
walkthrough.result: After one round, only the short-task team is available.
walkthrough.next: Choose another short task or reserve the team for a new opportunity.

prototype.firstStep: Build two team slots, three timed tasks and completion settlement without real multiplayer or a backend.
prototype.pitfall: Make completion, reward claiming and team release explicit states that cannot duplicate rewards.
prototype.test: Do players ever reserve a team for an expected task rather than always dispatch everyone?

mechanics.name: Farm reliably or push ahead
mechanics.summary: The next stage is tempting, but a familiar target may better fund the next breakthrough.
mechanics.rules: Repeat a reliably completed target to build resources, or attempt a harder new target. Progress can unlock better rewards, but time, failure or supply costs can slow accumulation. Use observed performance to return to farming, upgrade and try again.
loop: Observe yield and costs over time
decisions: Does barely beating a new enemy actually earn more than quickly repeating an old one?
Accept lower efficiency for a new drop or build reliable upgrades first?

parameters.name: Failure cost
parameters.effect: Losing only time encourages probing; losing supplies or equipment makes preparation more important.

parameters.name: Yield visibility
parameters.effect: Showing completion time, drops and consumption helps explain why harder need not be more profitable.

cases.implementation: Farm Mode stays in one zone earning gold; Progression Mode advances through zones until a boss cannot be beaten in time.
Players select combat areas or dungeons, repeating familiar enemies for materials or taking on harder targets; survivability and supplies determine whether the activity can continue.

mechanics.contrast: Clicker Heroes exposes a direct farming/progression switch; Melvor creates a similar loop through target-area, equipment and supply choices.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: harder targets wear equipment faster; show net earnings and repair costs so returning to an easier target is a meaningful option.

walkthrough.setup: An old target drops four coins each round; a new one takes three rounds and drops ten.
walkthrough.action: Farm the old target for three rounds, then spend the earnings on attack.
walkthrough.result: After upgrading, the new target takes two rounds, making its average yield higher.
walkthrough.next: Move to the new target and reassess at the next bottleneck.

prototype.firstStep: Build two targets, one automatic-resolution timer and an upgrade that affects speed.
prototype.pitfall: Show time and net yield rather than only enemy levels, so players can understand a stall.
prototype.test: After failing, do players know where to gather what they need and then retry?

mechanics.name: Swap neighbors to complete a match
mechanics.summary: Swap two positions while considering both the immediate clear and the board left behind.
mechanics.rules: Swap adjacent pieces to align enough matching pieces horizontally or vertically. Matched pieces disappear and pieces above fill the gaps; a swap that makes no match usually reverses. Search the new arrangement for the next useful move.
loop: Find a group missing one position
decisions: Take the easiest match or preserve it while setting up something larger?
A larger clear scores well, but does it affect the cells the goal requires?

parameters.name: Match threshold
parameters.effect: Higher thresholds require more preparation and stronger guarantees that useful moves exist.

parameters.name: Number of colors
parameters.effect: Fewer colors create frequent matches; more colors increase the time spent looking for an opening.

cases.implementation: Swap adjacent candies to align at least three of one color. Pieces refill, while the remaining moves constrain completion of the level goal.
Adjacent gem swaps create lines of at least three matching gems. Classic mode centers on scoring while keeping legal matches available.

mechanics.contrast: Candy Crush values swaps against a level objective and move budget; Bejeweled 3 Classic emphasizes continuing to score as the board changes.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: make board swaps and character movement spend the same action points, forcing a choice between earning healing resources and escaping danger.

walkthrough.setup: A row reads red, red, blue, with a red piece below the blue. Four moves remain.
walkthrough.action: Swap the blue piece with the red below it.
walkthrough.result: Three reds clear, the target count drops by three, and three moves remain.
walkthrough.next: New pieces create another incomplete group, so the next swap must be reconsidered.

prototype.firstStep: Build a six-by-six board with four colors, swapping, matching, refill and one collection goal.
prototype.pitfall: Random refill can leave no legal swaps; specify reshuffle or failure behavior first.
prototype.test: Can players explain why one swap advances the goal more than another?

mechanics.name: Trace a path through matching pieces
mechanics.summary: One drag selects a whole route; both length and endpoint can matter.
mechanics.rules: Trace through matching pieces using the allowed adjacency directions, then release to resolve the selected chain. Gaps and incompatible pieces constrain the route, creating choices about chain length, required targets and where the path ends.
loop: Read the routes created by refill
decisions: Choose the longest chain or a shorter path reaching a useful location?
Would clearing a bridge now split a large group needed next turn?

parameters.name: Allowed adjacency
parameters.effect: Orthogonal adjacency is easier to read; diagonal links greatly increase route options.

parameters.name: Color-switch nodes
parameters.effect: A few switch nodes connect color-separated regions, but legal continuations must remain clear.

cases.implementation: Connect two or more matching dots along horizontal or vertical neighbors; a square clears that color across the board.
Plan an attack path through same-colored enemies; grindstones allow the chain to change color and continue into another group.

mechanics.contrast: Two Dots rewards a closed square with a color clear; Grindstone turns the path into a character attack and adds color-switch junctions.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: use the traced chain as a scouting route that reveals map cells, requiring a safe camp endpoint to retain discoveries.

walkthrough.setup: Blue dots form two branches: the left reaches a target, while the right is longer.
walkthrough.action: The player links the four dots on the left.
walkthrough.result: The clear is smaller, but reaches the required target cell.
walkthrough.next: Refill creates a new opportunity to connect the right-hand region next turn.

prototype.firstStep: Make a five-by-five board with a reversible path preview and orthogonal links only.
prototype.pitfall: Corners can cause accidental selection; preview and backtracking need reliable behavior.
prototype.test: Do players deliberately shorten chains for a better endpoint or target cell?

mechanics.name: Clear a connected group with one tap
mechanics.summary: Rearrange the surroundings to join small groups, then decide when to collect them.
mechanics.rules: Tap an orthogonally connected group of matching blocks that meets the minimum size to clear the whole group. Other blocks move into gaps, potentially joining previously separated groups. The chosen group changes both immediate rewards and future connections.
loop: Compare immediate clearing with future connections
Tap the group to resolve it
Use the groups formed by movement
decisions: Clear a small divider to connect two large groups or collect an existing group now?
Is a small group beside the objective worth more than a distant large group?

parameters.name: Minimum group size
parameters.effect: A lower threshold reduces dead ends; a higher one emphasizes preparing the surroundings.

parameters.name: Gap movement
parameters.effect: Downward fall and horizontal column compression create different future connections.

cases.implementation: Tap at least two same-colored cubes to clear them; larger groups produce items such as rockets, bombs and disco balls.
Match two or more same-colored blocks to clear obstacles and rescue pets, balancing group size against rescue goals within limited moves.

mechanics.contrast: Toon Blast ties larger groups to special-item creation; Pet Rescue Saga ties clearing to pet rescue. The same input can serve different objectives.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a scanner reveals minerals under colored blocks. Clear a small group to reach a deposit now, or join a larger group to reduce extraction actions.

walkthrough.setup: Upper and lower red groups are separated by two blue blocks, with a collection target at the lower right.
walkthrough.action: Clear the blue divider so the red groups meet after movement.
walkthrough.result: The next action can clear a larger red group and approach the target.
walkthrough.next: The player chooses whether to collect now or connect a nearby smaller red group first.

prototype.firstStep: Build a five-by-six board with downward refill and a preview of the whole tapped group.
prototype.pitfall: Add a positional objective rather than rewarding group size alone, so planning can be observed.
prototype.test: Will players clear a small group to prepare a more useful larger one?

mechanics.name: Complete a line to reclaim space
mechanics.summary: Placed shapes consume room; completing a line returns that room to the player.
mechanics.rules: Place supplied shapes on a limited board. Filling a required row, column or region clears those cells. Every placement consumes future space, so immediate clears must be balanced against holes and room for the next piece.
loop: Inspect the piece and open cells
Fit the next piece into the reclaimed space
decisions: Clear one line to stay safe or build toward a larger simultaneous clear?
A tidy edge placement may leave a hole that later pieces cannot fill.

parameters.name: Piece preview count
parameters.effect: More preview supports multi-step plans; little preview favors flexible empty space.

parameters.name: Clear conditions
parameters.effect: Rows alone focus planning; columns or regions add intersecting clear opportunities.

cases.implementation: Move and rotate falling pieces to complete horizontal lines; Zone can suspend time to accumulate additional line clears.
cases.rights: Monstars / Resonair / Stage Games / Enhance / Tetris Holding

cases.implementation: Drag shapes onto a nine-by-nine board and clear completed rows, columns or three-by-three regions, without falling-piece time pressure.

mechanics.contrast: Tetris Effect compresses decision time through falling pieces; Blockudoku allows static placement and adds region completion.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: supplies occupy shaped inventory cells. Completing a row consumes those supplies for team healing, creating a choice between storage and reclaiming space.

walkthrough.setup: The bottom row has a two-cell gap; the current piece is a domino and the next is a square.
walkthrough.action: Place the domino in the gap.
walkthrough.result: The completed row clears, returning usable space.
walkthrough.next: Inspect the new boundary and place the square without creating isolated holes.

prototype.firstStep: Start with a static six-by-six board, three shapes and row clearing, without real-time fall.
prototype.pitfall: Rotation, previews and random piece supply all affect difficulty; hold two of them fixed initially.
prototype.test: Can players identify the awkward gap a placement would leave before committing?

mechanics.name: Merge matching items into the next tier
mechanics.summary: Merging upgrades an item while compressing several occupied cells into one.
mechanics.rules: Gather enough matching items of the same tier and consume them to create a higher-tier item. The result stays on the board and can enter the next merge. Space must be shared among ingredients, future outputs and temporarily unmatched pieces.
loop: Prepare the next group around the result
decisions: Merge now to free space or wait for more ingredients and a better batch yield?
Keep the result central for another merge or near an edge to reduce obstruction?

parameters.name: Inputs per merge
parameters.effect: More inputs increase storage pressure and the amount of space released by a merge.

parameters.name: Batch bonus
parameters.effect: Batch bonuses reward waiting, but excessive bonuses make small merges feel pointless.

cases.implementation: Merge at least three matching pieces into the next tier, such as grass into bushes and bushes into trees; upgraded pieces remain part of the spatial layout.
Three matching items produce one higher-tier item, while five produce two, creating a trade-off between waiting for a batch and clearing space.

mechanics.contrast: Triple Town couples merge placement to an increasingly occupied town; Merge Dragons explicitly rewards a larger batch with five-to-two conversion.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: merge three mature crops into one perennial, while all ingredients occupy farmland as they grow. Compare immediate harvest income with long-term space savings.

walkthrough.setup: Only two cells remain empty, and four same-tier seedlings are already stored.
walkthrough.action: The player merges three seedlings into one sapling.
walkthrough.result: The player gives up a five-item batch opportunity but immediately frees two cells.
walkthrough.next: The freed cells accept new ingredients, allowing another choice about saving for a batch.

prototype.firstStep: Build a four-by-four board with three item tiers and a fixed three-to-one rule.
prototype.pitfall: Do not start with dozens of merge chains; first test whether space pressure creates meaningful choices.
prototype.test: Can players say whether a merge was primarily for an upgrade or for space?

mechanics.name: Slide the whole board to merge numbers
mechanics.summary: One directional input affects many pieces, so one attractive pair cannot be considered alone.
mechanics.rules: Choose a direction to slide every movable piece. Compatible pieces merge when they meet, and a successful move introduces a new piece. Reclaimed space is continually consumed, so the player must preserve useful movement across the whole board.
loop: Resolve merges and the incoming piece
decisions: Would merging a large pair trap small unmatched numbers in a corner?
Free a cell now or preserve an ordered arrangement for the next tile?

parameters.name: Distance per input
parameters.effect: Sliding to the edge changes more at once; one-cell movement allows finer adjustments while incoming pieces consume room.

parameters.name: Incoming-piece preview
parameters.effect: Preview supports planning around the entry; unknown pieces require more flexible free space.

cases.implementation: Arrow-key input slides the board; equal values merge into a larger number and a valid move introduces a new low-value tile.
Each input moves tiles at most one cell; 1 and 2 combine into 3, then equal larger values combine, with a clue about the incoming tile.
cases.sourceLabel: Official Xbox game manual — indexed text
cases.rights: Sirvo / Asher Vollmer / Greg Wohlwend / Jimmy Hinson

mechanics.contrast: 2048 makes large board shifts per input; Threes emphasizes entry management and low-value pairing through one-cell movement and its 1-plus-2 rule.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: treat the board as a shipping crate. Merging equal parts shares packaging and lowers weight, while incoming cargo adds both weight and occupied cells.

walkthrough.setup: One row reads 2, empty, 2, 4, while other rows contain tiles too.
walkthrough.action: The player slides the board left.
walkthrough.result: The two 2s merge into a 4; other rows also shift, then a new tile enters.
walkthrough.next: The next direction must account for the whole board rather than only the new 4.

prototype.firstStep: Build a four-by-four number board with a fixed incoming sequence to test the readability of all four directions.
prototype.pitfall: Specify whether a newly merged tile can merge again that turn, or prediction and resolution will disagree.
prototype.test: Can players predict changes in at least two rows before an input?

mechanics.name: Set up gravity-driven cascades
mechanics.summary: Remove supporting pieces so falling pieces complete the next group.
mechanics.rules: After a clear, pieces fall into the gaps. If their new positions satisfy another match, resolution continues automatically. Players can prepare cascades using visible arrangements while distinguishing predictable falls from random refill outcomes.
loop: Predict where upper pieces will land
Choose a supporting group to clear
Resolve the sequence of falling matches
Inspect what remains after the cascade
decisions: Clear beside the target directly or clear below so upper pieces fall into a useful position?
Prefer a guaranteed two-step cascade or gamble on a larger one from random new pieces?

parameters.name: Refill information
parameters.effect: Fixed or visible refill makes cascades plannable; hidden random refill adds surprise and uncertainty.

parameters.name: Cascade reward growth
parameters.effect: Faster reward growth encourages setup, but excessive growth makes ordinary matches feel worthless.

cases.implementation: After gems clear, falling replacements can form another match, producing a cascade from one initiating move.
Candies refill cleared spaces, and chain reactions can contribute to the current level’s collection and clearing objectives.
cases.sourceLabel: Official store description and King controls guide

mechanics.contrast: Bejeweled 3 uses cascades for continued scoring; Candy Crush also makes their location relative to level goals matter.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: each clear generates a byproduct returned to a chosen column. The returning piece can complete the next cascade or obstruct the planned layout.

walkthrough.setup: Two upper blue pieces are one cell apart, while red support pieces prevent a third blue from reaching the gap.
walkthrough.action: Clear the red support group first.
walkthrough.result: The blue piece falls into place, completing and clearing another group.
walkthrough.next: The cascade leaves a new height pattern, requiring another prediction.

prototype.firstStep: Create three predictable two-step cascades on fixed boards, resolving each stage slowly.
prototype.pitfall: Animation should reinforce feedback without hiding which event caused the next match.
prototype.test: Can players identify the second clear before making the initiating move?

mechanics.name: Create a power piece with a match pattern
mechanics.summary: The shape of a match determines the tool it leaves behind.
mechanics.rules: A basic match clears pieces, while a longer line or corner pattern leaves a power piece. Players prepare the pattern, then choose when to use its effect. Clear creation positions and effect ranges make future use predictable.
loop: Find a match that can become a special pattern
Choose where and when to use it
decisions: Take a small ordinary match now or spend another move preparing a column-clearing tool?
Is a powerful piece worth creating if it appears far from the target?

parameters.name: Pattern-to-effect mapping
parameters.effect: A few fixed mappings are memorable; too many patterns make players dependent on hints.

parameters.name: Creation cell
parameters.effect: A predictable creation cell supports planning; random placement weakens spatial choices.

cases.implementation: Four in a line create a striped candy; a five-piece T or L creates a wrapped candy; five in a line create a color bomb.
A four-gem line forms a Flame Gem, a T or L forms a Star Gem, and a five-gem line forms a Hypercube, each with a different clearing effect.

mechanics.contrast: Similar patterns need not map to the same effect: a four-match creates a line-clearing tool in Candy Crush but a local explosion in Bejeweled 3.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: line, corner and long-line matches create suppression, armor-breaking and execution resources. Read the enemy’s posture needs before choosing a pattern.

walkthrough.setup: The target sits in the rightmost column; the left side offers an immediate three-match or a possible four-match setup.
walkthrough.action: The player sets up a four-match to create a vertical clear piece.
walkthrough.result: The power piece appears at the predicted cell as a tool for the next action.
walkthrough.next: The player now tries to position it in the target column or find a useful trigger.

prototype.firstStep: Start with basic three-matches and one four-match power piece, with a fixed previewable creation cell.
prototype.pitfall: Teaching many patterns and blast ranges at once can overwhelm the decision; test one first.
prototype.test: Will players reject an immediate ordinary match to prepare a useful future effect?

mechanics.name: Combine two power pieces into one effect
mechanics.summary: Using tools separately is convenient; saving them until they meet may transform the board.
mechanics.rules: Obtain two power pieces, bring them together and trigger their combined effect. The result can expand a range or spread an effect to other targets rather than merely activating both independently. Preparing the combination costs space and time.
loop: Preview and trigger the combined effect
Work with the newly opened board
decisions: Spend one tool on an urgent goal or save it for a stronger combination?
Does bringing the pieces together justify the moves compared with separate use?

parameters.name: Distinctness of combinations
parameters.effect: Larger numbers are simple to understand; a new behavior adds discovery but requires better previews.

parameters.name: Setup cost
parameters.effect: Restricted movement or separation increases waiting risk; combinations should not automatically dominate separate use.

cases.implementation: Combining striped and wrapped candies expands line clearing, while two color bombs can clear the whole board.
Rockets, bombs and disco balls can be used separately or combined for larger clearing effects.

mechanics.contrast: Candy Crush combines special candies through adjacent swaps; Toon Blast feeds power pieces made by group tapping into combinations. Acquisition changes the setup process.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: make the combined effect a two-step sequence, such as recolor then clear a color versus clear then recolor. The same tools serve different goals depending on order.

walkthrough.setup: A bomb and a rocket are separated by a column of ordinary blocks.
walkthrough.action: The player removes the divider so refill brings the tools together.
walkthrough.result: The combined preview shows a wider clear that reaches two objectives.
walkthrough.next: The player decides whether to trigger now or wait for another target to enter the range.

prototype.firstStep: Build two tool types and three pair combinations, highlighting affected cells before confirmation.
prototype.pitfall: Do not require memorizing a combination table; previews should explain why waiting is worthwhile.
prototype.test: Can players compare the concrete benefit of separate use with combined use?

mechanics.name: Clear support beneath cargo to reach an exit
mechanics.summary: The target is not cleared directly; remove what supports it to move it downward.
mechanics.rules: A target piece is collected only when gravity carries it to a designated exit. Clear supporting or nearby pieces to open its route. A large clear elsewhere may score well while doing nothing for delivery.
loop: Find obstacles between target and exit
Choose a clear that opens the route
Watch where the target falls and stops
decisions: Clear a small group directly below the target or create a tool that removes several layers?
If the exit is offset, reposition the target first or prepare another route?

parameters.name: Exit placement
parameters.effect: Several exits are forgiving; narrow or offset exits emphasize route preparation.

parameters.name: Fixed route obstacles
parameters.effect: Obstacles add staged planning, but passable cells must be easy to distinguish.

cases.implementation: Gummi Dragons must travel from higher cells to exits below; clearing candies and blockers releases them.
Donuts are collected at bottom exits marked by downward arrows; additional donuts can enter from above after those on the board are collected.

mechanics.contrast: Both turn clearing into transportation; Homescapes explicitly describes later targets entering in batches, allowing an opened route to be reused.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: make falling targets timed contract cargo. Different exits serve different customers, so delivery must be timely and reach the correct destination.

walkthrough.setup: A parcel rests above two layers of colored pieces, with an exit only on the right and five moves left.
walkthrough.action: The player clears a lower-right group to open a route toward the exit.
walkthrough.result: The parcel drops one level but stops on the final supporting piece.
walkthrough.next: The next move must address that support rather than chase a distant large match.

prototype.firstStep: Use one fixed board, one cargo target and one exit, with only clearing and gravity.
prototype.pitfall: Diagonal fall and portals can obscure prediction; begin with straight fall and clear exit markers.
prototype.test: Will players choose a smaller clear because it actually advances delivery?

mechanics.name: Hold duration sets jump height
mechanics.summary: Tap the same jump button for a low hop; hold it to reach a higher platform.
mechanics.rules: For a short period after takeoff, holding jump sustains the rise; releasing it ends the rise sooner. Choose when to release based on the ceiling and destination. Landing gives you another chance to shape the next jump.
loop: Land and adjust the next jump
decisions: With a low ceiling, release for a short hop or wait until you clear it before jumping high?
A high reward requires more airtime. Take it, or land safely sooner?

parameters.name: Hold window
parameters.effect: A longer window separates low and high jumps more, but makes timing harder to predict.

parameters.name: Rise reduction on release
parameters.effect: Stronger reduction makes short hops crisp; an abrupt cutoff can feel unnatural.

cases.implementation: Jump-button hold state affects rising speed. Short hops avoid ceilings, while a longer hold yields a higher arc. This entry isolates jump height, excluding dash refills.
cases.rights: Maddy Makes Games / Extremely OK Games

cases.implementation: The original developer explains that holding jump longer produces a higher jump, with the effective hold window adjusted by running speed. The Steam image supplies game context only.

mechanics.contrast: Celeste lets players shape jumps between platforms they can pause on; Canabalt also ties hold timing to a runner that keeps moving and changes speed.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: place low beams between two walls. Release quickly after a wall jump to avoid a beam, or hold longer to reach the next foothold.

walkthrough.setup: Teaching example: a one-tile step lies under a ceiling; a three-tile ledge stands beyond it.
walkthrough.action: Tap jump over the step, then hold jump after clearing the ceiling.
walkthrough.result: The first hop avoids the ceiling; the second reaches the high ledge.
walkthrough.next: The next platform is narrower, so reconsider the release timing instead of always holding.

prototype.firstStep: Build one room with a low ceiling and two platform heights; make taps and holds produce clearly different jump heights.
prototype.pitfall: If the two peaks barely differ, players may mistake the variation for randomness; separate the arcs first.
prototype.test: Have five new players cross the room twice; check whether they deliberately tap under the ceiling and hold for the high ledge on the second pass.

mechanics.name: Switch speed to control reach and landing
mechanics.summary: Running reaches farther; walking makes narrow approaches easier to control.
mechanics.rules: Switch between faster and slower movement. Speed extends horizontal reach but reduces reaction time near danger. Slower movement makes edges and narrow landings easier to align, so a single route calls for repeated speed changes.
loop: Cross the gap or narrow section
Change speed for the next obstacle
decisions: Build speed before a wide gap, or first walk closer to its edge?
Running saves time near a trapped landing, but should you slow down to verify the approach?

parameters.name: Speed difference
parameters.effect: A larger difference makes switching matter more, while increasing the cost of running on narrow paths.

parameters.name: Transition time
parameters.effect: Immediate changes support precise adjustment; gradual changes require reading the next obstacle earlier.

cases.implementation: A separate run input combines with jumping to cross larger gaps; players choose whether to keep running according to the landing.
Players can switch between running and walking and change the default movement mode. Narrow platforms and traps make speed changes near edges a practical choice.

mechanics.contrast: Super Meat Boy uses running to support continuous traversal challenges; Spelunky 2 also asks players to slow down around traps, pickups and unfamiliar terrain.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: recombine wide gaps and narrow trapped paths, showing a short preview from each entrance so players read ahead and adjust speed.

walkthrough.setup: Teaching example: a four-tile gap is followed by a one-tile-wide safe approach.
walkthrough.action: Run and jump across the gap, then switch to slower movement as you approach the landing.
walkthrough.result: You cover the distance and avoid rushing into the hazard beyond the landing.
walkthrough.next: The next gap is shorter: stay slow or accelerate toward a farther branch.

prototype.firstStep: Build a twenty-tile route with one wide gap, one narrow landing and one edge hazard; provide only run/walk switching and jumping.
prototype.pitfall: If running solves every obstacle without a tradeoff, walking has no decision value.
prototype.test: Record speed choices by section; check that the same player intentionally speeds up before the gap and slows before the narrow path.

mechanics.name: Bounce from a target into the next jump
mechanics.summary: A dangerous target can become a stepping stone if you hit it from the right direction.
mechanics.rules: A valid downward hit on a bounceable target launches the character upward. Align the contact and plan the next landing as soon as you rebound. Side contact or a missed hit does not provide the same boost.
loop: Use the rebound to gain height
Continue to a landing or another target
decisions: Take the safe ground route or use a moving enemy to reach a higher platform?
After bouncing, head for the exit or attempt another bounce for a nearby reward?

parameters.name: Valid contact area
parameters.effect: A wider contact area makes bouncing easier to read; a narrow one emphasizes alignment and timing.

parameters.name: Rebound height
parameters.effect: Height determines reachable destinations and the room available to correct a failed approach.

cases.implementation: A downward airborne nail strike against enemies, spikes or certain objects rebounds the Knight upward; the player actively times the strike.
Landing on some enemies produces a bounce. Bats or spiders can become stepping stones toward higher ledges, provided the player avoids dangerous contact directions.

mechanics.contrast: Hollow Knight requires an attack input and nail contact; Spelunky 2 primarily requires landing feet-first on an enemy. Similar upward feedback comes from different input requirements.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: show where an enemy will move on the next beat, allowing players to decide whether it will become a usable stepping stone across a pit.

walkthrough.setup: Teaching example: the exit is one tile above normal jumping reach; a slow flying target crosses the pit.
walkthrough.action: Wait until the target approaches the exit side, then jump above it and strike downward.
walkthrough.result: The rebound provides enough height to reach the exit ledge.
walkthrough.next: Another target is moving toward a reward; chain another bounce or land safely.

prototype.firstStep: Use one constant-speed circular target, one pit and one high ledge; implement only top-contact bouncing before adding combat.
prototype.pitfall: Without clear cues distinguishing top and side contact, bouncing can feel arbitrary.
prototype.test: Check whether, before a second attempt, players can explain where the target should be and from which direction they should approach.

mechanics.name: Time boarding and leaving a moving platform
mechanics.summary: The foothold moves, so both boarding and departure need a decision.
mechanics.rules: A platform follows a visible route or starts moving when boarded. Choose when to get on, then ride toward the destination. Its position relative to the target shapes the departure jump, while waiting may expose you to hazards.
decisions: Jump for the barely reachable platform now or wait until it is closer?
Leave before the platform reaches its endpoint, or wait for a shorter jump with a closer hazard?

parameters.name: Travel cycle and pauses
parameters.effect: Longer pauses ease boarding; continuous movement rewards anticipation.

parameters.name: Distance to the destination
parameters.effect: The closest distance determines basic reachability; changing distance makes early departure a meaningful option.

cases.implementation: Zip movers rush to their other endpoint when stepped on or grabbed, then return more slowly. Players choose both activation and departure timing.
cases.rights: Maddy Makes Games / Extremely OK Games

cases.implementation: Moving scaffolds carry players along a track across hazards; switches, platform position and destination geometry guide boarding and departure.

mechanics.contrast: Celeste zip movers are directly triggered by boarding and emphasize quick transitions; Portal 2 scaffolds work within test-chamber switches and route planning.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a platform moves only while powered by a beam. Set the beam route, then decide where to leave the platform and redirect its power.

walkthrough.setup: Teaching example: a platform travels between two ends; the high ledge is reachable only when it is near the right.
walkthrough.action: Board when it returns to the left, then jump as it approaches the right.
walkthrough.result: You reach the ledge while the platform returns, temporarily moving the way back farther away.
walkthrough.next: A reward ahead requires a second moving platform, whose cycle must be read afresh.

prototype.firstStep: Build one platform moving between two points, two fixed landings and one hazard; make its travel path clear.
prototype.pitfall: Jitter or unexpected displacement obscures the decision; stabilize carrying and departure behavior first.
prototype.test: Check whether players can identify the next boarding window and best departure section without trial jumps.

mechanics.name: Choose action timing while moving automatically
mechanics.summary: Forward motion is given; you choose when to jump, slide or act.
mechanics.rules: The character keeps moving forward, so stopping cannot remove the pressure. Recognizable obstacles approach in sequence. Choose action timing from their distance and speed, then read the next group immediately after passing the current one; mistakes end or reset a section.
decisions: An early jump seems safer, but will you land too soon in the following gap?
Use a riskier timing for a reward or focus on clearing the main route?

parameters.name: Look-ahead time
parameters.effect: Longer visibility supports sequence planning; too little turns play into memorizing obstacle positions.

parameters.name: Available actions
parameters.effect: One jump action emphasizes timing; multiple actions add recognition and switching at an input cost.

cases.implementation: The character runs automatically; the developer balances pressure through acceleration, roof gaps and obstacles that affect speed. Players mainly control jump timing and duration. The source discusses the original version.
The character automatically runs right while the player jumps, slides or kicks in response to obstacles. Authored levels let repeated attempts build a learned action sequence.

mechanics.contrast: Canabalt concentrates input on jumping across varying rooftops and speeds; BIT.TRIP RUNNER uses authored obstacle sequences that require switching among jumping, sliding and kicking.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: an automatic runner encounters a telegraphed attack at each doorway; jump over a low sweep or slide beneath a high beam.

walkthrough.setup: Teaching example: the character moves three tiles per second toward a low box, a low beam and a pit.
walkthrough.action: Jump over the box, slide under the beam after landing, then wait until near the pit edge to jump.
walkthrough.result: The three actions succeed without stopping, and the next obstacle group comes into view.
walkthrough.next: The next reward is higher, so decide whether to change jump timing to reach it.

prototype.firstStep: Build a twenty-second route at fixed speed with three recognizable obstacles; begin with two buttons for jumping and sliding.
prototype.pitfall: Do not randomize speed, spacing and obstacle types together at first; failure would become hard to interpret.
prototype.test: Check whether repeated failures occur where the next obstacle is unreadable; players should distinguish early inputs, late inputs and wrong actions.

mechanics.name: Retry the same short segment immediately
mechanics.summary: Make failure useful practice: change one action on the next attempt.
mechanics.rules: Divide a challenge into short action segments. Failure quickly restores the current segment without replaying completed sections. Use the freshly observed failure to adjust a jump or movement timing; completing the sequence advances to the next challenge.
loop: Return quickly to the segment start
decisions: After hitting the ceiling, release jump earlier or change where you take off?
Refine the nearly successful route or try a slower, safer one?

parameters.name: Retry segment length
parameters.effect: Short segments isolate a failure to one action; longer ones test consistency across a sequence.

parameters.name: Delay before control returns
parameters.effect: A short delay preserves fresh action memory, but removing failure feedback can obscure the cause.

cases.implementation: The official description emphasizes fast respawns. Room-scale challenges let players revise a short sequence of jumps, grabs and dashes without replaying the whole mountain.
cases.rights: Maddy Makes Games / Extremely OK Games

cases.implementation: A production-team interview explicitly describes short levels and instant respawns. Failed attempts quickly restart the small level, letting players revise their hazard-avoidance sequence.

mechanics.contrast: Celeste places retries in small rooms within a continuous journey; Super Meat Boy more often maps a retry to a separate short level. Both preserve learning in the player rather than requiring stat gains after failure.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: introduce one new obstacle rule per short room and briefly mark the previous collision point after failure, helping players propose and test a revised route.

walkthrough.setup: Teaching example: an eight-second section has two jumps; a late second takeoff hits a saw.
walkthrough.action: After failing once, retry from the segment start and change only the second takeoff to occur earlier.
walkthrough.result: You clear the saw; the previous failure has supplied useful information.
walkthrough.next: The next room relocates the landing, requiring a new sequence.

prototype.firstStep: Build three rooms that each take five to ten seconds to clear; restore control about half a second after failure while preserving clear collision feedback.
prototype.pitfall: Fast retries do not guarantee readability; hidden hazards or inconsistent reset positions still prevent learning.
prototype.test: Record five consecutive attempts; check whether players revise actions near the failure rather than repeating blind inputs from the start.

mechanics.name: Catch a ledge, then climb up or let go
mechanics.summary: Missing the top can still leave you hanging from its edge with a new choice.
mechanics.rules: Reaching a grabbable lip puts the character into a hanging state instead of continuing to fall. Climb up, jump away or drop below. The decision is a pause and transfer at an edge, rather than a sustained stamina climb across a wall.
decisions: A hazard is above: climb immediately or hang briefly to inspect it?
A lower landing is available: would dropping onto it be safer than continuing upward?

parameters.name: Catch tolerance
parameters.effect: More tolerance rescues near misses; too much makes distance judgments meaningless.

parameters.name: Actions while hanging
parameters.effect: Climb-only hanging offers fewer choices; dropping and jumping away create upward and downward routes.

cases.implementation: Jumping into a ledge allows hanging, followed by a jump onto the ledge or a down-plus-jump release. Catching an edge can also interrupt a dangerous long fall.
Building ledges serve as catchable traversal points that connect to climbing up and other movement. Official parkour updates include ledge-grab fixes and changes to movement momentum.

mechanics.contrast: Spelunky 2 presents explicit hanging, jumping-up and dropping choices; Dying Light 2 integrates catching into continuous first-person traversal across buildings.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a guard on a ledge telegraphs its attack area. Hang below it, then climb after the attack or release onto a lower route.

walkthrough.setup: Teaching example: you fall half a tile short of the upper surface, but can catch its lip; a small safe platform lies below.
walkthrough.action: Catch the lip and wait while an obstacle passes above.
walkthrough.result: The fall stops, giving you a chance to inspect two routes.
walkthrough.next: Climb once the obstacle clears or drop to the lower platform and continue around it.

prototype.firstStep: Build three ledges at different heights with catch, climb-up and release states; mark grabbable lips consistently.
prototype.pitfall: Automatic catches during an intended drop can feel unresponsive; define clear release and no-catch conditions.
prototype.test: Ask players to ascend and then reach a lower ledge; check whether they deliberately release rather than repeatedly jumping away at random.

mechanics.name: Lower the body and slide through a gap
mechanics.summary: Use existing speed to pass through low space, with room to recover at the exit.
mechanics.rules: Moving into a lower posture allows passage beneath obstacles that block a standing body. Entry speed and drag shape sliding distance. Choose where to start and recover to standing only where there is room; the posture changes physical clearance, not just animation.
loop: Recover or chain an action after exiting
decisions: For a long tunnel, build speed for the slide or take a higher but safer route?
A pit follows the exit: slide later or reduce speed early to leave stopping room?

parameters.name: Sliding drag
parameters.effect: Less drag preserves speed but makes overshooting a safe exit more likely.

parameters.name: Low posture height and recovery clearance
parameters.effect: The height difference defines usable passages; recovery clearance determines whether standing can cause snagging or ceiling penetration.

cases.implementation: Pressing crouch while sprinting initiates a slide and grants a small speed boost, connecting ground travel to subsequent movement.
Sliding supports low-posture traversal and can connect to other parkour moves; an official update specifically fixes getting stuck while sliding between tables and sofas.

mechanics.contrast: Titanfall 2 particularly uses sliding to chain speed and actions; Dying Light 2 traversal also highlights the need to recover safely after passing through low environmental spaces.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a high beam in a corridor lights up before firing. Slide beneath it, then decide whether to chain a jump as the beam ends.

walkthrough.setup: Teaching example: a low tunnel is four tiles long, with only two safe tiles beyond its exit.
walkthrough.action: Begin the slide one tile before the entrance, then reduce speed at the exit.
walkthrough.result: You pass beneath the ceiling, stop before the pit and regain standing room.
walkthrough.next: The next tunnel is longer, so reconsider the run-up distance.

prototype.firstStep: Give a rectangular character standing and low collision heights; add three tunnel lengths and adjustable sliding drag.
prototype.pitfall: Forcing a stand under a low ceiling can trap the character; define how the low posture persists until clearance returns.
prototype.test: Check whether players adjust the slide start to tunnel length and reliably return to standing after the exit.

mechanics.name: Commit to a downward slam
mechanics.summary: Do not wait to fall naturally: commit downward for a strong landing effect.
mechanics.rules: Trigger a rapid downward move in midair to turn an ordinary landing into an attack or a way to break terrain. Align first because correction is usually more limited during the slam. The changed enemy or route state determines what follows.
decisions: An enemy stands on dangerous ground: slam first or land beside it?
Breaking the floor opens an unknown lower area: do it now or inspect the current platform first?

parameters.name: Correction during descent
parameters.effect: Less correction rewards alignment before committing; more allows reactions to moving targets.

parameters.name: Breakable target rules
parameters.effect: Consistent materials or markings make routes readable; inconsistent rules encourage indiscriminate testing.

cases.implementation: An airborne downward dive attack combines descent with impact. After obtaining the Ram Rune, it can also break designated floors to open vertical routes.
Stomp sends airborne Ori rapidly downward, hitting targets below and breaking designated fragile ground to turn descent into a route-opening action.

mechanics.contrast: Dead Cells extends its basic dive with floor-breaking through a rune; Ori and the Blind Forest uses Stomp as an ability for both attacks and environmental interaction.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: show clearly marked thin floors on early routes. After gaining the slam, let players choose which floor to break first to open shortcuts into earlier areas.

walkthrough.setup: Teaching example: a thin floor lies below-left, spikes below-right and a moving enemy between them.
walkthrough.action: Move above the thin floor before triggering the slam.
walkthrough.result: The floor breaks and you enter a safe lower area, opening a new route.
walkthrough.next: A lower enemy approaches: seek height for another slam or keep your distance.

prototype.firstStep: Build one jumpable platform, two floor materials and one stationary target; clearly distinguish ordinary landing from deliberate slam impact.
prototype.pitfall: Do not make every floor breakable; a single slam could undermine the intended route structure.
prototype.test: Ask players to predict what happens to each floor before trying the slam; check whether material cues support the prediction.

mechanics.name: Move yourself and a carried object through obstacles
mechanics.summary: Reaching the destination yourself is not enough; the object must arrive too.
mechanics.rules: Deliver a physical object that retains its own position and collisions. Carry it, place it temporarily or send it across before following. Plan the routes of both character and object, rather than comparing total inventory weight.
loop: Carry, place or pass the object
decisions: Carry it along a longer safe route or send it across a gap and follow?
Leaving it on a switch opens a door, but will you need the object in the next section?

parameters.name: Actions available while carrying
parameters.effect: Keeping all actions is fluid; restricting some makes placing and transferring the object matter.

parameters.name: Recovery after losing the object
parameters.effect: A nearby reset preserves puzzle flow; a long retrieval can turn planning into repetitive hauling.

cases.implementation: Players carry cubes to devices such as weighted buttons, changing test-chamber routes through object placement. Both the player and the cube must reach usable positions.
In the later Mirror Temple section, the player carries the crystal containing Theo. Picking it up and throwing it lets the player sequence the crystal and their own movement through obstacles.
cases.rights: Maddy Makes Games / Extremely OK Games

mechanics.contrast: Portal 2 primarily changes routes through where a cube is placed on devices; Celeste emphasizes taking the same Theo crystal through a sequence of action obstacles.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: use linked portals to move a character and a crate. Some platforms support only the character and some switches require the crate, making their arrival order matter.

walkthrough.setup: Teaching example: a cube must reach an exit button; the character can jump a gap only while empty-handed.
walkthrough.action: Throw the cube onto the safe far platform, then jump across and pick it up again.
walkthrough.result: Character and cube reunite on the far side, making the route to the button usable.
walkthrough.next: Once the button opens the door, decide whether to leave the cube there or find another device to keep the route open.

prototype.firstStep: On one screen, build a pickup/place cube, a low platform and an exit button; add one gap that requires sending the cube before moving the character.
prototype.pitfall: Objects stuck inside terrain or lost in unreachable places force pointless restarts; define reset and anti-stuck behavior.
prototype.test: Check whether players can explain whether the character or object must move next, and recover from failure without repeating an already understood delivery route.

mechanics.name: Answer before the response window closes
mechanics.summary: The conversation continues even when you hesitate, so thinking uses up the chance to speak.
mechanics.rules: A conversation offers responses for a limited window. Choose a stance before it closes; otherwise a written default advances the scene instead of waiting forever. This mechanic concerns the deadline. Silence is one possible default, not a requirement.
loop: Weigh the responses within the window
Choose a line or accept the timeout
decisions: Answer safely now or risk losing the opportunity while thinking?
With incomplete information, should you still take a position and accept its commitment?

parameters.name: Response-window length
parameters.effect: Shorter windows add pressure; allow enough reading time and a timing adjustment.

parameters.name: Timeout outcome
parameters.effect: A clear default makes hesitation legible; a hidden random outcome can feel arbitrary.

cases.implementation: Many dialogue choices use a shrinking timer, requiring a response within the window before the story reacts.
Response prompts do not wait indefinitely: ignoring one can give Alex a default response or silence as the conversation moves on.
cases.rights: Night School Studio / screenshot via Android Central

mechanics.contrast: The Walking Dead emphasizes the decision with a visible countdown; Oxenfree places the opportunity inside a continuing conversation.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a merchant holds a contract offer briefly, requiring a stock check and a delivery commitment before the response window closes.

walkthrough.setup: A ferryman gives six seconds to decide whether to vouch for a traveler.
walkthrough.action: Before finishing the background note, the player chooses to vouch.
walkthrough.result: The traveler boards, and responsibility is recorded against the player.
walkthrough.next: At the next question, the player must decide whether to maintain that position.

prototype.firstStep: Build one question, three responses, an adjustable timer and one timeout branch.
prototype.pitfall: Long text with a short deadline tests reading speed more than decision-making.
prototype.test: Can players distinguish choosing a stance from simply failing to read in time?

mechanics.name: Choose silence and let the other person continue
mechanics.summary: Withholding an answer is a response, though it may not avoid consequences.
mechanics.rules: Provide an explicit no-answer path. The player withholds a position while the other person continues, interprets the silence or changes the question. Write meaningful feedback for silence rather than treating it as a missed button; the rule also works without a timer.
loop: Decide whether to reveal a position
Decide whether to keep withholding or speak
decisions: Is avoiding both a lie and a confession worth the resulting distrust?
