prototype.test: Change the days remaining and see whether players switch crops and explain the deadline.

mechanics.name: Irrigation coverage
mechanics.summary: Trade footprint and construction costs for less repeated watering.
mechanics.rules: Place irrigation devices so nearby crops receive water automatically. Device footprint, coverage shape and supply rules constrain layouts; uncovered plots reveal gaps.
decisions: Maximum planting density may obstruct harvesting; access still matters.
Covering today's plots or planning future supply trades immediate cost against expansion.

parameters.name: Coverage shape
parameters.effect: Cross, square and circular coverage create different gaps and tiling problems.

parameters.name: Supply dependency
parameters.effect: Requiring a source or tank turns placement into network planning.

cases.implementation: Different sprinkler tiers water fixed areas each morning without a tank connection.
Sprinklers also require water-tank coverage, so both crop coverage and supply coverage must be satisfied.

mechanics.contrast: Stardew primarily tests local coverage; Dinkum adds the spatial relationship to water infrastructure.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: irrigation follows elevation, making terraces and reservoirs part of farm efficiency.

walkthrough.setup: A five-by-five field contains twenty crops; each sprinkler waters four neighbouring cells.
walkthrough.action: Move two sprinklers inward to reduce overlap.
walkthrough.result: The preview marks automatically watered crops; some corners still need manual care.
walkthrough.next: Use the saved watering actions to expand, then check the new edges.

prototype.firstStep: Use a fixed grid, one cross-shaped sprinkler and wet/dry cells, with a live count of missed plots.
prototype.pitfall: Pressure, underground pipes and rotating heads add separate rules; postpone them until placement is engaging.
prototype.test: With a fixed sprinkler budget, can players reduce manual watering by repositioning existing devices?

mechanics.name: Fertilizer investment
mechanics.summary: Invest scarce materials before harvesting for faster or better returns.
mechanics.rules: Apply fertilizer under the planting rules, exchanging material cost for growth or quality. Effects may be mutually exclusive, and idle land or season changes can affect persistence; harvest timing and output reveal the benefit.
loop: Compare the benefit with its cost
decisions: Higher-quality sales or an earlier extra harvest depends on the time remaining.
Valuable crops justify fertilizer more easily but concentrate investment in one plot.

parameters.name: Benefit type
parameters.effect: Speed changes scheduling; quality changes sale and processing choices.

parameters.name: Persistence
parameters.effect: Persistent fertilizer favors permanent plots; expiring effects require ongoing investment.

cases.implementation: Fertilizers specialize in quality, growth speed or water retention; a plot cannot simultaneously use every type.
Standard fertilizer speeds the initial growth but does not accelerate later regrowth cycles of crops such as tomatoes and watermelons.

mechanics.contrast: The former offers alternative goals; the latter changes the value of investment between initial growth and regrowth.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: fertilizers use materials from different regions, each changing one crop trait and creating sourcing choices.

walkthrough.setup: You can buy one fertiliser: mature two days earlier, or improve crop quality.
walkthrough.action: With the season ending, choose faster growth to fit one more harvest.
walkthrough.result: The sale price stays the same, but the extra harvest may repay the fertiliser cost.
walkthrough.next: Recalculate at the start of the next season; the best choice may change.

prototype.firstStep: Use one crop and two mutually exclusive fertilisers. Show spending, harvest count and net return.
prototype.pitfall: Stackable percentage bonuses can reduce the decision to buying every affordable upgrade.
prototype.test: Test early- and late-season scenarios; see whether choices change for understandable reasons.

mechanics.name: Seed reinvestment
mechanics.summary: Reserve part of a harvest for the next cycle instead of selling everything.
mechanics.rules: Obtain next-cycle seeds from harvested produce or harvesting itself. Seed recovery may require processing, sacrificed output or probability; insufficient reserves force new purchases or exploration.
decisions: Selling now versus expanding later trades liquidity for future capacity.
Random seed return calls for a safety buffer, not just average-yield planning.

parameters.name: Seed return rate
parameters.effect: Returns below replacement demand require shops or exploration to sustain production.

parameters.name: Opportunity cost
parameters.effect: Sacrificing more saleable produce makes expansion compete with current income.

cases.implementation: The Seed Maker consumes eligible produce to generate seeds, making propagation an explicit allocation choice.
Harvesting can itself return seeds; gardening talents improve seed recovery and reduce replacement shortages.

mechanics.contrast: Stardew expands through machinery and sacrificed produce; Core Keeper sustains the loop through seed-return probability and skills.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: seeds adapt over generations, letting players sell valuable seed stock or retain it to expand production.

walkthrough.setup: You harvest six crops; each crop kept for seed is one you cannot sell.
walkthrough.action: Sell four to cover expenses and keep two for the next planting.
walkthrough.result: Cash rises, but the seeds retained limit the size of the next harvest.
walkthrough.next: At the next harvest, reconsider expansion against your cash needs.

prototype.firstStep: Start with Sell and Keep Seed controls and three rounds of bills; no movement or crop animation is necessary.
prototype.pitfall: Without near-term expenses, reinvesting everything may always dominate.
prototype.test: See whether upcoming bills change the amount retained instead of producing one fixed ratio.

mechanics.name: Regrowing crops
mechanics.summary: Establish a plant once, then collect repeated smaller payouts.
mechanics.rules: Some crops mature slowly at first but survive harvest and produce again after another interval. They occupy land and ongoing care in exchange for returns without buying new seeds every cycle.
loop: Decide whether to keep or replace
decisions: Early planting amortizes setup; planting near season end may offer little advantage.
Established crops yield reliably but can block crops better suited to current demand.

parameters.name: Initial maturity
parameters.effect: Longer setup rewards early planning and raises the cost of switching.

parameters.name: Regrowth interval
parameters.effect: Short intervals create a routine; long intervals support parallel activities.

cases.implementation: Crops such as blueberries regrow after the first harvest, while season changes still constrain their lifetime yield.
Tomatoes support repeated harvests; watermelons and pumpkins also place fruit on neighboring tiles, requiring room for vines.

mechanics.contrast: The shared investment loop gains an extra footprint constraint in Dinkum, so yield per plant is insufficient for comparison.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: prune regrowing crops for new orders, sacrificing one harvest to change later output.

walkthrough.setup: A mature berry plant yields every two days, while another crop currently sells for more.
walkthrough.action: Keep the berry plant while comparing total returns over the remaining days.
walkthrough.result: Harvesting leaves the plant intact and resets its next yield timer.
walkthrough.next: Reconsider replacement when an order changes or the season nears its end.

prototype.firstStep: Compare one regrowing plant with one single-harvest crop, separating first maturity from regrowth.
prototype.pitfall: Hidden long-term calculations encourage confusion; make the next few harvests visible.
prototype.test: Check that players understand the plot remains occupied and consider its established production before replacing it.

mechanics.name: Crop–substrate matching
mechanics.summary: A seed's viability depends on the ground beneath it.
mechanics.rules: Identify a seed's substrate requirements, then find or transport suitable ground. Incompatible tiles cannot support planting; the right setup turns exploration discoveries into repeatable production.
loop: Plant and expand a specialized plot
decisions: Build a remote farm or transport rare soil home depending on hauling cost.
Specialized plots improve reliability but are less flexible to repurpose.

parameters.name: Substrate rarity
parameters.effect: Rare substrates turn crops into exploration rewards rather than interchangeable shop goods.

parameters.name: Transport cost
parameters.effect: Cheap transport favors a central base; expensive hauling favors regional specialization.

cases.implementation: Carrock requires stone, Puffungi requires mold, and certain coastal crops require beach blocks.
Natural planting conditions vary by herb; clay pots and planter boxes offer more manageable cultivation alternatives.
cases.rights: Re-Logic; screenshot: Steam Community contributor (see source)

mechanics.contrast: Core Keeper emphasizes transporting terrain; Terraria also offers general-purpose containers to reduce later management overhead.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: soils from different mine layers grow different medicinal plants, making excavation waste essential greenhouse material.

walkthrough.setup: A newly discovered seed needs sand, but your home plots have ordinary soil.
walkthrough.action: Bring home two sand tiles and create a dedicated plot.
walkthrough.result: The same seed is invalid on ordinary ground and valid on sand.
walkthrough.next: After confirming growth, decide whether to expand or preserve space for other crops.

prototype.firstStep: Use two soil types and two seed types, with placement previews explaining incompatibility.
prototype.pitfall: A unique soil requirement for every seed creates a large memorisation burden; begin with shared categories.
prototype.test: After one failed attempt, can players choose the correct soil without outside instructions?

mechanics.name: Crop protection
mechanics.summary: Yield must be protected as well as grown.
mechanics.rules: External threats such as birds can destroy crops. Build protection, inspect coverage and close gaps as fields expand; missing plants turn prevention cost into a comparison with expected losses.
decisions: Small fields may tolerate occasional losses; expensive crops deserve priority.
Protective objects occupy productive space; the densest layout may be fragile.

parameters.name: Threat visibility
parameters.effect: Visible pests encourage intervention; overnight resolution emphasizes preparation.

parameters.name: Loss scale
parameters.effect: Occasional single-plant losses are forgiving; widespread destruction makes defense mandatory.

cases.implementation: Scarecrows stop crows from eating crops within range, requiring coverage checks as a field expands.
Birds threaten crops and scarecrows provide protection, linking the farm to surrounding wildlife.

mechanics.contrast: The same preventive investment can feel different when risk is communicated through coverage checks or visible wildlife.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: pests learn fixed patrol routes, so players adapt fences or install nonlethal deterrents.

walkthrough.setup: Four of twelve crops lie outside the scarecrow’s protection.
walkthrough.action: Move the scarecrow toward the expensive crops before buying another.
walkthrough.result: Protected tiles avoid this threat while uncovered tiles remain at risk.
walkthrough.next: Check coverage again after expansion so new edge plots are not exposed.

prototype.firstStep: Implement one periodic threat, one protection radius and a visible record of lost crops.
prototype.pitfall: Unexplained losses make it hard to distinguish incomplete coverage from a bug.
prototype.test: After one loss, can players locate the gap and reduce risk through placement?

mechanics.name: Long-term orchards
mechanics.summary: Trade a long maturation period and lasting footprint for recurring fruit.
mechanics.rules: Plant saplings or fruit, wait for maturity and harvest repeatedly. Trees occupy space with delayed returns, and growth conditions may differ from fruiting conditions; clearing them frees land but discards invested growth time.
decisions: When cash is scarce, trees tie up funds; over a long horizon they reduce repeated seed purchases.
Plant more trees for future yield, or leave a row open to make each harvest quicker?

parameters.name: Maturation time
parameters.effect: Longer maturity rewards foresight and makes relocation costly.

parameters.name: Fruiting season
parameters.effect: Seasonal fruit encourages variety; year-round fruit encourages steady logistics.

cases.implementation: Fruit trees require clear surrounding space while growing and produce in their season; locations such as the greenhouse can remove seasonal restrictions.
Players can bury fruit to grow trees that bear repeatedly, turning wild gathered fruit into a cultivated orchard.

mechanics.contrast: Stardew combines purchased saplings, growth clearance and seasons; Dinkum connects gathering to orchard expansion through planting fruit.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: graft a new variety onto a tree at the cost of temporary downtime, trading cash flow for future order flexibility.

walkthrough.setup: You have starting cash; a sapling takes several rounds to yield, while annual crops sell next round.
walkthrough.action: Plant one tree and keep the remaining money for short-term production.
walkthrough.result: The tree occupies land without income at first, then begins repeated yields.
walkthrough.next: Add trees once cash flow stabilises, leaving an accessible harvesting route.

prototype.firstStep: Use sapling, mature and ready-to-pick states plus recurring expenses to test the delayed return.
prototype.pitfall: Long waits become idle timers without other decisions; give players short-term cash commitments.
prototype.test: See whether players retain operating cash instead of buying saplings with every coin.

mechanics.name: Livestock care
mechanics.summary: Feeding and care make animals recurring producers with recurring needs.
mechanics.rules: Provide shelter, feed and routine attention, then collect eggs, milk or other products once animals mature. Growth and care influence output; a larger herd also increases feed demand and daily work.
loop: Process products or expand the herd
decisions: Before expanding the herd, secure feed rather than considering only the purchase price.
Spend today interacting with each animal, or pay to reduce feeding chores and preserve time for an outing?

parameters.name: Care–output relationship
parameters.effect: Quality-only effects are forgiving; total production shutdown creates mandatory daily chores.

parameters.name: Automation timing
parameters.effect: Late automation risks repetition; very early automation can weaken familiarity with individual animals.

cases.implementation: Animals require feeding; petting, mood and friendship affect products, while facilities can automate parts of the routine.
Keeping animals requires licenses, shelter, feeders and feed; players care for animals and collect resources such as eggs or milk.

mechanics.contrast: Stardew deepens individual care with friendship and mood; Dinkum foregrounds licenses and facility preparation.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: automate basic needs while individual care preferences unlock specialty products.

walkthrough.setup: You own three animals but have two portions of feed and an outing planned.
walkthrough.action: Refill the feed, then give your limited interaction time to the animal in poorer condition.
walkthrough.result: Animal condition improves; products or production progress make the care visible.
walkthrough.next: After collecting products, budget tomorrow’s feed before buying another animal.

prototype.firstStep: Start with three animal cards, a feed stock and daily care; use status indicators rather than complex behaviour AI.
prototype.pitfall: Breeding, illness, roaming and breed differences expand the scope; first test the daily care choices.
prototype.test: When time and feed are tight, do players delay expansion and change care priorities?

mechanics.name: Bite timing
mechanics.summary: Recognize a real bite and strike within a short window.
mechanics.rules: After casting, wait for a signal and strike when a real bite occurs. Variable waiting prevents rote timing; early or late action may miss. Bobber motion, sound or an icon makes underwater state readable.
decisions: Is the float merely twitching or truly sinking? Striking now may catch the moment or waste the cast.
After a bite signal, strike immediately or wait for confirmation and risk missing the window?

parameters.name: Response window
parameters.effect: Narrow windows emphasize reflexes; wider ones improve accessibility.

parameters.name: Signal contrast
parameters.effect: Subtle cue differences demand attention but can become tiring.

cases.implementation: Respond to the bite indicator and sound in time to enter the fish-catching minigame.
Fish approach and nibble at the bobber; strike when it genuinely submerges before beginning the fight.

mechanics.contrast: Stardew emphasizes an explicit prompt; Dinkum makes reading bobber behavior part of preparation.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: fog obscures the surface, making audio clearer at quiet but more distant fishing spots.

walkthrough.setup: The float twitches twice, but the fish has not committed to the hook.
walkthrough.action: Wait until the float clearly sinks, then strike.
walkthrough.result: A strike inside the valid window starts reeling; an early strike catches nothing.
walkthrough.next: After missing, cast again and use the feedback to read the next signal.

prototype.firstStep: Use waiting, nibbling, biting and escaped states with one button and learnably different signals.
prototype.pitfall: Postpone species and gear; unclear failure feedback makes extra content feel like more guessing.
prototype.test: After several attempts, can players identify early versus late strikes and improve?

mechanics.name: Line tension control
mechanics.summary: Release during resistance and reel during pauses.
mechanics.rules: Alternate reeling and release to bring the fish closer without exceeding line tension. Constant pulling risks a break; excessive release loses progress. Distance and tension feedback make the tradeoff legible.
loop: Repeat until the fish reaches you
decisions: Another pull closes the distance faster, but is there room for the next sudden struggle?
When the fish calms, reel immediately for progress or wait longer to lower tension further?

parameters.name: Tension recovery
parameters.effect: Fast recovery supports bursts; slow recovery demands restraint.

parameters.name: Resistance pattern
parameters.effect: Fixed patterns reward learning; variable patterns reward live feedback reading.

cases.implementation: Reeling while a fish struggles risks breaking the line; reel when it calms to close distance.
With the Legacy fishing minigame enabled, players reel around resting and struggling phases; this minigame is optional.

mechanics.contrast: Dinkum communicates the fight through the fish and line in the world; Core Keeper's legacy mode uses dedicated progress and tension displays.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: tougher line tolerates tension but occupies more inventory, trading reliability against expedition capacity.

walkthrough.setup: The fish is still far away, the tension gauge is high, and it starts struggling.
walkthrough.action: Release the reel to lower tension, then retrieve while the fish is calm.
walkthrough.result: The fish gets closer, but aggressive reeling raises the risk of a snapped line again.
walkthrough.next: Leave tension headroom before the next struggle and repeat.

prototype.firstStep: Use distance and tension values, calm/struggling fish states and one reel button.
prototype.pitfall: Random tension changes without warning turn release timing into guessing; begin with readable fish behaviour.
prototype.test: See whether players release before danger and catch faster as they learn the fish’s pattern.

mechanics.name: Tracking a moving fish
mechanics.summary: Keep a controlled zone over a moving fish to build catch progress.
mechanics.rules: Press and release to move a controlled bar over a fish icon. Gravity or inertia prevents instant positioning while the fish moves. Overlap builds progress; separation loses it, testing continual correction.
loop: Tap or hold to position the bar
Recover from errors and complete the catch
decisions: Chasing the current position can overshoot; anticipating direction changes is more effective.
Holding a likely zone or chasing every movement depends on how quickly progress drains.

parameters.name: Control-zone size
parameters.effect: A larger zone increases tolerance; a smaller zone emphasizes precision.

parameters.name: Control inertia
parameters.effect: More inertia demands prediction; less feels like direct cursor tracking.

cases.implementation: Keep the green bar over the fish icon until progress fills; fish species use differing movement behaviors.
Control a weighted yellow bar over the fish while a green bar shows catch progress.

mechanics.contrast: Both share a continuous-tracking prototype; differentiation comes from control response, fish behavior and surrounding equipment systems.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: magical fish create brief decoys, requiring memory of the real trajectory rather than following the brightest marker.

walkthrough.setup: The fish marker moves upward while your control bar is below it.
walkthrough.action: Hold to catch up, then use short presses to avoid overshooting.
walkthrough.result: Progress increases while the marker stays inside the bar and falls outside it.
walkthrough.next: Adjust your presses when the fish changes direction until capture progress fills.

prototype.firstStep: Build one vertical track, a gravity-driven control bar and one moving-marker pattern; no fishing scene is required.
prototype.pitfall: Frequent abrupt reversals hide control learning; make one movement pattern consistently readable first.
prototype.test: On repeated attempts, do players overshoot less and learn short presses to maintain position?

mechanics.name: Finding fish habitats
mechanics.summary: Make where to fish an exploration problem that can be reasoned through.
mechanics.rules: Use location, timing and environment to locate a target species, then update knowledge from catches. Better execution cannot compensate for the wrong habitat; clues and a journal turn trials into knowledge.
loop: Record results and narrow the search
decisions: Wait for a known favourable time, or investigate an unknown body of water?
After repeated misses, keep investing time or change the location, weather or time condition?

parameters.name: Number of conditions
parameters.effect: More location, weather and time requirements deepen planning but need clearer records.

parameters.name: Information from failure
parameters.effect: Clear mismatch feedback reduces blind trial; opaque randomness makes learning harder.

cases.implementation: Species depend on combinations of location, season, weather and time; not every condition applies to every fish.
Fishing spot, cast zone, rod, bait and day/night change available species and chances as more locations become accessible.

mechanics.contrast: Stardew emphasizes trips around seasons and weather; Graveyard Keeper also divides a single spot into selectable cast zones.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: restore wetlands to return fish species, making journal completion depend on habitat repair rather than repeated casts.

walkthrough.setup: The journal says the target likes rainy rivers; you have had no luck at a sunny lake.
walkthrough.action: Record the failed conditions and try the river when it rains.
walkthrough.result: New catches support or challenge the hypothesis and add to your habitat knowledge.
walkthrough.next: Use the new clue to plan the next trip with less blind trial and error.

prototype.firstStep: Use three fishing locations, two weather states and a few species rules, tested through a location-selection screen.
prototype.pitfall: Do not hide too many conditions at once; catches should be explainable through observable changes.
prototype.test: After two failures, can players suggest a different place or time instead of repeating the same attempt?

mechanics.name: Bait loadouts
mechanics.summary: Pre-cast consumables change waiting, catch odds and target selection.
mechanics.rules: Prepare and equip bait, spending a consumable for faster or more targeted catches. Different bait types have different effects and trip-wide costs; wait time and catch composition reveal their value.
decisions: Expensive bait saves time, but an ordinary target may not justify scarce materials.
Is shorter waiting or a better chance of the target species more valuable on this trip? Which effect is worth its cost?

parameters.name: Consumption probability
parameters.effect: Guaranteed consumption is predictable; probabilistic use creates stock uncertainty.

parameters.name: Targeting strength
parameters.effect: Strong targeting reduces unwanted catches; weak targeting preserves surprises.

cases.implementation: Standard bait reduces waiting, while targeted bait increases the chance of a chosen species, adding a purpose beyond speed.
Players choose bait in the fishing setup interface; bait combines with rod, zone and timing to influence potential catches.

mechanics.contrast: Stardew separates speed and targeting roles by bait type; Graveyard Keeper combines bait, rod and zone to determine potential catches.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: regional insects become bait, so daytime gathering routes determine which fish can be targeted at night.

walkthrough.setup: You seek a rare fish and carry cheap general bait plus costly targeted bait.
walkthrough.action: Confirm the location is suitable, then use targeted bait to reduce unwanted catches.
walkthrough.result: Each attempt spends bait; the catch distribution reveals whether it helps.
walkthrough.next: Switch back to cheap bait once the target is caught and save the rare bait.

prototype.firstStep: Use two clearly differentiated baits, visible stock and a catch log; omit the timing minigame initially.
prototype.pitfall: A pure success-rate ladder becomes a linear upgrade; bait types need different purposes and visible costs.
prototype.test: Do players change bait when the goal switches from earning money to catching a particular fish?

mechanics.name: Choosing a cast location
mechanics.summary: Consider range, angle and fish position before releasing the cast.
mechanics.rules: Adjust position or casting power to land the bobber in a useful spot. Short or misplaced casts may be less productive; landing points, surface markers and fish approaches provide spatial feedback.
decisions: The longest cast may miss a nearby special patch; farther is not always better.
Repositioning costs time but can prevent repeated unproductive waits.

parameters.name: Placement tolerance
parameters.effect: Large valid areas are relaxing; small hotspots reward aiming.

parameters.name: Recast cost
parameters.effect: Free recasts encourage practice; stamina or time costs add commitment.

cases.implementation: Casting range and distance from land matter, while bubble patches improve bite efficiency; players can adjust their cast.
Observe visible fish and place the bobber nearby, then wait for the fish to approach and bite.

mechanics.contrast: Stardew primarily optimizes water-tile conditions; Dinkum centers placement on visible swimming fish.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: current carries the bobber downstream, so players cast upstream to deliver bait behind cover.

walkthrough.setup: Fish gather near the right bank; the water straight ahead is farther away but quiet.
walkthrough.action: Move right and use less casting power to land near the fish.
walkthrough.result: The distance to the target is visible; a poor cast can be retrieved immediately.
walkthrough.next: Reassess your position and power when the school moves.

prototype.firstStep: Use a flat water area, a visible target circle and a charged cast arc, starting with a stationary target.
prototype.pitfall: Adding wind, moving schools and complex banks together makes missed casts hard to diagnose.
prototype.test: After three casts, can players deliberately adjust power and position to improve accuracy?

mechanics.name: Passive fishing traps
mechanics.summary: Replace moment-to-moment fishing with placement, waiting and collection routes.
mechanics.rules: Deploy traps in water, leave them to catch and return to collect, refill or repair. Quantity and upkeep constrain scale; location and revisit frequency determine practical yield.
decisions: A distant rich spot must justify its place in the whole collection route.
Too many traps can turn a casual side activity into an upkeep chore.

parameters.name: Capacity limit
parameters.effect: Low capacity encourages frequent visits; high capacity permits longer expeditions.

parameters.name: Maintenance type
parameters.effect: Baiting consumes resources; repairs create downtime, producing different rhythms.

cases.implementation: Crab pots normally require bait and yield a catch or trash the next day before being rebaited.
Crab pots catch passively, requiring management of location, capacity and service life alongside collection trips.

mechanics.contrast: Stardew emphasizes daily rebaiting; DREDGE combines placement with sailing routes and durability.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: traps also measure water quality, combining collection routes with pollution investigation.

walkthrough.setup: You have three traps; a distant bay yields well but takes a long round trip.
walkthrough.action: Place two along your daily route and one in the distant bay as a trial.
walkthrough.result: On returning, collect catches while paying travel and maintenance costs.
walkthrough.next: Compare total trip returns, then relocate traps that are not worth servicing.

prototype.firstStep: Use three map points with travel costs and timed trap inventories to test placement and collection.
prototype.pitfall: Too many compulsory chores turn planning into attendance; test whether servicing schedules allow flexibility.
prototype.test: Do players relocate traps based on the whole route rather than the highest yield at one spot?

mechanics.name: Fish-pond production
mechanics.summary: Turn a successful catch into the starting stock of a recurring production loop.
mechanics.rules: Stock a pond with caught fish, wait for breeding or collect roe, then decide how much stock to remove. Limited capacity creates a choice between preserving productive stock and selling immediately; species affect output value.
decisions: Selling rare fish provides cash now; retaining them may build long-term returns.
Choosing a species commits pond space and future maintenance priorities.

parameters.name: Reproduction rate
parameters.effect: Slow reproduction emphasizes stock preservation; fast reproduction supports mass production.

parameters.name: Expansion conditions
parameters.effect: Material requests add milestones; cash-only upgrades emphasize capital accumulation.

cases.implementation: Ponds usually hold one species that reproduces and requests items to expand capacity, while producing roe or other items.
Fish ponds breed fish and produce roe; fish can be removed with a rod to free space for further breeding.

mechanics.contrast: Stardew emphasizes staged item requests; Dinkum links removing fish and freeing space with roe production.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: upstream farming changes pond water quality, making crop planning and aquaculture coordinate.

walkthrough.setup: The pond is nearly full; selling every fish raises cash but removes its productive stock.
walkthrough.action: Take only some fish and leave enough breeding stock.
walkthrough.result: You earn money and free capacity while the remaining fish sustain future production.
walkthrough.next: Check population, orders and expansion needs before harvesting again.

prototype.firstStep: Use one capped pond, a breeding timer and a harvest-quantity choice, starting with one species.
prototype.pitfall: Postpone genetics, disease and multi-species ecology; first test the harvest-versus-retention balance.
prototype.test: When an urgent order appears, do players understand the future cost of emptying the pond?

mechanics.name: Timed fishing contests
mechanics.summary: Turn familiar fishing into a routing and efficiency challenge with a scoring window.
mechanics.rules: Catch qualifying fish within a time limit and submit results under the event rules. Practice, equipment and routing matter under the countdown; scoring decides whether quantity, a target species or rarity is optimal.
decisions: A better distant spot may not repay the travel time; plan around the scoring rules.
With few attempts left, risk a difficult high-scoring fish or keep catching easier fish reliably?

parameters.name: Scoring system
parameters.effect: Count scoring favors quick catches; value scoring favors riskier targets.

parameters.name: Preparation period
parameters.effect: Advance notice rewards preparation; surprise rules reward adaptation.

cases.implementation: The Festival of Ice includes a timed contest centered on casting into ice holes and catching enough fish.
cases.officialPage: https://pinion.jp/ガイド/stardew-valley各季節ごとのイベント-住民の誕生日一覧/

cases.implementation: Max hosts fishing competitions with event-specific scoring targets; players must record their results before the deadline.

mechanics.contrast: Stardew concentrates the contest in a festival setting; Dinkum connects event participation to fishing around the island.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: each round names a habitat trait rather than a fish, making journal knowledge guide the best route.

walkthrough.setup: Sixty seconds remain; small fish are nearby while high-scoring fish may be farther away.
walkthrough.action: Estimate travel and fighting time, then stay nearby for quick points.
walkthrough.result: Your score rises as time falls; every relocation costs scoring opportunities.
walkthrough.next: After scoring, review idle and travel time and revise the next route.

prototype.firstStep: Use two fishing spots, one countdown and one clear scoring rule; begin with a solo score challenge.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid combining opaque quantity, weight and rarity scoring initially; make points understandable.
prototype.test: As time runs low, do players change targets and abandon trips they cannot finish?

mechanics.name: Equipment-gated catches
mechanics.summary: Use equipment to unlock catch categories rather than merely speed up old tasks.
mechanics.rules: Prepare compatible gear for the target water or species before fishing is possible. Budget and carrying capacity constrain universal loadouts; inaccessible catches reveal future research or purchase goals.
loop: Return and use the new access
decisions: Refit for one rare target or carry a broader combination? The choice changes the purpose of the trip.
Pay now to access one new habitat, or earn with existing gear until a broader upgrade is affordable?

parameters.name: Equipment coverage
parameters.effect: Narrow coverage encourages loadout changes; broad coverage reduces returns but may create a dominant choice.

parameters.name: Loadout footprint
parameters.effect: Bulkier gear makes access coverage compete with cargo capacity.

cases.implementation: Rods support habitat types such as Coastal and Shallow and occupy designated boat slots; different capture methods cover different fish.
Three rods offer differing catch access; the chosen rod affects available species, so rod and bait choices should serve the target.

mechanics.contrast: DREDGE constrains loadouts through habitat types and boat slots; Graveyard Keeper changes catch access through rod–species compatibility.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a boat carries only two habitat modules, so clues guide which waters to leave out of each expedition.

walkthrough.setup: You discover deep-water fishing, but your boat has shallow-water gear and limited mounting space.
walkthrough.action: Return to port, remove an old tool and fit gear compatible with deep-water targets.
walkthrough.result: The previously unusable spot becomes accessible, at the cost of another capability.
walkthrough.next: Choose whether to keep the new gear or restore a general loadout for the next trip.

prototype.firstStep: Use three fishing-site categories and two equipment slots, explicitly showing missing capabilities.
prototype.pitfall: Separate eligibility from success chance; incompatible gear should not encourage pointless retries.
prototype.test: Can players plan the required refit and explain which existing capability they sacrifice?

mechanics.name: Shape-based packing
mechanics.summary: Let item silhouettes determine what fits.
mechanics.rules: Rotate and move differently sized items into a finite grid without overlap. Whether a remaining gap fits the next reward changes what you keep or discard.
decisions: Pack large items first or protect essential tools? Geometric efficiency need not mean tactical strength.
Reserve space for future finds or maximize immediate value?

parameters.name: Bag shape
parameters.effect: Irregular boundaries create local puzzles; rectangles make alternatives easier to compare.

parameters.name: Rotation
parameters.effect: Rotation reduces dead ends; fixed orientation rewards foresight.

cases.implementation: Loot occupies shaped grid space; expansion and packing determine the tools available for the next fight.
Each puzzle requires fitting all supplied items while meeting ammo and health conditions; using items in the right order frees space.

mechanics.contrast: Backpack Hero supports an evolving build; Save Room turns a fixed item set into a finite logic puzzle.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: intact artifacts occupy awkward shapes; dismantling saves space but sacrifices research value.

walkthrough.setup: An L-shaped space remains in your bag; a new sword occupies three cells.
walkthrough.action: Rotate the sword and move two potions into a corner to create a straight space.
walkthrough.result: The sword fits, but the space reserved for the next item is gone.
walkthrough.next: At the next pickup, compare value, shape, and essential supplies again.

prototype.firstStep: Use a small grid and five item shapes with dragging, rotation, and overlap feedback.
prototype.pitfall: Defer equipment stats until picking up, rotating, and putting items back feels reliable.
prototype.test: See whether players rearrange to preserve essentials instead of always discarding the largest item.

mechanics.name: Item adjacency bonuses
mechanics.summary: An item’s value changes with its neighbors.
mechanics.rules: Items trigger bonuses from adjacency, direction or nearby categories. Arrange useful connections within a limited bag, then use battle outcomes to assess the layout.
decisions: Surround one core item or support several smaller engines?
Is a stronger item worth breaking existing connections?

parameters.name: Effect direction
parameters.effect: One-sided effects add orientation puzzles; all-sided effects allow flexibility.

parameters.name: Stacking
parameters.effect: Stacking favors concentration; caps reward distributed layouts.

cases.implementation: Placement changes item effects; neighboring items can become the foundation of a build.
Arrange purchased items to create synergies that strengthen an automatically resolved battle.

mechanics.contrast: The former evolves a bag during dungeon exploration; the latter repeatedly couples shopping with between-round arrangement.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: cooling stones preserve adjacent potions while gunpowder destabilizes the same area.

walkthrough.setup: A gem boosts adjacent weapons, but potions occupy the space beside your weapon.
walkthrough.action: Move the potions and place the gem next to the weapon.
walkthrough.result: The weapon preview improves, but an awkward gap appears elsewhere.
walkthrough.next: With the next pickup, compare its individual strength with existing connections.

prototype.firstStep: Build six items and two adjacency rules with lines showing active effects.
prototype.pitfall: Limit resolution order before mixing adjacency, diagonals, direction, and chained effects.
prototype.test: Ask players to predict a bonus before placing an item and compare with the actual result.

mechanics.name: Carry-weight budgets
mechanics.summary: Capacity governs movement as well as storage.
mechanics.rules: Every carried item adds weight; exceeding capacity restricts movement. Compare usefulness to weight, then discard, cache or haul goods in separate trips, guided by the load meter.
decisions: Does bulky low-value loot justify another trip or a dedicated haul later?
Spend capacity on profit or on a safety margin?

parameters.name: Penalty curve
parameters.effect: A hard movement stop forces decisions; gradual slowdown makes risk easier to estimate.

parameters.name: Unloading distance
parameters.effect: Longer unloading routes make caches and route planning more valuable.

cases.game: The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim Special Edition
cases.implementation: Exceeding carry capacity restricts running and fast travel, creating a value-versus-weight trade-off.
The inventory has both slots and weight; encumbrance drains stamina when moving, forcing a lighter load.

mechanics.contrast: Skyrim primarily restricts movement modes; Valheim also ties load to stamina and retains a separate slot limit.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: rescuing an injured traveler consumes the same hauling budget as evacuation supplies.

walkthrough.setup: Your carrying limit is 20; you carry 18 and find ore weighing 5.
walkthrough.action: Drop 4 weight of common stone and take the ore.
walkthrough.result: Your load is within the limit, allowing normal travel at the cost of some materials.
walkthrough.next: Unload at base, then decide whether the remaining supplies justify another trip.

prototype.firstStep: Create ten weighted items with distinct uses, a load meter, and an overload slowdown.
prototype.pitfall: If value always scales directly with weight, decisions collapse into a fixed ranking.
prototype.test: Change the next mission’s needs and see whether kept items change beyond resale value.

mechanics.name: Slots and stack limits
mechanics.summary: Quantity can stack; variety still consumes slots.
mechanics.rules: Items fill finite slots and compatible items stack up to a cap; distinct types or qualities may stay separate. Choose between varied samples and bulk materials, using storage to free carrying slots.
decisions: Reserve the final slot for unknown loot, or carry a spare tool?
Keep a sample of many materials, or fill stacks with just a few types?

parameters.name: Stack cap
parameters.effect: High caps support bulk production; low caps shorten gathering routes.

parameters.name: Quality compatibility
parameters.effect: Separate quality stacks increase sorting pressure while highlighting valuable grades.

cases.implementation: Purchased upgrades add backpack slots; compatible type-and-quality stacks merge while tools occupy separate slots.
Special coin and ammo slots complement the main inventory, while quick-stack tools help move resources into chests.

mechanics.contrast: The former gates early gathering scale through bag upgrades; the latter eases item variety through specialized slots and sorting tools.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a survey needs one specimen per species; duplicates become stacked research material, separating variety from quantity.

walkthrough.setup: One slot remains; your wood stack is not full and new flower seeds lie nearby.
walkthrough.action: Merge the wood into its existing stack, then choose seeds or a spare tool for the free slot.
walkthrough.result: More wood costs no extra slot, while a new item type uses the last one.
walkthrough.next: Before another pickup, consider returning to storage to sort item types.

prototype.firstStep: Build a six-slot bag, three materials, and a stack cap with splitting and merging.
prototype.pitfall: Quality and binding states multiply item types; keep the initial distinctions clear.
prototype.test: Check whether players predict the slots a pickup needs and plan their return accordingly.

mechanics.name: Tool durability and maintenance
mechanics.summary: Tools wear out, making trip length a preparation decision.
mechanics.rules: Use or damage reduces durability until equipment becomes unusable. Carry spares, locate repair facilities or craft replacements; the durability meter brings each expedition closer to a maintenance stop.
decisions: A spare costs space but prevents an early return. Is it worth carrying?
Repair now for safety, or trust the remaining durability for one more vein?

parameters.name: Repair cost
parameters.effect: Free repair emphasizes routing; material costs also create resource sinks.

parameters.name: Break result
parameters.effect: Keeping broken tools encourages recovery; destruction increases preparation pressure.

cases.implementation: Depleted equipment can be repaired at an appropriate workbench or forge without spending materials.
Most ordinary tools have limited uses and disappear when exhausted, encouraging spare materials or replacements.

mechanics.contrast: Valheim makes maintenance a return-to-base rhythm; ordinary tools in Don’t Starve feed directly into crafting and material budgets.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: pick wear affects strike stability, while a temporary cave repair station extends expeditions.

walkthrough.setup: Your pick has three uses left; the vein needs five, and a spare occupies bag space.
walkthrough.action: Repair at the workbench first, freeing the slot that would hold a spare.
walkthrough.result: You leave later but can finish mining and carry another slot of resources.
walkthrough.next: After returning, inspect durability and choose repair or a spare for the next trip.

prototype.firstStep: Build one tool, fixed wear per use, one repair station, and a clear uses-remaining indicator.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid mere repair-click repetition; maintenance should affect preparation or routes.
prototype.test: Offer short and long trips and see whether repair and spare choices change.

mechanics.name: Consumable light reserves
mechanics.summary: Light provides safety at a supply cost.
mechanics.rules: Spend torches or fuel to sustain light while progressing toward depletion. Darkness changes danger or rules, creating a choice between relighting, pushing onward and returning; a light meter exposes remaining reserve.
decisions: Spend the final torch going deeper, or save it for the return?
With little light, take a familiar short route or explore a branch that may hold supplies?

parameters.name: Drain trigger
parameters.effect: Real-time drain creates execution pressure; movement-based drain favors planning.

parameters.name: Darkness rewards
parameters.effect: Extra rewards encourage risk; penalties alone emphasize preparation.

cases.implementation: Exploration reduces light; torches restore it, while darker conditions alter both danger and rewards.
An equipped torch continuously burns durability; attacks in complete darkness make backup light a survival resource.

mechanics.contrast: The former uses light as a risk-reward setting; the latter makes it an immediate nighttime survival requirement.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: photographing bioluminescent creatures requires darkness, but enough fuel must remain to relight safely.

walkthrough.setup: Your torch lasts another minute; a reward lies ahead and the exit is behind you.
walkthrough.action: Estimate the round trip and explore only the nearest room.
walkthrough.result: After one reward the light is visibly weaker, making further progress riskier.
walkthrough.next: Return to replenish light or accept the cost of darkness for one more stretch.

prototype.firstStep: Build a branching corridor, a consumable light source, and one clear darkness penalty.
prototype.pitfall: Poor visibility alone may only frustrate; explain which rules darkness changes.
prototype.test: See whether players choose to return before fuel runs out instead of waiting passively for darkness.

mechanics.name: Unknown-item identification
mechanics.summary: Risk a trial or spend resources for certainty?
mechanics.rules: Found items hide names or effects until examined, identified or used. Testing may consume the item or cause harm, but knowledge improves later decisions about the same kind.
loop: Decide its role in the loadout
decisions: An unknown potion may save an emergency or make it worse.
Spend scarce identification on valuable gear or on dangerous consumables?

parameters.name: Knowledge persistence
parameters.effect: Run-local knowledge renews uncertainty; persistent knowledge builds a long-term catalog.

parameters.name: Trial cost
parameters.effect: Cheap trials encourage experiments; costly trials increase the value of clues and identification tools.

cases.implementation: Potion and scroll appearances vary between runs; use and identification tools reveal their identities.
Examine unfamiliar artifacts to understand them; character states such as confusion affect examination, and understanding helps recognize the same kind later.

mechanics.contrast: The former reshuffles appearance-to-effect mappings; the latter emphasizes a character’s ability to understand unfamiliar technology.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: an alchemy shop can pay to identify ingredients or run small-dose trials, recording results for the current expedition.

walkthrough.setup: Your health is low; you have an unknown potion and one identification charge.
walkthrough.action: Identify the potion, then drink it after learning its effect.
walkthrough.result: You avoid a blind-drinking risk, but the next unknown item has no easy answer.
walkthrough.next: Remember its appearance so future potions of that type are recognizable.

prototype.firstStep: Build four potions with randomized appearances, an identification resource, and knowledge shared within the run.
prototype.pitfall: Limit harmful effects first; clue-free instant death offers little learnable judgment.
prototype.test: See whether players change identification priorities between safe and urgent situations.

mechanics.name: Card removal and draw density
mechanics.summary: Remove weak cards to draw desired combinations more often.
mechanics.rules: Manage a repeatedly drawn deck; permanent removal usually costs resources or requires a specific stop. Removing weak cards increases key-card frequency but may reduce coverage against varied situations.
decisions: Remove the weakest card or one that conflicts with the current plan?
A tiny deck is consistent, but does disruption make it fragile?

parameters.name: Increasing removal cost
parameters.effect: Rising fees limit rapid thinning and force priorities.

parameters.name: Starting redundancy
parameters.effect: More weak starters make early removal valuable; less redundancy makes decisions harder.

cases.implementation: Merchants remove cards for a fee, and some events offer removal; removing starters changes draw composition.
Players can pay to purge cards in shops or use dedicated map opportunities to focus a deck.

mechanics.contrast: Both treat subtraction as progression, but map access, fees and combat roles change the opportunity cost.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: archive irrelevant clue cards to improve the chance of drawing useful evidence during an investigation.

walkthrough.setup: Only two cards in a ten-card deck support your key move; a shop offers one paid removal.
walkthrough.action: Remove a frequently unused card instead of buying another card.
walkthrough.result: The smaller deck finds key cards more often but loses a fallback option.
walkthrough.next: Play several rounds, then decide whether to remove redundancy or fill a gap next.

prototype.firstStep: Create ten fixed cards, a visible draw history, and one paid removal opportunity.
prototype.pitfall: Make before-and-after draws comparable; probability text alone may not convey the effect.
prototype.test: Ask why a usable card was removed and check whether the intended combination appears more reliably.

mechanics.name: Budgeted ability loadouts
mechanics.summary: Owning every ability does not mean equipping them all.
mechanics.rules: Abilities consume capacity, forcing a choice between a few expensive powers and several small ones. Usually revised at safe points, each loadout is tested in play before the next adjustment.
decisions: Maximize damage, or trade some efficiency for survival or convenience?
Equip one costly powerful ability, or several small abilities for broader coverage?

parameters.name: Capacity growth
parameters.effect: Growing capacity expands combinations; fixed capacity preserves trade-offs.

parameters.name: Respec location
parameters.effect: Anywhere swapping supports local solutions; safe-point changes require anticipation.

cases.implementation: Charms have differing notch costs and are normally equipped at benches, limiting simultaneous effects.
Functions can be installed as active, upgrade or passive abilities, constrained by memory and slot types.

mechanics.contrast: Charms mainly combine passive effects; Functions also change roles between active, modifier and passive use.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a robot chip can become a scanner or an arm modifier, consuming a different budget in each role.

walkthrough.setup: You have five capacity: heavy offense costs three, while shield and scouting cost two each.
walkthrough.action: Before entering an unfamiliar area, choose shield and scouting over heavy offense.
walkthrough.result: Damage falls, but spotting danger and surviving mistakes becomes easier.
walkthrough.next: At the rest point, adjust the loadout to the threats encountered.

prototype.firstStep: Build five clearly differentiated abilities and a capacity cap, then test with two mission types.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid dozens of percentage bonuses; distinct purposes make capacity choices understandable.
prototype.test: Change the mission and see whether players reconfigure and explain their sacrifice.

mechanics.name: Recovering resources after death
mechanics.summary: Failure creates a retrieval mission to plan anew.
mechanics.rules: Death leaves resources in a dangerous location. After respawning, prepare a retrieval trip and weigh the recoverable value against the route’s danger; markers or remains keep the possibility visible.
decisions: Rush back lightly equipped or spend time preparing backup gear?
Is abandoning a small loss wiser than risking a chain of failures?

parameters.name: Repeated death rule
parameters.effect: Persistent remains reduce anxiety; replacing them increases retrieval pressure.

parameters.name: Recovery safety
parameters.effect: Offsetting recovery from the exact death point avoids traps; exact placement is harsher.

cases.implementation: Default death leaves carried items in a tombstone for retrieval; a later death does not simply replace the older tombstone.
Death leaves a Shade holding Geo; defeating it restores currency and Soul capacity, while another death replaces the old Shade.

mechanics.contrast: The former recovers physical supplies with persistent remains; the latter uses one Shade to create a sharper second-failure cost.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: shipwreck cargo drifts with tides; buy insurance or plan a recovery voyage yourself.

walkthrough.setup: You die deep in a cave; materials remain near a monster and you respawn at the entrance.
walkthrough.action: Take a spare weapon and return through a safer side route.
walkthrough.result: Recovering the materials reverses the loss, at the cost of preparation and travel.
walkthrough.next: Choose to leave or resume the unfinished objective using your remaining resources.

prototype.firstStep: Build one replayable level, a dropped resource bag, and a clear recovery marker.
prototype.pitfall: Define what a second death does to the old drop before allowing punishment to compound.
prototype.test: Test valuable and trivial drops and see whether players sometimes reasonably abandon recovery.

mechanics.name: Box pushing and positional traps
mechanics.summary: Before moving a box, consider where you can still stand.
mechanics.rules: Push boxes from adjacent cells to open routes or satisfy goals. A push may block access to the opposite side or trap a box, making position and action order central; undo supports experiments.
decisions: Solve the distant target first or clear working space?
Does this move preserve access for a later reverse push?

parameters.name: Undo scope
parameters.effect: Unlimited undo encourages experiments; limited undo adds pressure.

parameters.name: Box properties
parameters.effect: A few exceptions expand solutions; too many reduce readability.

cases.implementation: Boxes contain spaces; pushing them into and out of other boxes extends box pushing into recursion.
Pushable objects include word blocks, so moving them changes both routes and active rules.

mechanics.contrast: The former changes containment and space; the latter makes objects express rules.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: refrigerated warehouse crates must be pushed without blocking cold-air routes.

walkthrough.setup: A box faces its target beside a narrow passage.
walkthrough.action: Circle to the opposite side, preserve the passage, then push toward the target.
walkthrough.result: The target is satisfied and you can still reach behind the next box.
walkthrough.next: Check the standing space needed for remaining boxes, then move or undo a dead end.

prototype.firstStep: Build a small grid with two boxes, two targets, and single-step undo.
prototype.pitfall: Verify a solution by hand; extra boxes increase search without guaranteeing interesting choices.
prototype.test: See whether players preserve access and can explain why a corner push is irreversible.

mechanics.name: Changing gravity direction
mechanics.summary: Redefine down to turn obstacles into footholds.
mechanics.rules: Change character or world gravity to fall across routes that normal jumps cannot reach. Predict landing points, hazards and moving objects before switching; motion tests the prediction.
loop: Land and plan the next step
decisions: Switch early for reaction time or near an edge for a better trajectory?
Will a falling hazard reach the destination first?

parameters.name: Switch conditions
parameters.effect: Surface-only switching favors routing; midair switching favors control.

parameters.name: Affected scope
parameters.effect: Character-only gravity is readable; global gravity creates interactions.

cases.implementation: The character flips vertical gravity instead of jumping, finding landings among spikes and platforms.
Players rotate the environment to manipulate gravity, turning architecture, hazards and character positions into a physics puzzle.

mechanics.contrast: The former emphasizes quick reading and precision; the latter considers physical relationships in a rotated structure.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: shift greenhouse gravity to move water and seeds, securing fragile plants first.

walkthrough.setup: The exit is on the ceiling, with offset spikes between floor and ceiling.
walkthrough.action: Move below a safe opening, then reverse gravity toward the ceiling.
walkthrough.result: The character falls upward onto the ceiling platform instead of the spikes.
walkthrough.next: Treat the ceiling as your footing and choose a safe position for the next reversal.

prototype.firstStep: Initially reverse only the character’s vertical gravity in one room with static hazards.
prototype.pitfall: Reversing every object adds collision states; establish readable character control and camera behavior first.
prototype.test: Ask for the expected landing before each reversal to distinguish prediction from guessing.

mechanics.name: Paired portal connections
mechanics.summary: Make distant surfaces adjacent and rewire a route.
mechanics.rules: Place paired openings on allowed surfaces so objects entering one emerge from the other. Position, orientation and motion determine the result; replace portals to test spatial plans.
loop: Send a character or object through
decisions: Place an entrance near the goal or build entry speed first?
Will replacing a portal destroy a route still needed?

parameters.name: Eligible surfaces
parameters.effect: Restricted surfaces focus solutions; many surfaces widen the search.

parameters.name: Connection count
parameters.effect: One pair limits memory load; multiple pairs support collaboration.

cases.implementation: One portal pair links surfaces so spatial and momentum relationships bypass chamber obstacles.
Co-op gives each player a portal pair, creating coordinated multi-stage routes.

mechanics.contrast: The first trains individual understanding; the sequel’s co-op makes portal replacement a communication problem.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a logistics portal supports one link, requiring materials to take scheduled turns.

walkthrough.setup: A high ledge is unreachable; nearby floor and wall surfaces accept portals.
walkthrough.action: Place one portal beneath a drop and aim the other toward the ledge, then jump in.
walkthrough.result: Your falling speed carries through the other opening and launches you toward the ledge.
walkthrough.next: From the new position, rearrange the portals for the next obstacle.

prototype.firstStep: Start with paired 2D portals, velocity-direction conversion, and one valid surface type.
prototype.pitfall: Full 3D adds camera, crossing collisions, and recursive rendering beyond a simple teleport button.
prototype.test: Check whether players predict exit direction from orientation and repeat a traversal reliably.

mechanics.name: Rewinding time to change outcomes
mechanics.summary: Revisit the decisive moment and learn which states rewind.
mechanics.rules: Move time forward or backward to observe objects, characters and mechanisms. Exploit the order of states so a route or interaction becomes possible at a particular moment.
decisions: Is the obstacle about position or event order?
How can an object that resists rewind help?

parameters.name: Rewind scope
parameters.effect: Universal rewind is readable; selective rewind creates causal combinations.

parameters.name: Time resolution
parameters.effect: Continuous scrubbing allows fine timing; discrete phases simplify comparisons.

cases.implementation: Rewind enables retries and puzzles, while different worlds introduce distinct temporal behaviors.
Players mainly control time direction while characters follow set routes and interact at critical moments.

mechanics.contrast: Braid retains direct character control; The Gardens Between centers control on the event timeline.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: rewind one machine component until it synchronizes with parts still moving forward.

walkthrough.setup: A moving platform passes a door that closes just before you arrive.
walkthrough.action: Rewind to before the platform departs, adjust your departure, and advance time again.
walkthrough.result: You arrive before closure and understand the order of both events.
walkthrough.next: Use the discovered timing relationship to solve the next set of linked states.

prototype.firstStep: Record and replay the finite states of one character, one moving platform, and one door.
prototype.pitfall: Define which objects rewind; unrestricted physics and random events make replay consistency difficult.
prototype.test: See whether rewinding leads to a specific timing adjustment rather than repeating the same sequence.

mechanics.name: Routing beams to receivers
mechanics.summary: Move a few relays to complete an energy path.
mechanics.rules: A beam must reach a receiver to open a route. Adjust relays, reflectors or portal paths, avoid obstruction and check simultaneous requirements; visible beams reveal broken links.
decisions: Place a relay near the source or at a multi-target junction?
Will taking a relay close the door behind you?

parameters.name: Simultaneous targets
parameters.effect: Simultaneous targets demand networks; sequential ones favor routes.

parameters.name: Occlusion
parameters.effect: Character occlusion adds timing and cooperation; ignoring it favors static reasoning.

cases.implementation: Connectors establish sightline links between lasers and receivers to open barriers.
Beams use redirection cubes and portals to reach receivers that operate mechanisms.

mechanics.contrast: Talos emphasizes relay networks; Portal lets beam paths bypass normal spatial obstructions.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: mirrors light a cave farm, while moving irrigation devices can obstruct the beams.

walkthrough.setup: A wall blocks the light source and the receiver beside the door is dark.
walkthrough.action: Place a reflector at the corner to route the beam around the wall.
walkthrough.result: The receiver lights up and opens the door; removing the reflector breaks the beam.
walkthrough.next: Find a route through that preserves the beam, then tackle the next door.

prototype.firstStep: Use a 2D grid with one source, two rotating reflectors, and one receiver.
prototype.pitfall: Defer color mixing and moving blockers until the basic light path can be followed at a glance.
prototype.test: When the beam breaks, can players locate the break and move only the necessary object?

mechanics.name: Inferring visual puzzle rules
mechanics.summary: Teach a visual grammar through examples and feedback.
mechanics.rules: A consistent interface presents changing symbols. Infer rules from simple puzzles and test harder ones; failure invites comparison and revised hypotheses rather than random input.
decisions: Which differences affect the answer rather than decorate it?
Does the rule explain all solved puzzles or only the last?

parameters.name: Example order
parameters.effect: Isolate rules before combining them to reduce false learning.

parameters.name: Failure detail
parameters.effect: Specific errors are gentler; binary feedback requires stronger inference.

cases.implementation: Many panels use line drawing, with regional sequences teaching symbols and environmental clues.
Panels use on/off tile toggles; regions change the required patterns through themes and clues.

mechanics.contrast: Both teach rules through stable input; path drawing and tile toggling create different search spaces.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: use one field-notebook interface to infer new species’ habitat needs from known examples.

walkthrough.setup: The first three examples accept grouping matching colors together.
walkthrough.action: Hypothesize that color is the rule, then test it on a puzzle with a new symbol.
walkthrough.result: The answer is rejected, indicating a missing condition in the hypothesis.
walkthrough.next: Compare earlier examples, revise the rule, and try again.

prototype.firstStep: Design one clear rule, four teaching examples, and two puzzles that disprove plausible wrong hypotheses.
prototype.pitfall: The work is in example sequencing; complexity without distinguishing clues becomes guesswork.
prototype.test: Without explaining the rule, ask players to state it and solve a new puzzle.

mechanics.name: Turning visual relationships into geometry
mechanics.summary: Change how you see a scene to change its usable space.
mechanics.rules: Adjust a viewpoint or place an image so a visual relationship changes three-dimensional space. Move through the result to test scale, connections and obstruction.
decisions: Will joining distant platforms sacrifice a nearby route?
Enlarge a prop as a step or shrink it to fit a gap?

parameters.name: Result preview
parameters.effect: Clear previews reduce trial and error; uncertainty needs easy undo.

parameters.name: Editable objects
parameters.effect: Restricted objects help teaching; free editing expands solutions.

cases.implementation: Released objects change scale with perspective, turning familiar props into routes.
Placed photographs become explorable geometry, reconnecting or overwriting the scene.

mechanics.contrast: The former changes object scale; the latter converts whole pictures into space.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: photos complete miniature-city bridges but overwrite roads, requiring camera planning.

walkthrough.setup: Two distant platforms are separated; a picture depicts a walkway that could connect them.
walkthrough.action: Adjust the view and picture until the depicted walkway aligns with the visible edges, then confirm.
walkthrough.result: The picture becomes walkable space while replacing part of the original scene.
walkthrough.next: Walk through to verify the connection, then choose another spatial relationship to change.

prototype.firstStep: Use one fixed viewpoint and one authored bridge image to validate a single image-to-space transformation.
prototype.pitfall: Arbitrary image-to-3D conversion, occlusion, and collision are costly; constrain viewpoints and assets initially.
prototype.test: Check whether players predict the new route and overwritten area, then retain spatial orientation.

mechanics.name: Folding terrain to connect routes
mechanics.summary: Fold distant terrain together to build a route.
mechanics.rules: Fold or unfold a paper world to connect separated paths. Folding hides areas and changes links, requiring coordinated character positions and mechanism states before proceeding.
decisions: Will a fold connect the goal but hide an essential entrance?
Where must the character stand before the next fold?

parameters.name: Folding freedom
parameters.effect: Preset folds are readable; more options increase spatial search.

parameters.name: Two-sided information
parameters.effect: Viewing the reverse reduces memory demands; hiding it requires prediction.

cases.implementation: Fold the paper world to rearrange paths and guide the protagonist through environmental puzzles.
Manipulate pop-up-book folds to change structures and paths for the traveler.

mechanics.contrast: Paper Trail emphasizes overlapping terrain; Tengami emphasizes layered pop-up mechanisms.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: the map doubles as a folding bag; closing a road frees storage but cuts access.

walkthrough.setup: The character is on the left and the exit on the right, with a gap between their paths.
walkthrough.action: Fold a permitted corner so the path edges connect.
walkthrough.result: The route connects, but the folded paper covers an earlier entrance.
walkthrough.next: Move to a useful position, then decide whether to unfold or make another fold.

prototype.firstStep: Build two foldable regions using discrete grid connections rather than free-form paper physics.
prototype.pitfall: Keep character layers and walkable edges consistent before arbitrary angles or many overlapping folds.
prototype.test: See whether players position the character before folding and predict which route gets covered.

mechanics.name: Decoding language from context
mechanics.summary: Infer meaning from behavior, pictures and repeated symbols.
mechanics.rules: Compare unknown writing with scenes, behavior and recurring phrases to propose meanings. New contexts support or overturn guesses; translations make directions and history usable for further investigation.
decisions: Is a symbol a name, action or category, and which explains more?
Proceed with an uncertain translation or seek another clue?

parameters.name: Validation timing
parameters.effect: Immediate confirmation shows progress; delay preserves archaeological uncertainty.

parameters.name: Suggested meanings
parameters.effect: Suggestions reduce difficulty; free entry emphasizes inference.

cases.implementation: Observe peoples and their writing, record guesses and build understanding through context.
Study inscriptions, select translation hypotheses and test them against later discoveries.

mechanics.contrast: Chants centers living communication; Heaven’s Vault embeds translation in uncertain historical reconstruction.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: trade using pictures first, then learn local language to detect hidden contract terms.

walkthrough.setup: An unknown symbol appears beside a well and again in a conversation about handing over water.
walkthrough.action: Tentatively record it as “water” and use that guess on the next sign.
walkthrough.result: The new context fits, strengthening the guess; a contradiction would require revision.
walkthrough.next: Find repeated words and use the growing translation to choose routes or respond to characters.

prototype.firstStep: Design six symbols, three corroborating scenes, and an editable personal dictionary.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid a huge language first; each word needs enough context for inference rather than pair memorization.
prototype.test: Present a new sentence using learned words and see whether players interpret it and act accordingly.

mechanics.name: Reconstructing events from evidence
mechanics.summary: Connect visible facts into a testable account.
mechanics.rules: Inspect revisitable scenes for people, objects, dialogue and timing, then assign identities, actions or causes. Validation tests the account against evidence; contradictions prompt another visit.
decisions: Anchor reliable identities first or propose a complete story?
Are clothing and accents only tendencies, and is there corroboration?

parameters.name: Validation granularity
parameters.effect: Per-field feedback reduces stalls; grouped checks discourage brute force.

parameters.name: Revisit cost
parameters.effect: Quick revisits encourage cross-checking; costly ones become memory tests.

cases.implementation: Infer crew identities and fates from death scenes and audio, recording them for grouped confirmation.

cases.game: The Case of the Golden Idol
cases.implementation: Inspect scenes for words and clues, then fill an explanation to reconstruct actions and causes.

mechanics.contrast: Obra Dinn emphasizes identities across scenes; Golden Idol turns words into explicit event reconstructions.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: run a detective agency with limited investigative funds and alternative evidence paths to the same conclusion.

walkthrough.setup: A scene contains a broken cup, two testimonies, and a receipt with a conflicting time.
walkthrough.action: Compare the receipt time to rule out one stated sequence of events.
walkthrough.result: One hypothesis conflicts with the evidence while another fits all three clues.
walkthrough.next: Record the supported relationship and revisit the scene for the missing final clue.

prototype.firstStep: Build one static scene, three people, six clues, and a fillable conclusion.
prototype.pitfall: Verify that evidence supports a unique answer before more people and text multiply consistency work.
prototype.test: Ask for evidence behind each conclusion; add clues wherever success comes from trying every option.

mechanics.name: Gift preferences and allocation
mechanics.summary: Allocate scarce gifts to characters for affection or practical rewards.
mechanics.rules: Choose a recipient and an item. Preferences, gift limits or story gates determine the benefit; dialogue, relationship records and return gifts inform the next allocation.
decisions: Give a rare gift to a favorite character or someone offering immediate utility?
Test an unknown preference or repeat a safe choice?

parameters.name: Preference spread
parameters.effect: Larger differences reward remembering individual traits.

parameters.name: Gift allowance
parameters.effect: Lower limits make allocation meaningful but add waiting.

cases.implementation: Villagers have loved and hated gifts, normally limited to two per week; birthdays amplify their effects.
Most giftable characters return a Keepsake for their first Nectar; a shared gift resource shifts the decision toward which reward to unlock first.

mechanics.contrast: Stardew emphasizes matching items to people; Hades emphasizes allocating one resource across people.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: gathering materials can become gear or gifts that unlock a trainer’s moves; relationship investment sacrifices equipment progress.

walkthrough.setup: You have one rare fruit and two relationships to maintain, with different preferences.
walkthrough.action: Give the fruit to the person known to like it and reserve a common gift for the other.
walkthrough.result: Their response confirms the preference and raises the relationship, consuming the rare gift.
walkthrough.next: Update your preference notes and allocate the next set of gifts.

prototype.firstStep: Build three characters, six gifts, and recorded liked, neutral, and disliked reactions.
prototype.pitfall: Defer extensive dialogue; make preferences observable and memorable instead of pure trial-and-error lookup.
prototype.test: With too few gifts, see whether players allocate by preference and goals rather than routine equal distribution.

mechanics.name: Daily contact rhythm
mechanics.summary: Limited daily conversation rewards turn checking on friends into a routing decision.
mechanics.rules: Find a character and talk. Repeating the same interaction usually cannot farm its daily benefit; dialogue and affinity provide feedback while travel consumes time.
decisions: Detour for one person or visit several nearby friends?
Keep time for income or maintain relationships?

parameters.name: Daily reward limit
parameters.effect: A once-daily limit prevents grinding but needs varied dialogue.

parameters.name: Character accessibility
parameters.effect: Dispersed schedules add routing; gathering places reduce friction.

cases.implementation: Daily conversation raises friendship; some relationships decay on days without contact, with exceptions at relationship milestones.
The first daily chat improves a relationship; repeating it gives no equivalent gain, while gifts and other interactions provide separate options.

mechanics.contrast: Stardew adds maintenance and decay exceptions; Portia places chat among several low-cost daily social actions.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a delivery route can include visits to regular customers; affinity requires an actual conversation rather than merely passing a doorway.

walkthrough.setup: One free period remains today; one friend is on your route and another is at a distant dock.
walkthrough.action: Visit the distant friend and skip another gathering trip today.
walkthrough.result: You get a conversation and new dialogue at the cost of production time.
walkthrough.next: Tomorrow, plan visits around the characters’ schedules again.
