prototype.firstStep: Use three characters with fixed schedules, three daily periods, and one meaningful daily interaction per person.
prototype.pitfall: Repeating identical lines turns relationships into check-ins; add visible schedule or dialogue variation.
prototype.test: See whether players adjust routes for relationships instead of gaining progress through repeated clicking.

mechanics.name: Relationship-gated scenes
mechanics.summary: Unlock character scenes through sustained interaction, turning progress into visible change.
mechanics.rules: Invest interaction time to build a bond; scenes may also require a date, location or presence condition. The event reveals character information or rewards and establishes the next milestone.
decisions: Finish one character’s story or sample several?
Seek the event after reaching its threshold or encounter it naturally?

parameters.name: Milestone spacing
parameters.effect: Longer gaps require stronger scene payoffs.

parameters.name: Trigger transparency
parameters.effect: Hidden requirements encourage discovery but can stall invested players.

cases.implementation: Heart events commonly require friendship thresholds plus location or time conditions; raising affinity does not immediately play every scene.
Player-driven Social Links advance through time together and scenes; characters can have date, social-stat or other Social Link prerequisites.

mechanics.contrast: Stardew embeds scenes in everyday spaces; P4G makes bond progression compete for calendar slots.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a companion scene reveals a new route rather than a separate reward room, giving an old map a new use.

walkthrough.setup: A character reaches a relationship threshold and is expected at the station in the evening.
walkthrough.action: Move other activities earlier and visit the station that evening.
walkthrough.result: A new scene reveals something about the character and opens the next relationship goal.
walkthrough.next: Use that understanding to choose the next interaction.

prototype.firstStep: Build one character, two relationship stages, and one clear time-and-place trigger.
prototype.pitfall: Hidden trigger conditions can look like stalled progress; provide understandable hints.
prototype.test: After reaching the threshold, can players find the scene unaided and recall what it revealed?

mechanics.name: Companion approval
mechanics.summary: Companions judge choices differently, creating trade-offs inside the party.
mechanics.rules: Make decisions in quests and dialogue. Relevant companions approve or disapprove according to their own values, changing future relationships rather than a universal morality score.
decisions: Stay in character or accommodate a favorite companion?
Which companions make this mission socially risky?

parameters.name: Feedback visibility
parameters.effect: Immediate feedback teaches preferences but encourages approval farming.

parameters.name: Departure threshold
parameters.effect: Strict departure rules make conflict matter but penalize experimentation.

cases.implementation: Companions maintain individual approval ratings; many dialogue choices and actions trigger character-specific reactions.
Quest decisions and dialogue affect companion approval, while gifts offer another route to influence relationships and associated interactions.

mechanics.contrast: Both encode personal values; Origins also offers gifts as another relationship-repair channel.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: retreat saves the party but disappoints an honor-driven companion, occasionally putting tactical and personal goals in conflict.

walkthrough.setup: One companion values promises, another payment; an employer offers more money to change the target.
walkthrough.action: Keep the original promise and explain your reasoning.
walkthrough.result: One companion approves and the other complains, changing their relationships differently.
walkthrough.next: Before continuing, choose companions and consider discussing the disagreement.

prototype.firstStep: Build two companions with conflicting values, three difficult choices, and separate response records.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid obvious good-versus-evil choices; give both positions understandable reasons.
prototype.test: Ask players to predict both responses and see whether they understand the values yet choose independently.

mechanics.name: Dialogue persuasion checks
mechanics.summary: Make persuasion an action with preparation, failure and branching consequences.
mechanics.rules: Choose persuasion, intimidation or another argument. Skills, clues and random outcomes govern success; failure creates a new situation or forces an alternative approach.
decisions: Attempt persuasion now or return with evidence?
Choose the best odds or the line that fits your character?

parameters.name: Retry rules
parameters.effect: Retries reward preparation; one-shot checks heighten commitment.

parameters.name: Failure content
parameters.effect: Alternative failure paths encourage attempts more than simple locks.

cases.implementation: Persuasion is Charisma-based; many dialogue options require ability checks whose odds depend on skills and available bonuses.
Active checks include white and red checks; white checks can reopen under conditions, while red checks generally offer a single attempt.

mechanics.contrast: BG3 emphasizes builds and bonuses; Disco’s retry categories reshape the decision to attempt a check now.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: scene observation produces clues used both in a logic puzzle and in persuasion, reducing reliance on grinding a speech statistic.

walkthrough.setup: A guard refuses entry; persuade him now or first find a letter proving your identity.
walkthrough.action: Get the letter, then choose an argument supported by it.
walkthrough.result: Preparation changes the check; success grants entry, while failure requires another route.
walkthrough.next: Proceed on success or seek further evidence and alternatives.

prototype.firstStep: Build one conversation, one collectible clue, and an alternative route after failure.
prototype.pitfall: Show which preparation helps; opaque dice alone make failure difficult to understand.
prototype.test: See whether players seek evidence to improve their chances and continue after failure.

mechanics.name: Shared-activity itineraries
mechanics.summary: Plan a sequence of shared activities within a limited budget.
mechanics.rules: Invite an eligible character and choose places and activities. Preferences, time and activity budgets constrain the itinerary; reactions and relationship outcomes reveal compatibility.
decisions: Choose a known favorite or try something new?
Concentrate the budget or plan several small experiences?

parameters.name: Activity budget
parameters.effect: Tight budgets create trade-offs; generous ones favor wandering.

parameters.name: Preference clues
parameters.effect: Clear clues reward observation; opaque preferences encourage lookup tables.

cases.implementation: Playdates and dates include dining, conversation and minigames; activities consume action points and affect the outing’s mood.
Invite eligible villagers to a movie and choose a snack for them; characters have different movie and snack preferences.

mechanics.contrast: Portia emphasizes allocating action points across activities; Stardew’s cinema focuses on matching movies and snacks to individual preferences.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: plan a picnic route and cook with ingredients gathered along the way; both preparation and routing shape the outing.

walkthrough.setup: Two date periods remain; your partner likes quiet, and the budget buys two ordinary activities or one costly one.
walkthrough.action: Start with a park walk, then use the response to decide whether to visit a busy restaurant.
walkthrough.result: The response reveals preferences while consuming time and budget.
walkthrough.next: Adjust the remaining itinerary and remember useful choices for the next outing.

prototype.firstStep: Build one character, four activities, limited time and budget, and clear feedback after each activity.
prototype.pitfall: Defer bespoke minigames for every venue; test itinerary order and preference information first.
prototype.test: After the first response, see whether players revise the plan and explain why.

mechanics.name: Faction reputation
mechanics.summary: Track separate faction opinions so one action can have conflicting consequences.
mechanics.rules: Complete tasks, help or harm groups, each tracking a separate attitude. Titles, hostility, dialogue and abilities signal changes and influence future allegiance.
decisions: Will an immediate reward close another faction’s opportunities?
Does mixed fear and respect fit better than simple approval?

parameters.name: Reputation dimensions
parameters.effect: Two dimensions preserve mixed attitudes; one axis is easier to read.

parameters.name: Cross-faction effects
parameters.effect: Stronger spillovers make allegiance more strategic.

cases.implementation: Factions track reputation separately; positive fame and negative infamy can produce mixed reputations, and hostility may lead to attacks.
Faction reputation uses Favor and Wrath as separate scales; progression can unlock associated abilities.

mechanics.contrast: New Vegas emphasizes social access and hostility; Tyranny also connects relationship directions to ability rewards.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: selling supplies to the army worries the merchants’ guild; reputation changes market access and forces long-term customer choices.

walkthrough.setup: A guild and smugglers both want the shipment; helping one affects the other’s attitude.
walkthrough.action: Deliver to the guild for payment, giving up the smugglers’ route information.
walkthrough.result: Both groups record the action independently, changing later prices or access.
walkthrough.next: For the next task, decide whether to commit further or repair the other relationship.

prototype.firstStep: Create two factions, three consequential tasks, and two later options affected by reputation.
prototype.pitfall: Keep consequences traceable; too many factions and hidden numbers obscure cause and effect.
prototype.test: See whether players consider future access or trade opportunities when choosing the current task.

mechanics.name: Secrets as leverage
mechanics.summary: Turn discovered secrets into resources to expose, exchange or retain.
mechanics.rules: Discover secrets through observation or investigation, then expose them or demand a concession. Targets may comply or refuse; public knowledge can destroy exclusive leverage.
decisions: Cash in now or retain leverage for later?
Will exposing a target also remove your bargaining advantage?

parameters.name: Secret lifetime
parameters.effect: Expiring secrets demand action; permanent ones encourage hoarding.

parameters.name: Refusal consequences
parameters.effect: Automatic exposure makes threats credible but reduces flexibility.

cases.implementation: Discovered secrets can be used for blackmail to obtain hooks that pressure character interactions; the secret’s nature affects the leverage.
The landlord gathers incriminating information by spying on tenants, then may report, blackmail for money or conceal it.

mechanics.contrast: CK3 turns secrets into political leverage; Beholder ties the trade-off closely to household expenses and tenants’ lives.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: an information shop sells anonymous summaries or named evidence; summaries pay less but preserve future investigation opportunities.

walkthrough.setup: You discover a manager concealed an invoice and need access to his warehouse.
walkthrough.action: Privately offer silence in return for one warehouse visit.
walkthrough.result: The manager may accept or refuse; public disclosure removes the exclusive leverage.
walkthrough.next: Use the response to decide whether to retain, spend, or expose the secret.

prototype.firstStep: Build one discoverable secret, a target with a need, and retain, trade, and expose actions.
prototype.pitfall: Track who knows and whether disclosure occurred; inconsistent states undermine negotiation.
prototype.test: See whether players save leverage for later and understand the irreversible cost of disclosure.

mechanics.name: Dynastic marriage
mechanics.summary: Connect political resources through family ties, balancing alliances and succession.
mechanics.rules: Compare eligible characters and acceptance conditions, then arrange a marriage. Character movement, family ties or alliances change, with consequences beyond the current generation.
decisions: Gain a powerful ally or retain a valuable character?
Does immediate military value justify future family changes?

parameters.name: Character transfer
parameters.effect: Post-marriage residence determines whether the deal costs talent.

parameters.name: Tie persistence
parameters.effect: Ties that lapse when people die require ongoing renewal.

cases.implementation: Marriage or betrothal between sufficiently close relatives of two rulers can establish an alliance; eligibility depends on their family connections.
Diplomatic marriages can send or receive family characters, making character transfer and diplomatic relations part of the bargain.

mechanics.contrast: CK3 embeds marriage in generational succession; Three Kingdoms makes it an explicit tool of character movement and diplomacy.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: allied artisan families share apprenticeship slots, making each alliance a decision about who inherits specialized skills.

walkthrough.setup: Your family has a strong heir; two marriages offer either military allies or better family continuity.
walkthrough.action: Compare residence and descendants’ affiliation, then choose the arrangement fitting your long-term plan.
walkthrough.result: The family network changes, trading immediate alliances against future continuity.
walkthrough.next: As the next generation grows, arrange relationships around the changed family structure.

prototype.firstStep: Use character cards for two families, four people, and explicit post-marriage affiliation rules.
prototype.pitfall: Inheritance, relationship restrictions, and multiple generations interact; limit generations and allowed relationships initially.
prototype.test: Before confirmation, ask who leaves and who inherits to check that outcomes are predictable.

mechanics.name: Relationship commitment
mechanics.summary: Make confession, dating and separation explicit actions beyond affinity growth.
mechanics.rules: Build affinity, then initiate a specific relationship transition. Eligibility need not guarantee acceptance; a clear response changes available interactions and makes commitment deliberate.
decisions: Maintain a familiar bond or risk rejection to progress?
When is a commitment worth its scarce item cost?

parameters.name: Acceptance certainty
parameters.effect: Clear thresholds reduce frustration; probabilistic acceptance adds uncertainty.

parameters.name: Exclusivity
parameters.effect: Exclusivity adds weight but limits exploring multiple stories.

cases.implementation: A bouquet initiates dating after the affinity threshold; marriage requires further conditions and a Mermaid’s Pendant.
A Heart Knot is used to confess and may be rejected; dating unlocks relationship interactions, and a separate item can end the relationship.

mechanics.contrast: Stardew’s key items act as milestone switches; Portia retains uncertainty in confession acceptance.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a companion formally joins an expedition after preparing a commemorative dinner together, turning a relationship transition into shared action.

walkthrough.setup: You know the character well, but a formal commitment requires a special item.
walkthrough.action: Prepare the item and propose the new relationship at an appropriate moment.
walkthrough.result: An explicit acceptance or rejection follows; success opens new interactions.
walkthrough.next: Continue under the new relationship status and decide how much time to invest next.

prototype.firstStep: Build two relationship statuses, one proposal action, one prerequisite, and clear acceptance or refusal.
prototype.pitfall: Ensure status changes available interactions; a renamed meter alone conveys little commitment.
prototype.test: Check whether players understand the current status and what the proposal would change.

mechanics.name: Price discovery
mechanics.summary: Infer acceptable prices from customer reactions instead of a fixed answer sheet.
mechanics.rules: Set an asking price and watch acceptance and reactions. Higher prices improve individual margins but may lose sales; use observations to update the next quote.
decisions: Secure a low-price sale or risk losing it to learn the ceiling?
Does one high-price sale generalize to other customers?

parameters.name: Feedback precision
parameters.effect: Detailed reactions narrow the price range; vague feedback preserves uncertainty.

parameters.name: Customer variation
parameters.effect: Different budgets prevent a single solved price but increase complexity.

cases.implementation: Set shelf prices and infer value from browsing reactions that indicate bargains, acceptable prices or overpricing.
Quote prices to customers and observe acceptance; willingness to pay and budgets mean base item value alone does not determine a sale.

mechanics.contrast: Moonlighter embeds testing in shelf browsing; Recettear embeds it in individual transactions.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: rare ore lacks a universal price; miners test small sales to workshops and gradually map demand across industries.

walkthrough.setup: You do not know the ore’s price ceiling; at 20, the first customer buys immediately.
walkthrough.action: Raise the next piece to 30 and observe the customer.
walkthrough.result: The customer hesitates and leaves: no sale, but a narrower likely price range.
walkthrough.next: Use stock and cash needs to choose an intermediate price or return to the lower price.

prototype.firstStep: Build one product, three customer budgets, and clear expensive, acceptable, and bargain reactions.
prototype.pitfall: An exact answer removes discovery, while wholly random reactions prevent learning.
prototype.test: See whether players adjust prices from previous reactions instead of changing them arbitrarily.

mechanics.name: Haggling
mechanics.summary: Improve a deal before closing through reactions, timing or concessions.
mechanics.rules: Adjust terms around a specific item. The player must stop between gaining more value and losing the deal; immediate feedback indicates negotiation progress.
decisions: Push for more when the deal is already profitable?
Close safely or invest more effort for a better result?

parameters.name: Negotiation tolerance
parameters.effect: Low tolerance raises tension; high tolerance supports experimentation.

parameters.name: Execution demand
parameters.effect: Timing emphasizes dexterity; turn-based offers emphasize reading and valuation.

cases.implementation: The haggling minigame uses clicks as a moving indicator crosses valid zones to change the deal; the player can choose when to finish.
Negotiate with varied customers through offers and counteroffers while judging item value and acceptance.

mechanics.contrast: Potion Craft turns negotiation into execution; Dealer’s Life 2 emphasizes appraisal and reading customers.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a restaurant bargains for discounts by promising future orders, tying today’s cheap purchase to later menus.

walkthrough.setup: The seller asks 100 for an item you value at 120, but you need cash for other purchases.
walkthrough.action: Offer 80, then raise it to 90 after a negative response.
walkthrough.result: The seller is willing to close; pressing further might save money or lose the deal.
walkthrough.next: Accept or leave, then carry the remaining budget into the next transaction.

prototype.firstStep: Build a short negotiation with a seller’s minimum price, limited patience, and three offer actions.
prototype.pitfall: Let feedback indicate proximity to a limit instead of hiding outcomes behind opaque randomness.
prototype.test: See whether players voluntarily close after a discount and explain the risk of continuing.

mechanics.name: Supply-driven market prices
mechanics.summary: Let trading change subsequent prices, making the market responsive to players.
mechanics.rules: Observe prices, then buy or sell. Trading and production alter supply and demand; repeated selling can reduce the seller’s own margins, feeding information into the next decision.
decisions: Lock in a return now or wait for demand?
Will expanding production erase its attractive price?

parameters.name: Price elasticity
parameters.effect: Large changes from small trades emphasize timing and manipulation.

parameters.name: Market scope
parameters.effect: Shared markets strengthen competition; regional markets reward transport.

cases.implementation: Resource prices react to player trades, encouraging cheap input purchases or production of scarce goods.
City commodity prices change with supply and demand, so selling large quantities alters the profitability of further sales.

mechanics.contrast: Offworld’s shared real-time market makes rivals direct influences; Patrician ties pricing to cities and voyages.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: excessive mining depresses a town’s local ore price, forcing changes to gathering routes and manufacturing uses.

walkthrough.setup: The market lacks wood and pays 10 per unit; you hold a large stock.
walkthrough.action: Sell a small batch and inspect remaining demand and the new price.
walkthrough.result: The added supply lowers the price, reducing the average return of selling everything.
walkthrough.next: Wait between batches, sell another good, or accept the lower price for immediate cash.

prototype.firstStep: Build two goods, visible stocks, a simple supply-demand pricing rule, and periodic demand updates.
prototype.pitfall: Set price bounds and trading spreads to avoid an unlimited buy-sell exploit.
prototype.test: After a large sale, do players understand their price impact and adjust later quantities?

mechanics.name: Regional arbitrage
mechanics.summary: Move goods between places to earn the spread after travel costs.
mechanics.rules: Compare purchase and sale prices across locations, then choose cargo and a route. Capacity, supplies, hazards and demand constrain profit; the net return matters more than the headline spread.
decisions: Does the distant spread cover extra risk and supplies?
Fill the hold with value or reserve emergency capacity?

parameters.name: Travel overhead
parameters.effect: Ongoing supplies eliminate routes that look profitable only before travel.

parameters.name: Regional scarcity
parameters.effect: Greater local differences make discovering markets worthwhile.

cases.implementation: Port shops offer different goods and prices; trade profits must account for fuel, supplies and voyage hazards.
Buy and sell across Hanseatic cities to exploit local supply differences while managing ships and transport.

mechanics.contrast: Sunless Sea binds routes to survival risk; Patrician emphasizes expanding a continuing commercial network.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a mountain clinic pays well for herbs, but the fastest route requires light climbing gear, putting cargo volume against delivery value.

walkthrough.setup: Port A sells salt for 5 and port B buys it for 9; supplies cost 10 per trip.
walkthrough.action: Load ten salt units and choose the safer route.
walkthrough.result: Sell for 90, subtract 50 for stock and 10 for supplies, and earn 30 net.
walkthrough.next: Compare return cargo and demand elsewhere to plan the next net return.

prototype.firstStep: Use three locations, three goods, fixed capacity, and visible travel costs, with menu-based transport.
prototype.pitfall: Validate trade decisions before free sailing, combat, and dynamic economics expand the project.
prototype.test: Add a high-spread, high-cost route and see whether players compare net returns.

mechanics.name: Shop display allocation
mechanics.summary: Make limited display positions a selling decision rather than dumping all stock.
mechanics.rules: Choose goods and display positions, then observe sales during opening hours. Display space and restocking time are limited; stored items do not get equal exposure.
decisions: Display expensive goods for margin or cheaper goods for turnover?
Does protecting rare stock justify using premium display space?

parameters.name: Display capacity
parameters.effect: Few positions sharpen assortment choices; many reduce rotation.

parameters.name: Position differentiation
parameters.effect: Functional differences create layout decisions; identical slots mostly decorate.

cases.implementation: Shelves sell items; showcases target wealthy customers and protect the displayed goods from thieves.
Arrange displayed stock and shop decoration, then handle customer transactions during opening periods.

mechanics.contrast: Moonlighter gives showcases customer and security functions; Recettear integrates display with broader shop management.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: antique displays offer different lighting and protection, so fragile valuables trade entrance visibility for safety.

walkthrough.setup: Two display slots must serve cheap popular goods and an expensive rare item.
walkthrough.action: Display one of each and observe sales speed and remaining stock.
walkthrough.result: The cheap goods sell out while the rare item remains, revealing the cost of occupying a slot.
walkthrough.next: Restock the popular item or give the rare one more time.

prototype.firstStep: Build two shelf slots, four products, and customers with differing preferences; allow restocking during opening hours.
prototype.pitfall: Separate placement effects from pricing effects so sales changes remain explainable.
prototype.test: Allow only one restock and see whether observed sales change the display choice.

mechanics.name: Interpreting customer requests
mechanics.summary: Infer a need from natural language and match it with product properties.
mechanics.rules: Customers may describe symptoms, tastes or uses instead of naming a product. Infer constraints, choose or craft a match, and learn from acceptance, rejection or extra payment.
decisions: Meet the minimum or spend rare inputs on preferences?
When several answers fit, favor cost or character context?

parameters.name: Request ambiguity
parameters.effect: Moderate ambiguity creates inference; missing clues create guesswork.

parameters.name: Valid alternatives
parameters.effect: Several valid answers reward creativity; one emphasizes recognition.

cases.implementation: Customers request effects and sometimes extra constraints; unmet required conditions block purchase, while optional ones increase payment.
Orders may name a drink or describe a flavor; players consult recipes and mix drinks, influencing customer reactions and dialogue.

mechanics.contrast: Potion Craft frames requests as effects and constraints; VA-11 HALL-A also carries the serving result into narrative.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: an adventurer wants to remain unnoticed in snowy mountains; a tailor can satisfy that through different combinations of warmth, color and quiet materials.

walkthrough.setup: A customer asks for a refreshing drink that is not too sweet, without naming one.
walkthrough.action: Identify both conditions and choose an affordable recipe with suitable flavors.
walkthrough.result: The customer accepts and comments on the flavor, showing which requirements were met.
walkthrough.next: The next customer describes another need; use the learned attributes to match it.

prototype.firstStep: Build five products with two clear attributes, six natural-language requests, and explanatory feedback.
prototype.pitfall: Start with a finite set of authored descriptions; unrestricted language makes rule validation difficult.
prototype.test: After rejection, can players identify the missed condition and select a genuinely matching product?

mechanics.name: Timed delivery contracts
mechanics.summary: Assess capacity before accepting an order that binds planning to a deadline.
mechanics.rules: Choose an order with quantity, quality or collection conditions and a deadline. Produce and deliver for payment; overcommitment creates conflicts in materials, equipment or schedules.
decisions: Take a lucrative challenge or a safe small order?
Will buying materials to rush erase the margin?

parameters.name: Deadline slack
parameters.effect: Short deadlines emphasize scheduling; long ones emphasize resource allocation.

parameters.name: Failure cost
parameters.effect: Lost opportunity encourages trying; reputation penalties demand caution.

cases.implementation: Commerce Guild commissions require specified items by a deadline and reward money, workshop reputation and client relationship gains.
Special Orders can require newly collected items as well as delivery, with order-specific deadlines and rewards; stored goods do not always satisfy every objective.

mechanics.contrast: Portia connects contracts to workshop growth; Stardew’s Special Orders redirect activities over a period.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a festival fireworks order requires several production stages; early delivery lets residents decorate sooner, offering visible feedback beyond money.

walkthrough.setup: A contract needs six tools in two days; daily capacity is four and some materials are missing.
walkthrough.action: Check materials and production time, then accept and schedule purchases.
walkthrough.result: Production occupies equipment, while delivery pays out and other jobs wait.
walkthrough.next: Review remaining materials and time before selecting the next contract.

prototype.firstStep: Build two machines, three deadlines, and a visible daily production schedule.
prototype.pitfall: Avoid surprise deadline changes; expose the main constraints before acceptance.
prototype.test: Offer a lucrative but infeasible contract and see whether players reject it.

mechanics.name: Debt and cash-flow pressure
mechanics.summary: Use debt obligations to separate earnings from money actually available to spend.
mechanics.rules: Earn income through business or work, then cover debt and continuing costs. Surplus can improve efficiency, but overinvestment may leave too little cash for the next cycle.
decisions: Upgrade immediately or reserve cash for settlement?
Take safe work or riskier jobs to escape debt sooner?

parameters.name: Repayment cadence
parameters.effect: Fixed deadlines create sprints; ongoing fees create efficiency pressure.

parameters.name: Bankruptcy consequence
parameters.effect: Recoverable failure supports experiments; resets amplify repeated work.

cases.implementation: The item shop must repay an inherited loan, requiring enough money at repayment milestones while sustaining future trading.
Salvaging ships earns money against a large corporate debt; equipment upgrades enable more valuable work.

mechanics.contrast: Recettear applies pressure through repayment milestones; Shipbreaker uses debt to frame long-term labor and progression.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a repair shop can repay equipment loans early or upgrade tools, using order history to judge which better improves cash flow.

walkthrough.setup: A payment of 100 is due in three days; you have 80 and an upgrade costs 50.
walkthrough.action: Reserve cash for repayment and take reliable smaller jobs.
walkthrough.result: Growth is slower, but you meet the deadline without a cash shortage.
walkthrough.next: After payment, estimate the next cash requirement before upgrading.

prototype.firstStep: Build a seven-day calendar, one debt deadline, two jobs, and one productivity investment.
prototype.pitfall: Make income, costs, and due dates visible; hidden charges undermine planning.
prototype.test: Check whether players distinguish total earnings from spendable cash and reserve funds for deadlines.

mechanics.name: Auction bidding limits
mechanics.summary: Maintain a valuation while rivals raise the price.
mechanics.rules: Inspect a lot and current bid, then raise or withdraw. Winning is not automatically profitable: compare cost with resale or strategic value before the auction settles.
decisions: Does denying a rival justify paying above personal value?
Is time spent bidding tempting you to exceed your limit?

parameters.name: Valuation uncertainty
parameters.effect: Incomplete information increases both bargains and overpayment.

parameters.name: Bid increments
parameters.effect: Large increments shorten auctions but reduce fine probing.

cases.implementation: Auctions contest advantages such as claims or patents, requiring bids to be weighed against economic capacity and strategic value.
Players can acquire goods at auctions, with business value depending on appraisal and purchase cost rather than merely winning.

mechanics.contrast: Offworld auctions change competitive leverage; Dealer’s Life 2 emphasizes later commercial returns.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: auction ruin maps whose value depends on each explorer’s skills, giving the same lot different values to different buyers.

walkthrough.setup: You value the item at 120; the bid is 90 and increments are 10.
walkthrough.action: Bid 100; the opponent offers 110, leaving you to consider 120.
walkthrough.result: At 120, winning leaves no expected resale profit.
walkthrough.next: Withdraw and keep funds for an item with more margin.

prototype.firstStep: Create three items with estimated values and two computer bidders with different limits.
prototype.pitfall: Distinguish valuation clues from actual value; omniscient opponents can feel unfair.
prototype.test: See whether players abandon a long bidding contest instead of treating victory as profit.

mechanics.name: Programmed trade routes
mechanics.summary: Turn repetitive trading into routes and cargo rules, managing exceptions instead of every trip.
mechanics.rules: Choose stops, cargo and ships, then configure loading or trading at each stop. Ships repeat the route; shortages, congestion and hazards prompt revisions, so automation still needs oversight.
decisions: Use one long circuit for utilization or several short routes for resilience?
Add a ship or improve loading and stop order?

parameters.name: Rule granularity
parameters.effect: Quantity and price rules add flexibility and setup cost.

parameters.name: Travel predictability
parameters.effect: Stable travel supports precise planning; hazards demand buffers.

cases.implementation: Trade routes assign islands, cargo and ships for repeated loading and unloading; waypoints can adjust the sailing path.
Convoys can trade automatically along configured town sequences, using commodity trading settings that the player revises over time.

mechanics.contrast: Anno often uses routes to sustain production networks; Patrician emphasizes continuing trade between city markets.
mechanics.combination: Design proposal: a town postal service combines mail and freight routes; relationships unlock shortcuts, while overloaded runs miss promised delivery times.

walkthrough.setup: Port A produces wood, port B consumes it, and a ship carries ten units per trip.
walkthrough.action: Set the ship to load ten at A, unload at B, and return.
walkthrough.result: The ship loops automatically, but slow demand at B leaves cargo aboard on the return trip.
walkthrough.next: Inspect inventory changes, then adjust quantities or add a third stop.

prototype.firstStep: Build three ports, one ship, and load, unload, and wait commands using discrete time steps.
prototype.pitfall: Handle shortages, full holds, and rejected cargo before adding fleets and complex routes.
prototype.test: Create a deliberate bottleneck and see whether players diagnose it from stock and trip logs.
